title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 adding two new features soon
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are here, and later this year they’ll get even more powerful with two new features: Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are here, and later this year they’ll get even more powerful with two new features: Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Here are the details.

#1: Siri Recap

Siri AI is a major tentpole of watchOS 27, and later this year there’s a powerful Siri addition coming to Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. It’s called Siri Recap.

Here’s what it does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

Siri Recap seems like the kind of feature that no one was necessarily asking for, but it could add valuable utility if the privacy protections are done right. You can read the finer details around privacy in Apple’s white paper here.

#2: Live Rewind

Live Rewind is another ‘Audio Intelligence’ feature coming to the new Apple Watch models later this year. It provides a more direct way to revisit something that was just said.

Here’s how it works per Apple:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Like Siri Recap, Apple has in-depth details on Live Rewind’s privacy protections outlined here. For me personally, the utility of Live Rewind seems less obvious beyond accessibility needs. But I’m interested to see how it works in its finished form.

Apple is expected to introduce both new Apple Watch features in watchOS 27.3, which should launch in beta very soon.

title: 1Password will let AI agents use your passwords without seeing them
snippet: As AI agents continue to get more capable, account credentials are becoming more of a hang-up. 1Password is today offering its solution – giving AI agents the ability to use your passwords without actually seeing them, all while leaving you in control. more…
fullText:
As AI agents continue to get more capable, account credentials are becoming more of a hang-up. 1Password is today offering its solution – giving AI agents the ability to use your passwords without actually seeing them, all while leaving you in control.

“1Password for Agents” is a new way to connect your password vault to your AI agents, all while leaving things secure. This works be connecting an AI agent like Meta’s Muse to 1Password and letting the agent ask for permission to sign into a website, at which point 1Password will provide the needed information on your approval. 

The actual sign-in is handled by 1Password, not the agent, with your credentials remaining hidden to the agent. 1Password explains:

1Password for Agents lets AI agents sign in without receiving or seeing the credential. When an agent reaches a sign-in form, it uses a unique digital key to verify its identity to 1Password. The person sees which credential it needs and why, and then chooses whether to approve the request. If approved, 1Password fills it directly into the sign-in form. Once the website accepts the login, 1Password removes the credential so the agent can’t read or reuse it as it continues the task.

The process also leaves the rest of your password vault inaccessible to the agent.

	

While there’s still a level of trust, this solution seems far safer than just handing an AI agent your passwords. Right now this integration is limited to Muse and Grok Bot, but support for more agents is in the works, including OpenAI Dots and Anthropic Claude Duet.

title: Anthropic, Suno Sued for Unlawfully Using Songs by Madonna, Johnny Cash, Joni Mitchell
snippet: Companies are accused of training their AI models using copyrighted music and lyrics.
fullText:
The Man in Black couldn’t have imagined this. AI companies Suno and Anthropic face a combined $338 million in lawsuits for allegedly using songs and lyrics by Madonna, Johnny Cash and Joni Mitchell to train their artificial intelligence systems.

Reservoir Media Management, a music rights company, filed two separate lawsuits on Oct. 21. In one of them, Reservoir accuses Suno of scraping 1,050 copyrighted songs — including Cash’s Ring of Fire, Mitchell’s Both Sides Now and Madonna’s Papa Don’t Preach. Suno is a platform where users can generate an AI song using only a text prompt.

In the other lawsuit, Reservoir accuses Anthropic of using copyrighted lyrics from 853 songs to train its Claude family of AI models. Some of the songs mentioned in that lawsuit include Mitchell’s Big Yellow Taxi, Billy Strayhorn’s Lush Life and Evanescence‘s Bring Me to Life.

			

More from CNET

“We disagree with the allegations and intend to defend this case vigorously,” a representative for Anthropic told Billboard.

Representatives for Suno and Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Reservoir seeks $186.4 million in damages from Suno and $151.4 million from Anthropic. Both lawsuits accuse the companies of copyright infringement, circumventing restrictions such as logins and paywalls and stripping song credits of title, writer and publisher data.

Anthropic was also sued last week for violating copyright for reportedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train Claude. The company has been sued more than a dozen times for copyright infringement — most notably in a $1.5 billion settlement over allegations that it trained its AI on millions of pirated books. Suno also faces several copyright infringement lawsuits, including a second from Sony Music and Universal Music Group.

Reservoir founder and CEO Golnar Khosrowshahi told Music Business Worldwide that the AI music industry can’t be allowed to exploit songwriters’ work.

“When we believe their work has been exploited without authorization, we will hold AI platforms legally accountable to ensure those rights are upheld,” Khosrowshahi said. “We will continue to advocate for a framework that supports technological progress while protecting the creative work at the heart of our industry.”

Lawsuits are piling up

Copyright infringement — of news articles, music, books and art  — has become a major issue, with several AI companies accused of ingesting mountains of data to train AI models such as Claude, OpenAI’s GPT, Google’s Gemini and Elon Musk’s Grok. There’s even a website, the AI Lawsuit Tracker, that counts 145 copyright infringement lawsuits — more than half of the overall cases against AI companies.

AI models are trained when their companies feed a vast amount of data — text, images, music, videos and software code — into their AI systems. With all that data, as well as synthetic data generated by computers, AI models can learn to generate words, images and video that may appear human-created.

In the lawsuit filed last week, Reservoir said Suno has already admitted to copying “essentially all music files of reasonable quality that are accessible on the open internet,” a statement Suno made in court during a 2024 suit brought by Universal Music Group, Sony Music Entertainment, and Warner Music Group.

This summer, a hacker cracked into Suno’s code and revealed that the company allegedly scraped music and lyrics from platforms like YouTube Music, Deezer, Genius and stock music libraries. The hack showed more than 2 million clips in a folder called “youtube_music,” as well as thousands of hours of music from the lyrics database Genius HQ, the music streaming service Deezer, and the stock music site Pond5.

In the lawsuit, Reservoir says that Suno is not truly a platform for people to create music and “was instead always meant to replace the artists whose works were being unlawfully copied by directly reaching those artists’ listeners with AI-generated substitutes which copy the originals.”

Anthropic allegedly stripped credits

Reservoir also accused Anthropic of using a text-extraction tool called Newspaper, which removes copyright notices from written material. Reservoir said Claude is partly trained on lyrics collected from Common Crawl, a web crawler that, during its crawls, inadvertently picks up lyrics from licensed sites such as Musixmatch and LyricFind.

title: Samsung can’t decide between a larger Galaxy Z Fold 9 or one with worse specs, and neither can I
snippet: Following a smash hit in the smaller and wider Galaxy Z Fold 8, Samsung is obviously weighing its options behind the scenes when it comes to sequels. According to one leaker, the company is currently deciding between adding another Galaxy Z Fold 9 with a larger display, or one with lesser specs, and I can’t decide which one I want to see either. more…
fullText:
Following a smash hit in the smaller and wider Galaxy Z Fold 8, Samsung is obviously weighing its options behind the scenes when it comes to sequels. According to one leaker, the company is currently deciding between adding another Galaxy Z Fold 9 with a larger display, or one with lesser specs, and I can’t decide which one I want to see either.

Leaker Lanzuk on Naver says that Samsung is adding more options to the Galaxy Z Fold 9 lineup next year after the Galaxy Z Fold 8 garnered “much better response than expected” (translated). It’s all-but-official that Samsung is expanding the lineup – we’ve heard this repeatedly at this point – but exactly what joins the lineup remains unclear.

This latest rumor suggests two possibilities. 

The first is a larger version of the Galaxy Z Fold 8, a “Galaxy Z Fold 9 Plus,” the leaker suggests. This wouldn’t be an Ultra device, but rather would share the same wide form factor as the standard Fold 9, just with a larger pair of displays.

	

The other option is a “Galaxy Z Fold 9 FE” which would downgrade the specs to achieve a lower price point. Samsung tried this with the Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE to essentially no success, but the company’s cuts on that device were far from compelling on a form factor that was already in decline.

Samsung is said to be testing both form factors and “a decision will be made soon,” but only one of the two would move to production and a full release. 

9to5Google’s Take

Personally, I’m split here. I’ve been using the Galaxy Z Fold 8 as my daily smartphone since its launch, and the size is certainly one of its most attractive features. On the one hand, I’d love to have a larger version for better media consumption and multitasking, but I also think Samsung would run into diminishing returns with a larger size. The wider form factor wouldn’t scale nicely to a larger size too, I think.

Meanwhile, a more affordable version seems like a clear win. This form factor has so clearly resonated with customers, and having an option that makes strategic cuts to hit a price of say, $1,400, would be a home run. However, given Samsung’s existing struggles with profitability amid RAMageddon and ever-rising prices, that also feels unrealistic.

I’m very torn on which would be the better option. Which one would you prefer?

title: iOS 27.2 now available: Here’s everything new for iPhone
snippet: iOS 27.2 is now available to everyone after six weeks of beta testing. The update was released on Monday, bringing multiple new iPhone features. Here’s everything you need to know. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 is now available to everyone after six weeks of beta testing. The update was released on Monday, bringing multiple new iPhone features. Here’s everything you need to know. 

Why iOS 27.2 and not iOS 27.1?

Apple released iOS 27 on September 14, bringing a ton of new iPhone features, including Siri AI. iOS 27.2 entered beta testing just two days later on September 16.

What happened to iOS 27.1? iOS 27.1 was exclusive to the iPhone Duo, which was released last week and shipped with iOS 27.1. With iOS 27.2, the software update paths have converged and all iPhones will be on the same page going forward.

iOS 27.2 new features

New Siri AI features

Siri AI was the big new feature in iOS 27, and iOS 27.2 expands the feature in multiple ways. First, Siri AI is now available in these five languages: 

French

Japanese

Korean

Portuguese

Spanish

Second, iOS 27.2 also adds several new features to Siri AI. From Apple’s release notes: 

Siri AI can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week

Siri AI can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List

Excluded Apps lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one setting

Granular text selection lets you select and copy just the part of a Siri response you need

Dual Capture mode for Group FaceTime

In iOS 27, Apple added a new Dual Capture feature for FaceTime that lets you have your front and rear cameras active at the same time. The person on the other end of the call will see you as well as whatever you’re looking at. iOS 27.2 expands this feature to Group FaceTime calls for the first time.

Dual Capture requires an iPhone 17 or later, and everyone on the call needs to be running iOS 27.

Also in iOS 27.2, FaceTime now supports adding a third party sign language interpreter or live captioner to a call. 

Apple Podcasts

In Apple Podcasts, the “Up Next” queue has been refreshed with two new dedicated rows: New Episodes and Continue Playing. The New Episodes list shows the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing shows in-progress episodes, organized by most recently played. 

Additionally, episode lists also now use color-matched backgrounds based on the podcast art.

TV app changes 

There are two changes to the TV app included in iOS 27.2. First, the update adds Multiview support to iPhone for the first time. This lets you watch up to four live sports streams simultaneously, including MLS, F1, and MLB. 

The Apple TV app in iOS 27.2 adds support for profiles for the first time. This feature has been available on tvOS for several years, but this is the first time it has come to iPhone.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

Suggestions in Messages

Suggestions in Messages, which feature Apple tested in iOS 27 but removed before the update was released, have returned in iOS 27.2. This feature adds quick shortcut buttons to Messages, making it easy to add things to apps like Calendar and Reminders with a single tap. 

Apple Music rebrand 

iOS 27.2 introduces a new brand identity for Apple Music. This includes a new app icon, seen above. There are also various interface tweaks throughout the Music app. For example, the red interface accents are now blue. 

This is part of a larger Apple Music rebrand that the company debuted last week. 

iPhone Duo features

iOS 27.2 adds two new features for iPhone Duo: 

Support for Apple Pencil (USB-C)

Edge Light: add a ring light around the edge of your display to illuminate your face during calls. 

More tidbits

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground. 

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments. They can also display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos. 

The Friends tab in the Games app provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages. 

There are small interface tweaks to the Clock app, including smaller a.m. and p.m. labels. 

iOS 27’s Call Context feature, which surfaces information right on your screen when calling a business, has been expanded to include anniversaries.

Security fixes

iOS 27.2 also includes a ton of security fixes, as Apple outlines on its website. There are security fixes in apps like Mail and Safari, as well as Apple Intelligence, the Neural Engine, and more. 

Wrap up

Report counters soft demand rumors

In a report released today, Counterpoint Research says iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max sales in the US fell 4% during their first three weeks of availability compared to the first three weeks of iPhone 17 Pro series sales last year.

The report noted that Japan saw a whopping 27% drop in sales, with demand weakening “as exchange rates amplified the price increases.”

China, on the other hand, saw a 29% increase in sales, while other markets collectively recorded a more modest 3.1% increase.

The report doesn’t break down what that means in units, or millions of units, but it does offer some context on what drove these regional differences.

Here’s Counterpoint:

A regional breakdown shows that the global 3.1% growth was concentrated in specific markets. China posted the strongest growth, with sales rising 29% YoY. This was driven by better early supply compared with last year and by price increases on competing flagship models from Chinese Android OEMs. Excluding China’s contribution, the global sales growth rate would have been far weaker. The US and Japan experienced a YoY decline, affected by higher prices compared with their predecessors. In the US, consumers largely do not perceive meaningful improvements over the previous models in either features or design, while in Japan, demand has contracted as exchange rates amplified the price increases.

Today’s report also includes another interesting tidbit: According to Counterpoint, the iPhone 18 Pro Max accounted for a slightly smaller share of Pro-series sales compared to last year’s iPhone 17 Pro series, which the firm attributed to higher prices and stronger demand for the smaller Pro model in emerging markets:

The iPhone 18 Pro Max accounted for 56% of sales within the iPhone 18 Pro series, a slight decrease from 57% last year. This can be attributed to the higher prices compared with last year, as well as the fact that the sales growth in emerging markets such as India and Southeast Asia skewed more toward the Pro models.

As to how, or whether, the iPhone Duo had any effect on these shifting numbers, the report didn’t address that directly, since the device launched after the three-week period covered by the data. However, Counterpoint Associate Director Sujeong Lim raised the possibility that it could affect Pro Max sales going forward:

“Whether China’s outperformance reflects durable demand or front-loaded buying will become clearer in the coming weeks. The recovery of US and Japanese volumes, and whether the iPhone Duo launching in Week 43 will generate incremental demand rather than cannibalising Pro Max, are the two most consequential near-term variables.”

title: Galaxy Watch user reports burn overnight; this isn’t the first time
snippet: One Galaxy Watch 5 Pro user reported burns and blisters on their skin after sleeping with their watch under what can only be considered normal operation. more…
fullText:
One Galaxy Watch 5 Pro user reported burns and blisters on their skin after sleeping with their watch under what can only be considered normal operation.

A post on Reddit shows blisters and red marks on a Galaxy Watch 5 Pro user’s arm (via Android Authority). Red marks and irritation aren’t all that uncommon for users, but they’re generally categorized as contact dermatitis. The blisters are new, though.

They claim the watch was on their wrist from the moment they went to bed after charging it to full, but that the battery had drained by the time they woke up. A dead battery might indicate the Galaxy Watch 5 Pro was active enough to burn through the 590mAh cell throughout the night. The user also notes their watch refused to power on after the incident.

When a lithium-ion battery depletes itself in a matter of hours, it puts off some considerable heat. So a burn this bad sits nowhere outside the realm of possibilities.

	

This isn’t the first time we’ve seen reports like this. Samsung’s Galaxy Watch lineup is, for the most part, consistently safe. We’ve tested them for years and have never had overheating issues that leave visible markings on skin. Still, reported battery issues are not all that uncommon. It’s even affected the Galaxy Ring.

Users have reported suspected overheating with their Galaxy Watch Ultra, Watch Ultra 2, Galaxy Watch 8, and a few other models in the past, but none of them seem to have affected the user as much as the most recent Watch 5 Pro report. An argument could be made for contact dermatitis on some older posts, but this report holds more water – or fluid.

What’s your experience with skin irritation from Samsung’s watches? Tell your story in the comments.

title: Google will target ads based on Gmail, Photos data if Personal Intelligence is enabled
snippet: If you’re an Android user, you’ve probably trusted Google with mountains of your own personal data over the last couple of decades. Now, a new privacy policy update suggests that the company is finally dipping into that data to target personalized ads, and you can’t opt out with disabling Personal Intelligence. more…
fullText:
If you’re an Android user, you’ve probably trusted Google with mountains of your own personal data over the last couple of decades. Now, a new privacy policy update suggests that the company is finally dipping into that data to target personalized ads, and you can’t opt out with disabling Personal Intelligence.

As spotted by Android Authority (via The Verge), Google’s new privacy policy update — which went into effect one week ago on October 16th — adds new language surrounding how the company uses data from Gmail, Drive, and Photos to target ads. Previously, the policy specifically stated that personalized ads were not “based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos,” but following this change, the sentence no longer stops there. Google now continues on with a pretty big caveat: “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”

	

Obviously, that sentence reads about as intentionally vague as possible, so let’s draw a clearer circle around it: this is a change that revolves around Google’s AI initiative, and the choice the company is referring to here is the decision to enable Personal Intelligence across your account. Personal Intelligence first began rolling out in beta at the start of this year, and allows for Gemini to share data between various apps, including Gmail, Photos, Search, Drive, and more.

You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.

In other words, while Google hasn’t explicitly revealed your cloud storage, inbox, or photo collection to advertisers, it has opened the door to allowing advertisers to target ads based on that connected content as it appears in spaces like Search. The company still says advertisers won’t be able to see personally identifying details, including your name and email address, to advertisers without your permission; that language remains unchanged from previous policy versions.

	

Personal Intelligence remains opt-in (for the time being), but if this sort of change freaks you out, you might want to verify your Google account settings are where you want them to be. To do so, head to Data & privacy under your My Account page, selection Personalization settings, then select Manage Personalized Recommendations in Search services. You can also disable Personalized Recommendations entirely by clicking the Turn off button on this page.

title: Next week’s MacBook Pro could be huge upgrade, but with one problem
snippet: Apple has a fully redesigned MacBook Pro launching next week that promises to be a major upgrade, except in one key area. more…
fullText:
Apple has a fully redesigned MacBook Pro launching next week that promises to be a major upgrade, except in one key area.

New MacBook Pro will reportedly have no performance boost, use current M5 Pro and Max chips

Next week on October 28 at its ‘Pro and tell’ event, Apple is expected to unveil a redesigned MacBook Pro with major improvements.

The new model is rumored to feature:

brand new industrial design

significantly lighter and a bit thinner

OLED display

touchscreen

Dynamic Island

no notch

wildcard: possibly a C2 cellular modem

If most or all of these rumors prove true, it’s going to be a big upgrade for the MacBook Pro.

But there’s one crucial area that’s not expected to improve: performance.

Per Mark Gurman, the new MacBook Pro will include the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips that first debuted nearly eight months ago. That means a product that specializes in performance is going to offer zero performance boosts.

It’s an odd move, and reportedly the result of Apple skipping M6 Pro and Max chips altogether in favor of fast-tracking the M7 Pro and Max for 2027.

Considering how expensive the MacBook Pro is already, and the premium this new model is likely to bring, we may be looking at a ~$2,999 starting price for a model that’s no faster than before. 

	

Perhaps Apple will replace the current M5 Pro and M5 Max models entirely at the same price point. I would love that, but it’s probably wishful thinking in our memory-crisis moment. 

Overall, I’m fascinated to see how Apple pitches the new MacBook Pro to prospective upgraders. Will Pro users who passed on M5 Pro and M5 Max chips earlier this year all of a sudden be convinced now? We’ll have to wait and see.

title: Report: Apple gains ground in China as smartphone shipments hit 14-year low in Q3
snippet: Rising memory prices continue to weigh on the global smartphone market, with shipments in China alone falling 10% year over year in Q3. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Rising memory prices continue to weigh on the global smartphone market, with shipments in China alone falling 10% year over year in Q3. Here are the details.

Apple gains ground despite market downturn

A few days ago, IDC reported that smartphone shipments in China fell 15.4% year over year in Q3 2026, with Apple increasing its share of that total to 17.8% despite a 4.3% decline in iPhone shipments.

The report echoed the broader global trend, with IDC estimating that worldwide smartphone shipments fell a record 22% year over year during the quarter, while Apple recorded the smallest decline among the top five manufacturers, at just 4%.

Now, a new report from Counterpoint Research paints a similar picture of China’s smartphone market in Q3, although its estimates differ somewhat from IDC’s.

According to the report, smartphone shipments in China hit a 14-year low during Q3 2026, with a 10% decline year over year.

Apple, on the other hand, accounted for 19.5% of smartphone shipments in China during the period, a 4.8-percentage-point increase year over year. The company was second only to Huawei, which held a 21.3% share, up 5.3 percentage points from a year earlier.

In fact, these were the only two among the top six brands to gain shipment share year over year, with vivo down 2.8 percentage points to 15.2%, OPPO down 1.3 points to 15.1%, Xiaomi down 1.6 points to 13.5%, HONOR down 2.2 points to 12.7%, and other manufacturers collectively down 2 points to 2.8%.

Notably, Apple went from sixth to second place in overall shipments, which Counterpoint attributes in part to the strong launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series:

Apple ranked second with a 19.5% market share in Q3. The iPhone 18 Pro series saw a strong launch in China, with sales in the first three weeks up 23.5% YoY compared with the iPhone 17 Pro series. The delayed launch of the base iPhone 18 may have encouraged some consumers to trade up to the Pro models, supporting their early sales momentum.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint noted that rising smartphone prices are leading consumers to delay upgrades, wait for promotional periods, or turn to refurbished devices, potentially putting further pressure on demand in Q4.

snippet: A Redditor used Claude Code AI to build a Mac temperature monitor app and found that the machine was running much hotter than expected. fullText:
A Redditor used Claude Code AI to build a Mac temperature monitor app and found that the machine was running much hotter than expected. Claude reported that it found a crypto miner using more than 1,000% of the CPU cycles – then added an unprompted comment denying having installed it.

Some Redditors were understandably suspicious of Claude’s spontaneous comment that it wasn’t responsible for installing the rogue app …

Redditor UntilHEX shared the Claude report on the reason for the overheating (via Macworld).

“Most important: your Mac is running a cryptominer that I didn’t put there. While checking sensor accuracy | saw xmrig using about 1175% CPU, roughly 12 cores. That is why your temperatures are so high, with the CPU peaking at 112°C.”

About all that seemed to be missing from Claude’s comment was the word “totally.”

Redditors had split views on the suspicious-sounding comment, but it seems more likely to be a training artifact than an AI gone rogue.

title: iFixit tears down iPhone Duo, finds possible causes of early screen failures
snippet: iFixit’s teardown of the iPhone Duo is up, revealing some interesting (and some worrisome) details about what it calls the most repairable foldable phone yet. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
iFixit’s teardown of the iPhone Duo is up, revealing some interesting (and some worrisome) details about what it calls the most repairable foldable phone yet. Here are the details.

You know the drill: new iPhone, now iFixit teardown

iFixit’s much-anticipated teardown of the iPhone Duo is now live. Among the many interesting findings of its disassembly process, perhaps the most positively surprising one is its repairability score: the iPhone Duo gets a 5 out of 10, which iFixit says is the highest score it has ever given a foldable smartphone.

Granted, this is a provisional score, pending the availability of replacement parts, but it’s still an encouraging result for Apple’s first foldable.

As usual, the teardown is very detailed, and I encourage you to watch the video below and read iFixit’s in-depth blog post here.

Unsurprisingly, much of the teardown focuses on the hinge, which is the biggest news of this iPhone. As iFixit notes, Apple’s patents had already been offering clues about its design for years. Still, now that it’s here, the teardown reveals an even more intricate and fascinating mechanism than those filings suggested.

iFixit’s teardown starts with its now-traditional fluorescent dust test, which lets the team track how dust particles enter the device as they disassemble it.

The iPhone Duo has an IP68 rating, which means it’s dust-tight and can withstand submersion in water up to 6 meters deep for 30 minutes.

Right off the bat, they notice that the hinge starts making crunchy sounds after the dust test. As the teardown progresses, though, they find that relatively little dust has made its way into the hinge, especially compared to other foldable phones they’ve tested.

The hinge itself features an intricate combination of gears, springs, and interconnected metal joints, along with a waterdrop design that makes room for the display to bend without folding too sharply. This waterdrop design is rather commonplace for foldable phones by now, though Apple’s implementation adds some interesting engineering tricks of its own.

Apple also uses curved guides to control how the joints move, to reduce the stress placed on the display as the phone opens and closes.

About those screen failures

Speaking of stress, however, iFixit has found some possible culprits for the early screen failures reported by iPhone Duo owners, many of whom have described hearing a crunch while folding or unfolding the device, followed by bright lines appearing across the inner display.

Interestingly, many of the reported failures appear to occur around the same area of the display, near the transition between the opening for the cable connecting the two halves and the central hinge support.

Using CT scans, teardown footage, and Apple’s patents, iFixit built a 3D model of the hinge to investigate the possible causes of the damage.

One possibility is that a central support bar isn’t retracting properly as the phone closes, potentially putting excessive pressure on the display. Another involves the curved rails that guide the hinge’s movement, which rise above the surrounding components during folding and could, in theory, interfere with the screen if they fail to move as intended.

iFixit also points out that several structural edges and components converge around the affected area, potentially concentrating stress on the delicate display layers.

iFixit’s teardown doesn’t definitively establish what’s causing the failures, but the similarities between the reported damage and the hinge’s internal geometry give the team some promising leads for further investigation.

Other interesting tidbits

iFixit’s teardown also takes a closer look at the iPhone Duo’s matte nano-texture display, which Apple explains helps disguise the crease by scattering reflected light. Under a microscope, the team found a surface covered in tiny rounded bumps that diffuse reflections, making the crease less noticeable.

Another interesting discovery came from examining the display’s pixels under a microscope. iFixit noticed that some of the subpixels are oval-shaped and oriented in different directions, rather than following a uniform pattern.

iFixit noted that an Apple patent suggests that this arrangement could help reduce diffraction artifacts, potentially making the crease even less noticeable. The teardown blog post offers a fascinating look at the pattern and how Apple may be using it to make reflections less distracting.

And speaking of pixels, iFixit also examined the area above the inner display’s selfie camera. Much like the under-display infrared camera on the iPhone 18 Pro, the Duo uses a modified pixel pattern with larger gaps that allow light to reach the camera underneath. In this area, the pixels also become rounder and more regularly arranged.

Lastly on the display, iFixit notes that the bezel surrounding the inner screen can be removed without breaking, thanks to Apple’s use of clips rather than relying entirely on adhesive. The outer display is also surprisingly easy to remove, which is particularly good news, given that several internal repairs require removing it first.

	

Moving on to the batteries, iFixit shows how Apple has positioned the two cells, one beneath the back glass and the other beneath the outer display (which means that replacing both requires opening up both halves of the phone). The larger battery has a capacity of 11.567 Wh, while the smaller one is rated at 7.506 Wh, for a combined 19.073 Wh.

iFixit also praises Apple’s use of electrically releasable adhesive on both batteries, allowing them to be removed without forceful prying. The team called it the best battery-removal experience it has seen in a foldable smartphone.

The teardown also explores the iPhone Duo’s new logic board design, the display’s multiple layers and how they move independently to accommodate folding, and you can watch it in full below:

title: Google says Gemini 4 Argon ranks well behind Claude and GPT-6 for Android coding
snippet: Google has updated its Android Bench list for showing how good AI models are at Android coding assistance, with Gemini 4 Argon ranking way behind that of the latest Claude and GPT models. more…
fullText:
Google has updated its Android Bench list for showing how good AI models are at Android coding assistance, with Gemini 4 Argon ranking way behind that of the latest Claude and GPT models.

The Android Bench was introduced early this year as a way for Android developers to get a quick way to see what AI models were best suited to Android coding assistance based on a test from Google. That test took into account aspects of AI use that are specific to Android coding and best practices in Android development. As Google has continued its tests and ranking new models, it has also included the average cost as a part of the benchmark so that developers can make the best decision for their needs.

With the October 26 update, Google has added the reasoning level used for each model, as well as adding results for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, as well as Google’s own Gemini 4 Argon.

Currently topping the chart is Claude Sonnet 5.5, with a pass rate of 40% and a completion rate of 80.9%. Claude Opus 5.5, added to the list in early October, comes in second place. 

	

OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol might be the most interesting addition here, coming in at a pass rate of 29.3% and completion rate of 82.8%, but a cost of just $99.50 compared to Claude’s $1,574.90 cost for its first place finish. 

But it’s Google’s own Gemini 4 Argon that makes a rather underwhelming debut, sitting well behind other frontier models in fifth place. It lags behind Claude Fable 5.1 at a mere 21.3% pass rate, 81.8% completion rate, and an average cost of $267.70. 

In a report shortly after Google’s announcement of Gemini 4 Argon, some internal voices claimed that the model “struggles to handle certain coding tasks,” though Google stood by its capabilities.

title: Discord is making its public communities more searchable, and people have concerns
snippet: In December, messages from Discord's public discoverable servers will begin appearing in search engine results.
fullText:
Discord announced on Tuesday it will make some conversations in its public servers searchable and easier to find on the internet. The new update targets conversations in “Discoverable Servers,” public Discord servers that administrators have made eligible to appear in the platform’s Server Discovery feature.

The aim is to help people find useful information that might otherwise remain buried in Discord conversations to a wider audience. 

According to Discord, more than 63,000 Discoverable Servers host discussions on everything from gaming strategies and fandoms to language learning and niche interests. By making some of these conversations searchable, Discord hopes to extend the reach of its communities beyond the platform itself.

The move also taps into the appeal of traditional internet forums, where users can find answers by searching through publicly accessible discussions. Gaming communities could draw attention to walkthroughs, developers could reach more people with technical advice, and content creators could attract new audiences without relying solely on Discord’s internal discovery tools.

Image Credits:Discord

Starting November 16, every Discoverable Server will have its own web page, which may feature automated summaries of discussions in active public channels. Beginning in mid-December, selected messages from public channels may also appear in search engine results.

Server administrators will be able to choose which channels are included, while individual members can opt out of having their messages made publicly searchable. Published messages will not display usernames or avatars. Private servers, direct messages, and group direct messages are excluded.

The announcement has sparked backlash over privacy. Some users are concerned about exposing conversations to audiences far beyond their original context, arguing that posting in a public Discord server does not necessarily mean users want their messages to be discoverable across the wider internet. 

Others have raised concerns about whether these conversations could be used to train AI models. Similar arguments emerged during controversies surrounding Reddit’s data-sharing practices and AI training, when users questioned whether their posts and comments should be used to train AI without their explicit consent or compensation.

Discord says users can manage their preferences in settings, while server administrators retain control over which channels participate. Notably, the option to make messages discoverable is turned off by default in the EU, U.K., Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea because of legal restrictions. Teen users are also excluded from the feature.

title: Samsung reportedly slashes production plans for millions of Galaxy phones
snippet: As RAMageddon rages on, brands are making tough choices including price hikes and refocused lineups. According to a new report, Samsung plans to cut production for millions of entry-level and mid-range Galaxy phones. more…
fullText:
As RAMageddon rages on, brands are making tough choices including price hikes and refocused lineups. According to a new report, Samsung plans to cut production for millions of entry-level and mid-range Galaxy phones.

ETNews reports that Samsung is cutting production of Galaxy A smartphones by “approximately 20%.” The cuts are being made to reallocate those resources for Samsung’s flagship products, as those pricier products are more likely to make a profit in current market conditions. For mid-range devices, inflated costs of memory and chipsets now make up around half of the overall cost of production.

This 20% cut to Galaxy A devices is said to account for roughly 10 million units, with further cuts planned going into 2027 (translated):

Component orders for the fourth quarter have decreased by about 20% compared to the production plan at the beginning of the year. On an annual basis, this represents a decrease of about 10 million units. The situation is critical as Samsung Electronics’ Mobile Communications (MX) division is suffering a loss this year… The stance is to cut Galaxy A series production by more than 10% next year as well.

While Samsung does make less on its Galaxy A series, the company’s entry-level and mid-range devices make up a huge share of Samsung’s overall sales. The best-selling Samsung phones are almost always entry-level or mid-range Galaxy A devices, though the Galaxy S26 series finally broke that record earlier this year.

title: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
snippet: Massive note conversions reveal the true extent of Amazon's ownership in Anthropic.
fullText:
Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital are expected to return billions.

Yet according to Anthropic’s S-1, none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders’ table. That’s highly unusual. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed. The reason is Anthropic’s size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo’s roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures.

While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners. Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO.

Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company. Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic. Instead of taking stock upfront, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale.

According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30. That is Anthropic’s entire debt load. But as Anthropic’s valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable. Amazon’s own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30.

As the value of Amazon’s convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books. It reported the adjustments on its income statement under “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs,” a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The charge is non-cash, meaning no money left the company. 

Amazon’s notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, according to the S-1. But a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic’s “partially diluted” share count, a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options. Amazon can waive the cap. Notes that can’t convert will stay outstanding and convert in later quarters, subject to the same limit.

But the notes are only part of Amazon’s holdings. It further invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock (a type of equity), in the second quarter, according to Amazon’s quarterly report for the period ended June 30. Amazon did this by investing $5 billion in each of Anthropic’s last two funding rounds. Combined with the $8 billion it invested in the notes from 2023 through 2025, that brings Amazon’s total investment to about $18 billion.

Beyond its stock gains, Amazon will also continue to earn significant revenue from Anthropic, which has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over the next 10 years. 

Google, too, is set for a major windfall from both the listing and its cloud computing deals with Anthropic. The search giant held about 14% of Anthropic as of early last year, according to court filings that were reported by The New York Times, and has invested more since, including $10 billion in April. (Google was likely diluted in subsequent and massive funding rounds, with PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes telling TechCrunch he estimates its current stake at closer to 5.6%.) It has also secured at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from the Anthropic through 2033.

While VCs set for massive paydays have little reason to complain, the S-1 makes it clear that the biggest winners of Anthropic’s IPO may well be tech giants like Amazon, which backed a would-be rival early on and now sell it much of the computing power it runs on. 

The S-1 itself warns that some of those cloud providers also build rival AI models and that they may not always want the same things that Anthropic does.

fullText:

Whether you’re launching your first startup, navigating your next funding round, or preparing to scale, this is your chance to get actionable strategies, make valuable connections, and learn what it really takes to build a successful company.

Don’t wait until the event doors open and prices go up. Secure your ticket now and save up to $100 before you miss your chance.

7 days until game-changing founder insights take over the venue

TechCrunch Founder Summit is a one-day founder 101 bootcamp designed to help you tackle the real challenges of building and growing a startup. No generic advice. No guessing what comes next. Just practical insights, candid conversations, and connections that can move your business forward.

Two Q&A breakout stages. Two interactive roundtable rooms. One full day of founder insights from scaling experts. Explore the full agenda and get ready for a day packed with:

Actionable breakout sessions covering fundraising, hiring, product-market fit, AI strategy, and growth.

Candid roundtable discussions where founders can dig into real challenges and get direct insights from experienced operators and investors.

High-impact networking powered by Braindate, giving you opportunities to connect with fellow founders, investors, and experts through one-on-one and small-group conversations.

Official Boston Side Events that extend the conversations and help you build relationships with the local startup community throughout the week.

Image Credits:Halo Creative

Meet the leaders helping founders build what’s next

From venture capital and AI to enterprise technology and startup growth, Founder Summit brings together experienced leaders who have navigated the challenges founders face every day.

Here are some of the expert voices joining us on November 4:

Kent Bennett, Bessemer Venture Partners: Learn how to validate customer demand, identify meaningful product-market fit signals, and avoid scaling before your startup is ready.

Vineet Edupuganti, Cogent Security: Learn how to attract ambitious talent, build trust through transparency and feedback, and turn individual drive into a high-performing team.

Chase Garbarino, HqO: Discover the advantages and challenges of building and scaling a category-defining company outside of a major hub, instead of in Silicon Valley.

Dave Balter, True Ventures and Edisyl: Learn how to sharpen your startup pitch, communicate your value clearly, and earn the next conversation with investors in this pitch session.

Tina Tosukhowong, TDK Ventures: Discover how investors evaluate startups for category leadership by assessing economics, scalability, competitive positioning, and commercial timing.

These are just a few of the leaders bringing practical insights to the event. Check out the full speaker lineup here.

Only 7 days left to save up to $100 before doors open in Boston

title: Samsung’s open-ear Galaxy Buds On cost $229 in the US, launching next month
snippet: After launching in Korea earlier this month, Samsung has confirmed that its open-ear Galaxy Buds On will cost $229 in the US and will go on sale early next month. more…
fullText:
After launching in Korea earlier this month, Samsung has confirmed that its open-ear Galaxy Buds On will cost $229 in the US and will go on sale early next month.

Galaxy Buds On are clip-style, open-ear earbuds that are designed to be super lightweight and let you hear music, podcasts, and more without blocking sound from the world around you. The form factor has been used by other brands, but is new to Samsung’s lineup.

The company announced Galaxy Buds On earlier in October in Korea, touting Gemini Live integration, 9.5-hour battery life, automatic volume adjustments, and more. Today’s announcement also calls out features like “Intelligent Clear Call” and “Quick Voice Memo,” as well as Bixby integration for searching through recordings “hands-free.” There’s also gesture support for answering/declining calls, dismissing alarms, and more.

Galaxy Buds On are available solely in black and the earbuds have the same case design as Galaxy Buds 4/Pro. 

	

Pricing lands at $229 in the US, making these Samsung’s second-most expensive pair of wireless earbuds behind the $249 Galaxy Buds 4 Pro. Galaxy Buds 4 are $179. Pre-orders open today with shipping in “early November” – a specific release date has not been confirmed. 

Are you getting a pair?

title: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max was exciting until I found out about the price
snippet: RAMageddon sucks folks. Over the past few weeks I’ve been using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, a phone I’ve been pretty enthralled by, but its price tag really killed the hype on this one. more…
fullText:
RAMageddon sucks folks. Over the past few weeks I’ve been using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, a phone I’ve been pretty enthralled by, but its price tag really killed the hype on this one.

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is €1,799. You’re not reading that wrong. This non-foldable, MediaTek-powered Android flagship costs just a little bit less than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (€1,999). 

It’s not really Oppo’s fault, and it’s not like the company is alone in this struggle. A comparable Galaxy S26 Ultra in Europe isn’t much cheaper at €1,769, and Xiaomi is also rumored to be running into wildly high prices for its next launch in Europe too. This is just the current state of the tech industry as a whole, largely thanks to AI companies. 

But the reactions to Oppo’s pricing have not been quiet, and not just for the European model. Some users on Reddit mention how Oppo’s price matches the latest iPhone 18 Pro Max, how pricing in some regions is disproportionately high, and how you can still get the Find X9 Ultra for less. And I’m right there in that same train of thought.

	

As mentioned in our review, you’ll be happy with the Find X10 Pro Max. It performs well, has great cameras, and killer battery life, but this price tag really stings in a market where prices are already exceptionally high. 

Review: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a gut punch in a post-OnePlus world

Mirroring that last example, I’d happily go for the Find X9 Ultra, especially if I could get it for less. Even the Find X9 Pro seems like a better deal for many – some have pointed out that last year’s flagship has more memory and a bigger battery in Europe for hundreds less. You can get a Find X9 Pro in Europe right now for around €1,000~, way less than the newer model.

Find X9 Pro and Ultra both deliver more phone for less money

You might be able to get the Find X10 Pro Max for a deal, though. Some UK buyers point out offers they were able to take advantage of, but nothing changes that Oppo’s latest flagship is very expensive. 

Have you been considering the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max? Would you pay full price for it? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Re:Build, which spun out Slate Auto, raises $2.1B
snippet: The manufacturing accelerator bills itself as "America’s answer to Shenzhen."
fullText:
Re:Build, the Massachusetts-based manufacturing accelerator that spun out EV startup Slate Auto in 2023, has raised $2.1 billion 

The company said Tuesday that it will use the funding to “expand Re:Build’s capacity to manufacture hard tech products and launch new industrial startups,” which will “ensure the most innovative products can be made in America for generations to come.” The investment was led by General Catalyst and JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group. Other investors weren’t disclosed.

The funding round comes as increasing attention and capital is flowing to the idea of building up manufacturing and supply chains in the United States, especially as a hedge away from China.

“We started Re:Build because the deindustrialization of America is an economic failure and national security risk,” Re:Build co-founder Jeff Wilke said in a statement. “This capital allows Re:Build to go faster and further than would otherwise be possible, and build a great manufacturing business and a platform for American industrial leadership. The products and companies emerging from our ecosystem prove we can help restore America’s industrial might.”

General Catalyst’s CEO Hemant Taneja echoed those sentiments in a statement, saying, “General Catalyst has long believed that rebuilding American industrial capacity is one of the most important economic and national security imperatives of our time.”

Taneja added: “To compete with China, re-industrialize the U.S., and revitalize the towns and jobs that have been left behind, we need platform companies that can operate at genuine scale — and we need our innovation ecosystem to learn how to build hardware again.”

Founded in 2020, Re:Build bills itself as “America’s answer to Shenzhen,” and it has numerous ties to Amazon. It was co-founded by Wilke, who was Amazon’s former commercial CEO. Wei Gao, a longtime Amazon VP and technical adviser to Bezos, is Re:Build’s chief digital and product officer. Multiple other Re:Build executives also worked for the e-commerce giant. 

Re:Build claims to have “launched hundreds of products and production systems” over its six-year existence. The company tends to operate two ways: It enters partnerships with industrial companies to “design, engineer, and manufacture products at scale across verticals including aerospace and defense,” and it incubates startups in “critical, underserved markets.”

Re:Build says its network of companies employs more than 2,100 people in the U.S. and houses more than 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity.

Wilke and his co-founder Miles Arnone came up with the idea of Slate Auto in 2022 and decided to spin it out in order to help it attract more capital. The company has since gone on to raise at least $1.4 billion, including funding from Bezos’ family office, in an attempt to build an ultra-low-cost, bare-bones pickup that can be customized to a customer’s liking.

title: Disruptive raises $10B fund to make big bets on at least 10 companies
snippet: Disruptive has made headlines in recent years for pouring money into companies like chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

11:55 AM PDT · October 27, 2026

Image Credits:Altayb (opens in a new window) / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

The Dallas-based investment firm Disruptive, whose past bets include Palantir, Airbnb, and Spotify, announced a $10 billion fund to back at least 10 late-stage companies, with checks of up to $1 billion, it said Tuesday.

It’s one of the biggest fundraises of the year so far, aiming to back (what else?!) the capital-intensive fields of AI and defense. The Wall Street Journal first reported earlier this month that the firm was seeking to raise the fund and by then had already secured at least $7.5 billion in capital commitments. 

The firm was founded in 2012 by Alex Davis, grandson of billionaire oil magnate Marvin Davis.

This is technically the firm’s first blind-pool fund, meaning investors commit money without knowing which companies it will back. Until now, the firm raised money through deal-by-deal special purpose vehicles. Disruptive has nonetheless made headlines in recent years for pouring money into companies like chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs. Bloomberg reported that the firm told LPs it has returned more than $6 billion on the roughly $1.9 billion it has put into startups. 

According to the Dallas Business Journal, the new vehicle is the largest venture fund raised in Texas history.

fullText:
Tech is in a weird place right now. There are plenty of exciting developments in AI, tons of new hardware, and rapidly growing ideas, but it’s all surrounded by the effect today’s tech is having on society. So, what tech is making you happy right now?

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

This article spawned from my time recently with new tech including Googlebook, the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, and the Mac Mini that I recently purchased.

Let me explain.

	

In the 10+ years I’ve been working in this industry, Googlebook is the first big launch that left me unable to find the upsides. Even after reviewing the otherwise excellent HP Googlebook 14, I’m still struggling to find anything to be optimistic about. And that largely boils down to the timing, as we discussed in last week’s Weekender issue. Googlebook is not only a platform that’s less capable than its competitors, but also wants to demand more from customers for it, all in a time where our resources as customers are more strained than ever. That same train of thought also comes into the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max that I reviewed earlier this week. It’s a great smartphone, one I think I’ll keep using for a while yet, but it’s also obscenely expensive, not really to the fault of Oppo directly. That’s just the tech industry we’re dealing with right now – heck, it’s the economy as a whole we’re dealing with right now.

So, that Mac Mini I bought. That came out of a limited-time deal where the M4 Mac Mini was $650. I’m still a Windows guy at the end of the day, but as PC components only become harder to find and, frankly, to afford, a $650 Mac Mini was by far the most logical way for me to eke more out of my gaming PC that’s already overdue for some component replacements. 

All of that is to say, the tech industry right now is full of a lot of tougher choices when it comes to the bottom line. As a reviewer, that’s been a tough conversation to balance, and it has me thinking not just about how we’ll interact with new devices going forward, but also where to find the optimism in the tech I’m using.

Here are some recent examples of tech that have brought me a smile:

The Oppo Enco X4 earbuds that I used alongside the Find X10 Pro Max are the harder-to-buy sibling to the stellar OnePlus Buds Pro 3, and they’re just utterly wonderful to use with such an excellent sound profile. 

As I’ve been working up my review of the Fitbit Edge, I’m reminded just how much I’ve come to adore the Fitbit Air for its simple and refreshing take on a wearable – I look forward to going back to it soon. 

There’s delight in the simplest ideas; the Statik Powerstand cable I went hands-on with this week immediately sparked a bit of joy from the moment I picked it up, knowing I’d just found a new staple for my bag. 

So, that’s my question to you.

What tech is making you happy right now? Is it a new gadget you picked up, or just the simple fact that your existing device is still up and running? Regardless of your outlook on the tech industry as a whole right now, it’s a stressful time out there, so let’s all focus on the positives for a minute…

title: Halloween Candy Prices Take a Scary Bite Out of Shoppers’ Budgets
snippet: Americans could spend over $4 billion on Halloween candy this year.
fullText:
If you can’t afford a trip to a haunted house this spooky season, just swing by the supermarket candy aisle for a nasty scare. The price of sweets jumped over the last few years, soaring even faster than the average inflation rate, according to a recent report from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, with higher ingredient costs as the primary villain.

October is important for candy sales, as shoppers stock up for parties, trick-or-treaters, or — let’s be honest — personal consumption.

“The biggest purchasing days are still ahead, with about 35% of Halloween seasonal sales expected this week,” a Hershey Company spokesperson told CNET.

			

More from CNET

Chocolate treats have become especially expensive, as a recent global cocoa shortage squeezed the market while candy companies were preparing shipments for Halloween. 

But despite chilling prices, chocolate is still making its way into Halloween bags and buckets. 

“Trick-or-treat participation intent is in line with last year,” the Hershey spokesperson said. “Confection remains a resilient category.”

Money monstrosity

Americans will likely spend over $13 billion on Halloween this year, the National Retail Federation reports. That’s almost twice the $6.9 billion people spent on the holiday 11 years ago, in 2015.

“Consumers continue to make Halloween a spending priority, but they are also approaching the season with affordability in mind,” Allison Zeller, a National Retail Federation vice president, said in a statement. 

Candy remains the favorite purchase, with 95% of Halloween shoppers planning to snag some this year, followed by decorations, costumes and greeting cards, according to the National Retail Federation. In 2026, shoppers are expected to spend over $4 billion on Halloween candy alone.

An Oct. 20 report from research group Groundwork Collaborative broke down which candy prices have risen the most this year. The Mondelez Sour Gummy Candy variety pack, which jumped 39% in price, and Hershey seasonal Peanut Butter Cups, which saw a 23% increase, are this year’s most expensive Halloween candy compared with last season. 

The squeeze doesn’t stop in the candy aisle — utility bills and other essentials are climbing, too. A Consumer Reports survey from earlier this month found that one in five American families has cut back on groceries due to rising energy costs. 

“If you’ve been waiting until now to get your Halloween goodies, you’re right to do so. Halloween sales hit the high street and online two or three days before Halloween as stores try to clear stock,” says James Bricknell, CNET commerce managing editor.

“If you’re all set for this year, do what I did last year and grab a bunch of costumes and decorations the day after Halloween,” he adds. “Then, you can store them ready to go for Halloween 2027.”

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Julian Dossett
						

						

							Writer						
					

											

								

											Julian is a contributor and former staff writer at CNET.

title: iOS 27.2 just upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new
snippet: Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27 last month, but this week’s release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27 last month, but this week’s release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And now iOS 27.2 has introduced four more. 

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s new:

you can now edit captions for your photos and videos

comments can be edited too

there’s a feature to prevent adding duplicate photos to an album

the app can display a reminder before albums expire, so participants can save photos before they’re gone

To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

#2: SynthID watermarking to identify AI-modified photos

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated. 

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

What do you think of the latest Apple Photos changes in iOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

snippet: T-Mobile is launching T-Mix, a new trio of plans that come with your choice of 16 popular services bundled in, like Netflix, Apple TV, Xbox Game Pass, YouTube Premium, and more. more…
fullText:
T-Mobile is launching T-Mix, a new trio of plans that come with your choice of 16 popular services bundled in, like Netflix, Apple TV, Xbox Game Pass, YouTube Premium, and more.

T-Mobile is at it again, launching a trio of slightly confusing new plans called T-Mix. These plans all include the basics (unlimited talk/text/data, T-Satellite, and T-Mobile Tuesday) and have a tiered list of included bundled services you can choose from. In other words, no more subscribing to a plan that includes something you don’t use. All plans have a 4-line maximum per plan.

	

The basic plan starts at $55 per month and includes one line with your choice of one of the following services: 

Apple TV

DoorDash DashPass

500 Delta SkyMiles per month

Google AI Plus

Hulu (with ads)

Netflix Standard (with ads)

Pandora Plus

Paramount+ Essential

SiriusXM All Access

YouTube Premium Lite

Upgrading to the $75/month plan lets you choose from one in the list above plus either Apple Music Individual, Google AI Pro, Pandora Premium, Xbox Game Pass Premium, or YouTube Premium.

	

T-Mobile also has a T-Mix Loaded plan that starts at $95/month and lets you add one or two more bundled services, including Netflix Standard, Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, ESPN Unlimited, and Netflix Premium. Here’s the full chart if you’re up for studying:

title: Amazon’s New Digital Picture Frame Is Clever and Classy
snippet: The frame, available in real wood finishes, is the first-ever with Amazon Alexa built in and offers unlimited storage for Prime members.
fullText:
Amazon just dropped its first-ever digital picture frame, right in time for the holiday gifting rush, along with a whole batch of new Echo-based gadgets. We got a peek at the Alexa Photo Frame at a launch event in New York, and it has a few neat tricks and design touches you won’t find on most frames.

The big standout is that the frame syncs automatically with Amazon Photos and picks out the “best” shots for you, so you’re not stuck watching all 300 photos from your upstate leaf-peeping trip on repeat. We love the idea, but we haven’t tested it yet, so we can’t say how well it curates.

	

			

	

			

									

						Smart Home Gift Buying Guide 2026: Upgrades Everyone Will Love					

							

		

The first smart frame with Alexa built in

Alexa prompts fetch the exact photos or photo types you want to see. 

Amazon’s frame, which comes with unlimited storage for Prime members, is the first with Alexa built in, so you can ask to see photos of certain people, places or events.

			

More from CNET

“Alexa, nobody believes me that I met Dolly Parton at Costco; please bring up the selfie,” is one example for locating photos.

You can also use AI-style prompts to create a specific slideshow, such as “show pictures of the kids” or “absolutely no pictures of the kids, please.” 

We’ve tested generative AI frames before, and most left us wanting more. SwitchBot recently came out with a second-gen AI frame model, but we haven’t seen anything like this Alexa hybrid approach before, which makes us really want to try it out.

High-definition picture that adjusts to changing light

Brightness automatically adjusts as ambient light changes.Amazon

The 10-inch high-definition, semi-matte, anti-glare finish was impressive, making photos look more like a physical photo than a screen, and they show clearly from almost any angle. A clever light sensor automatically adjusts the screen brightness from day to night.

The wood frame may be the best part

The frame comes in birch or walnut wood.

What first caught our eye was the textured, soft-white matting and the real wood frames, available in walnut, lighter birch or black. If you’ve browsed digital frames online, you’ve likely noticed a trend: drab black plastic designs with little warmth or visual appeal. Amazon’s wood options are a welcome departure from the norm, even if they cost more.

You can add voice notes to photos for some reason

Perhaps the strangest feature is the ability to add voice notes to accompany images as they pass across the screen to “capture the story behind the moment.” I suppose this might enhance the picture-frame experience in some cases, but I can’t think of many. 

Pricing and availability

The frame comes in three finishes, including two wood options, and begins shipping Dec. 16.Amazon

The Alexa Photo Frame is available starting today. It costs $200 for black plastic and $229 in one of two wood finishes, walnut or birch.

title: Amazon’s New Echo Lineup Goes in the Opposite Direction of Apple HomeView
snippet: While Apple’s first home screen is small, Amazon is going bigger and more TV-oriented than ever before — but that comes with high prices.
fullText:
Apple made a big splash early this October with its massive smart home announcement, including new Siri AI features, the company’s first smart display called HomeView and the long-awaited smart speaker, the HomePod Mini 2.

Now Amazon’s here with its new Echo lineup, and we’re all comparing these smart speakers and smart displays with what Apple is offering. What’s interesting is that Amazon is taking a completely different path with its new home devices — especially the latest Echo Show, which is currently available for preorder. Here’s what that means and why it matters for potential buyers this holiday season.

Amazon’s Echo Show 16 is everything the HomeView is not

The Echo Show 16 is different from the HomeView in nearly every way. Amazon

Apple’s first smart display relies heavily on Siri AI and audio features as a selling point, with a design a bit like the Echo Show 11. During Apple’s announcement, I noted this created dissonance since the 7-inch screen is too small to easily watch the latest Apple TV shows, or much else, even if the audio is excellent. That’s one reason companies like Amazon have been making Echo Show devices bigger and bigger.

			

More from CNET

Read more: How Does Apple’s HomeView Smart Display Look Against the Competition?

Now with the Echo Show 16, Amazon is embracing the idea of a second TV device for the kitchen or hallway more fully than ever. This new Show ditches the big speaker for a series of small woofers and tweeters (and a stand design perhaps pointedly reminiscent of Mac computers).

I’ll have to listen to the result in person, but it looks like Amazon is backing away from the 360-degree, room-filling sound for something that acts more like a traditional TV, while still including the touchscreen, camera and mic of past smart displays. It supports wall mounting if you’d rather not use a stand.

The Echo Show 16 backs up its new size and design with a built-in Fire TV platform, something previously limited to only larger, wall-mount-only Echo Shows. Fire TV not only makes it easier to access Amazon Prime content, but also handles third-party apps and more complex controls better.

You can spring for an upgraded display on the Echo Show 16, but it will cost even more.Amazon

Those deeply invested in catching up on shows or sports can upgrade to an enhanced Nanomatte display designed to cut glare and improve color accuracy. While Apple is a bit coy about which third-party apps will be supported alongside Apple TV, Amazon says the Echo Show will support Netflix, Disney Plus, YouTube, HBO Max/Peacock, Tubi and Pluto, which should reassure streaming fans.

The drawback to all this new tech is the price, something Apple HomeView fans will know well. While the small-screened HomeView starts at $299, Amazon’s Echo Show 16 starts at $499.99, and the Nanomatte display bumps the price up to $569.99. Plus, you’ll want a compatible stand, which starts at $69.99 but can go up to $150, so you can see how prices quickly rise.

That high price is a tough sell for anyone who already has a smart display or is leaning toward the HomeView, but people looking for a second Fire TV screen may find it more palatable. I want to test them both out before I make an ultimate recommendation.

Amazon adds an Echo camera to compete with the HomePod Mini 2

Amazon’s added a camera to its studio speaker, although I’m not sure it’s a good idea.Amazon

The Echo Show 16 wasn’t the only Amazon device aimed at Apple’s latest releases. The company also announced a new Echo Studio model, starting at $249.99 and comparable to Apple’s HomePod Mini 2 — with one big difference. This latest Studio comes with a built-in, nearly invisible home camera.

Amazon says the camera is meant to gather visual intelligence for Alexa, which rings privacy warning bells to me, but the camera could let the voice assistant answer questions about what’s happening in the room when users are away or offer live views, sort of like a mini security camera.

I’m not convinced this camera add-on is worth it, but it does help Amazon differentiate the Studio from the $149 HomePod Mini 2, which might otherwise seem similar to the casual buyer.

Amazon also announced a noncamera Echo Dot, more affordable at $99.99, upgraded with an AZ3 custom-designed silicon chip for faster Alexa responses, and a kid’s version of the same model.

And while Apple may have showed how the iPhone Duo could be used as an impromptu alarm clock, Amazon showed up with its own dedicated smart clock, the aptly named Echo Time, a round, dial-like smart display meant to serve as a nightstand clock with the addition of Alexa Plus. It includes unique smart alarm features to help manage waking up in a slower fashion. But again, Amazon is setting prices very high at $199.99 for the clock.

Alexa Plus is ready to duel with Siri AI

Alexa Plus has new tricks to go along with the new display.Amazon

I’d be remiss not to talk about Alexa Plus and how the AI voice assistant is now going head-to-head with Apple’s Siri AI. Both add new capabilities to the new smart displays. Siri AI gets home control functions and an easier way to display information pulled from emails, text messages and other iPhone sources.

Alexa Plus, meanwhile, will have a new interface on the Echo Show 16, which ditches the old transcription visual (which I kind of liked) and replaces it with an interactive display that can pull up visuals, videos, events and more as you talk with Alexa. Each conversation gets its own Card icon, so you can revisit and pick up past conversations as needed. Alexa also has a new Home Map mode which acts like a living layout of all your smart devices, letting you control what‘’’s on or off, room by room.

I already like Alexa Plus a bit more than Siri AI, even if the voice assistant gets a little too talkative, and now I’ll have new experiences to test out. Of course, cost is yet again a factor here: Apple notes that more advanced Siri AI features do require iCloud Plus subscriptions, although it’s still light on details. Alexa Plus, meanwhile, is free with an Amazon Prime subscription, but otherwise, it costs a steep $20 per month for most features.

Final thoughts

Ultimately, Apple is treading carefully with its first-ever smart display, but that tiny screen is a tough sell for me. Amazon, meanwhile, is betting big that people want a second TV experience in their display and are willing to pay for it. Both AI voice assistants are showing up with new tricks I can’t wait to try.

Meanwhile, Amazon is trying out new avenues in the smart home, like giving its flagship smart speaker a built-in camera — which I’m dubious about — and releasing targeted screens for alarms, picture frames and more. It’s all very expensive, which gives Apple a surprise advantage for the holidays, but Amazon’s vision is strikingly different, so I’m not sure they’re after the same audience.
