title: Amazon debuts the Alexa Photo Frame and Echo Time smart clock, plus other upgraded devices
snippet: Amazon's other new decides include an upgraded Echo Dot, an Echo Studio with visual intelligence features, and the Echo Show 16.
fullText:
Amazon unveiled five new Alexa devices today, including two new kinds of hardware: the Alexa Photo Frame, a smart picture frame, and the Echo Time, a smart alarm clock.

The Alexa Photo Frame is Amazon’s foray into the world of digital photo displays, a product category that has transcended from a clunky, last-minute holiday gift to a sleek, attractive way to look through your camera roll.

Aura is responsible for much of the growth in this category, so it’s no coincidence that the Alexa Photo Frame has a similar aesthetic feel: The screen is much easier on the eyes than the old, bright photo frames from years past. The device is said to be specifically calibrated for sharing photos, featuring a semi-matte, anti-glare display that makes it look more like a Samsung Frame TV than a laptop screen. 

Also like Aura, the Photo Frame’s 10-inch screen looks like matte photograph, helping it blend in with other artwork on your wall.

Amazon’s new device, though, adds the value of integration with users’ existing Amazon accounts. Prime members get unlimited storage on Amazon Photos, and Alexa+ is supposed to intelligently choose how and when to display photos.

“It knows to choose photos where you’re smiling and the lighting is right, and it matches the season you’re in, so you see last year’s family Halloween costumes in October instead of the middle of spring. It also knows what to skip, like screenshots and receipts,” Amazon said in a press release. You can also add voice notes to photos, and images sync automatically as you take them.

The Alexa Photo Frame is on sale now, and starts at $199.99 in Black, and $229 in Birch or Walnut wood.

Image Credits:Amazon /

Meanwhile, the Echo Time clock seems to be a response to the growing sentiment that people don’t want to rely on their phones for alarms, setting morning reminders or checking the weather.

“Millions of customers start and end their days with Alexa—checking the weather and turning on the lights from bed in the morning or winding down with white noise at night,” Amazon wrote. “But the bedroom asks for something different from a device than the kitchen or living room does—so we designed an Echo specifically for it.”

Amazon says that the Echo Time, which costs $199.99, or $209.99 for a Kids version, has opt-in sleep sensing tools. You can choose to set a smart alarm feature that wakes you up anywhere between 10 to 60 minutes of your alarm, and can wake you when it detects you’re in a lighter phase of sleep, so that it’s less jarring to begin your day. 

Like the popular Hatch alarm clocks, the clock can also mimic sunrise features to ease you awake.

Image Credits:Amazon /

Amazon also showed off updates to its existing lines of devices. We now get the Echo Show 16, a new Echo Dot, and Echo Studio with Home Camera.

The biggest upgrade to the Echo Dot is that it now includes a built-in smart home hub, which also includes an eero Wi-Fi extender that adds up to 1,000 square feet of coverage, helping it connect to lights, locks, and thermostats around your home. The new Echo Dot is also powered by Amazon’s custom AZ3 silicon chip, which is said to make it better at on-device processing to speed up conversations with its AI, Alexa+.

Amazon says its most advanced speaker, however, is the Echo Studio with Home Camera. This speaker doubles as a camera so you can check on your home while you’re out, and also has visual intelligence features.

“Alexa can also see and understand what’s in front of the camera and help you in real time,” Amazon explained. “Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors.”

The Echo Dot is available at $99.99, and the Echo Studio with Home Camera costs $249.99. 

Finally, Amazon unveiled the new Echo Show 16, which includes a 16-inch display. Amazon says the device has a 10% larger viewing area than its predecessor, but with a 40% smaller frame. It has Fire TV built in, plus Smart Home tools like Family Organizer. It can also function like a digital photo frame.

The Echo Show 16 is available for pre-order for $499.99.

The arm seems limited to verified users, or those with a paid subscription to X Premium. Reactions, unsurprisingly, have been less tha … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

After Elon Musk warned that “advertisers who post ads that are ugly, shrill, strident or overstate claims about their product will be barred from advertising” on X earlier this month, the platform now appears to be using a jarring animated arm that reaches across the screen to draw attention to the “promote” button while users are composing a post.

Many X users have seen and shared images of the unsettling promotional tool, including The Verge’s Tom Warren, but it doesn’t appear for everyone on the platform. The arm seems limited to verified users, or those with a paid subscription to X Premium. Reactions, unsurprisingly, have been less than positive. “I’ve never promoted a post and HATE this screen takeover,” said Sheel Mohnot, while Jesse Middleton likened it to a Halloween prank. “I wish I could explain how jarring this hand and animation was in the @X app. It was truly shocking, almost like a Halloween gag, but I’m pretty sure it was real.”

Using the paid promote feature extends the reach of an X post to a larger audience based on their location, interests, or demographics, including those not currently following a user’s account. Posts that have been promoted look like other posts on X but are branded with a “promoted” or “ad” label.

title: Google Messages rolling out Enhanced Protection mode against spam and scams
snippet: Following the announcement earlier this month, Google Messages for Android is rolling out an Enhanced Protection mode to counter spam and scams. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement earlier this month, Google Messages for Android is rolling out an Enhanced Protection mode to counter spam and scams.

To date, Google Messages has offered Standard Protection to block “spam and suspected harmful links.” Enhanced Protection introduces “Advanced detection to prevent spam and scams.” There are three core features at launch.

Scam Detection will leverage “cloud Gemini models to evaluate complex message context and understand a scammer’s intent more quickly when you’re in a conversation with an unknown sender.” Compared to the existing on-device detection, this approach is better at identifying “novel and sophisticated attacks.”

It uses Android’s Private AI Compute feature to encrypt messages and process them in a secure space that is “private to you and not available to anyone else, including Google.”

	

Meanwhile, enhanced link protections use the on-device Gemini Nano model and real-time web signals to evaluate whether an unfamiliar link is trustworthy before you tap. This feature is available on the Pixel 10+, Samsung Galaxy S26 series, Z Flip 8, Z Fold 8, and “other select devices.”

	

The final update redesigns warnings to give you additional time and more context to “pause before tapping links” sent by numbers not in your contacts.

Enhanced Protection is an opt-in feature. To enable, go to Google Messages settings > Protection & safety. Instead of an on/off toggle, you’ll find three options:

Enhanced protection

Standard protection

No protection (not recommended)

We’re seeing this available with the latest Google Messages beta (version 20261020_00_RC00).

fullText:

Friday, October 23, 5 p.m. ET: Practice 2

title: New iPad mini vs previous model: Here’s everything new
snippet: Apple unveiled a new iPad mini today, and it’s a big upgrade over the previous model. Here’s everything new. more…
fullText:
Apple unveiled a new iPad mini today, and it’s a big upgrade over the previous model. Here’s everything new.

Design: Thinner, reduced bezels, camera repositioned, and new colors

The new iPad mini look similar to the previous model, but also fresh and more modern thanks to two main design changes:

It’s thinner than ever, with a depth of 5.4mm compared to 6.3mm on the last model

Bezels are now 24% smaller than before

You may or may not notice, but the new mini is also slightly more narrow, measuring 132.6mm wide vs 134.8mm. And it weighs less: 255 grams vs 293 for Wi-Fi models.

The front-facing Center Stage camera is now positioned on the landscape side of the device rather than portrait.

Apple now offers the iPad mini in two colors: Midnight and Starlight. Previously more options were available, including Space Gray and Starlight, but the latest colors still have an updated look.

Display: Larger display with OLED, optional nano-texture

Thanks to the reduced bezels, the new iPad mini now has a larger, 8.5-inch display. The previous model’s was only 8.3 inches.

Perhaps a more significant change is that the display is OLED, a big upgrade from the LCD technology used before. Apple says this enables “pixel-level lighting control for much deeper blacks and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vivid and accurate imagery.”

The display gets much brighter than before too, with peak brightness of 1200 nits, double the previous max of 600. Standard SDR and HDR brightness is 600 nits, up from 500. It also supports 1-nit minimum brightness for use in dim environments.

Apple now lets you optionally choose a nano-texture display on 256GB models and up. iPad mini has never previously offered nano-texture.

Performance: A20 Pro vs A17 Pro

The new iPad mini has an A20 Pro chip, Apple’s most powerful mobile processor that first debuted in iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. The previous generation had an A17 Pro. Per Apple:

A20 Pro delivers a giant leap in performance for iPad mini, significantly boosting graphics and AI-intensive tasks. It is built using Apple’s latest 2-nanometer process technology and a new package inspired by M-series chips. Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core, iPad mini delivers up to 4.5x faster AI performance than the previous generation — perfect for AI tasks ranging from running on-device models in creative apps to running local LLMs. And with the latest graphics architecture, including dynamic caching and hardware-accelerated mesh shading and ray tracing, graphics performance jumps by up to 2.7x — great for gaming and 3D rendering. A20 Pro also features up to a 6-core CPU for up to 60 percent faster multithreaded performance for everyday tasks like editing photos and working across apps.

A20 Pro also brings 2x increase in unified memory bandwidth.

One key detail worth noting is that the new iPad mini uses a binned A20 Pro chip in all but the high-end 512GB model. Not only does the binned chip have only 5 CPU cores rather than 6, it also lacks the Dual 16-core Neural Engine. Instead, you get the standard 16-core Neural Engine.

So if you’re comparing performance, Apple’s “up to” quotes refer to the 512GB model.

Acoustic Display speakers and IP67 water and dust resistance

Instead of the previous traditional stereo speaker setup, the new iPad mini uses “an innovative Acoustic Display” for audio, which Apple says delivers:

an even better audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content. Specially designed woofers are paired through the display to produce punchier bass and more volume. In addition, custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs.

The Acoustic Display has a sealed enclosure which enables iPad mini to offer IP67 water and dust resistance. This makes it more versatile than before.

Wireless connectivity, fast charging, and more

Apple’s N1 and C2 chips comes to the iPad mini, enabling the following connectivity improvements:

New iPad mini

Previous iPad mini

Wi-Fi

Wi-Fi 7

Wi-Fi 6E

Bluetooth

Bluetooth 6

Bluetooth 5.3

Cellular

Apple C2

Qualcomm

Additionally, though Apple didn’t give specific fast charging details for its last iPad mini, the new model supports: “Up to 50% charge in 30 minutes with a 35W adapter or higher.”

Finally, Apple also notes that the new iPad mini “supports extended display mode when connected to an external display, great for users multitasking with windowed apps.” Previously only mirroring was available, whereas this sounds like a full-fledged extended display feature.

Pricing and availability

	

As with nearly every other product these days, the iPad mini is getting more expensive with today’s updates. It now starts at $699, up from the previous $599 starting price. 

Pre-orders for the new iPad mini will open this Wednesday, October 28 at 10:10 a.m. PT and orders deliver on Friday, November 6.

title: Google Wallet rolling out notifications feed, support for more digital passports [U]
snippet: After the stacked card list redesign, Google Wallet for Android is gaining a notifications feed and support for more passports. more…
fullText:
After the stacked card list redesign, Google Wallet for Android is gaining a notifications feed and support for more passports.

On the homepage, you’ll see a notification bell icon next to the profile switcher in the top-right corner. Tapping opens a feed with “updates about items in Wallet.” 

Earlier this month, the company said it was introducing an “in-app message center in Google Wallet.” This new feature is still rolling out via a server-side update.

Meanwhile, Google Wallet is adding support for more digital passports. Officially referred to as an “ID pass” in the app, usage varies by country. US passports can be used at TSA security via NFC or QR code scanning. 

	

Update 10/23: Following Brazil, Singapore, Taiwan, United Kingdom, and the United States of America, we’re starting to see the ability to add Estonia, Ireland, Italy, and Spain.

The new countries are not widely rolled out yet.

To add a passport, tap the ‘plus’ FAB at the bottom of Google Wallet > IDs & personal info > ID pass. The registration process involves scanning your passport info page and security chip. Afterward, you have to record a video of your face. You’ll get a notification once verification is complete.

title: Ace Combat 8 Elevates High-Voltage Dogfights With Wistful Melodrama
snippet: The latest Ace Combat game feels like a polished, punchy airborne adventure — unapologetically anime in its storytelling and a joy to play.
fullText:
Up in the digital skies, I sortie with my squad (sortie, that was the word), staying quiet as they sound off over comms. A stalwart lecturer, a daredevil peacenik and a stoic rocker drifted off the edges of my wings (they’ll back you up if you bring them home). We cruise ahead, lighthearted bickering layered over views of the clearest blue over blankets of puffy white. A contact hits the edge of our radar, orders come spilling in from below, and as one, we peel off to find our enemy in the air (I can almost feel the wind).

The prologue kicking off Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, the latest game in the fighter jet combat franchise that debuted in 1995, is riddled with voiceovers loftily espousing the aviator’s philosophy of communing with the skies. It’s a little much, I thought, as I struggled to adjust to the game’s controls. By the time I rolled credits around 25 hours later, the aircraft in my hangar were extensions of my digital body. I was up in the clouds alongside my nameless pilot and their squadmates. 

As my first Ace Combat game, it’s unclear to me how much Wings of Theve retains and how much it innovates on its predecessors. That fresh perspective, and especially my inexperience with flight simulator games of all stripes, makes my wholehearted embrace of Ace Combat 8 all the more special. If you’ve been waiting to dive into a game flying jets around a fictional warzone, Wings of Theve could enchant you as it has me. 

			

More from CNET

That’s partially a credit to the controls and gameplay, but it’s the earnest melodrama established in the game’s intro that builds and builds over each mission. Plucked from the ocean by the crew of an old aircraft carrier serving as the last hope of an invaded nation, you’re thrown into the sky in a ridealong with a legendary pilot. Targeted by an enemy ace, you go down, but get fished out of the water alone – with the pilot’s soul riding along with you, issuing wise parentheticals about the new squad you’re assigned to lead, about war, about flying itself. 

In stakes, in setting, in characters, in echoed themes, in bombastic set pieces and midmission moments your attention is pointedly drawn to, the word that comes to mind when describing Ace Combat 8 is anime. (That’s a compliment.) Characters speak their minds in hushed whispers or loud barks, but always from beliefs welling in their chests. These missives come crackling over the radio, amplifying high-tension jet combat between metal machines with a spotlight on the humans at the controls. 

Missions span attacking land, air and sea targets.

Those big beliefs slam head-on into massive enemy vehicles, land- or airborne colossi bristling with weapons, another staple from anime skilfully deployed to ratchet up the challenge and spectacle. It should be silly to send your quartet of jets against land battleships (literal naval vessels footed with rows of tank treads), but their menacing blister of guns cracks the sky open with explosions, a sinful interruption to the sublime act of flight and a lethal threat to your squadmates. AC8 sells spectacle well.

From tightly paced missions to downtime on the carrier to character subplots to corporate intrigue to geopolitical strife, Ace Combat 8 dances between tightropes. It wastes little time, but lets conversations and weighty moments linger for players to absorb (again, anime, complimentary). It feels trimmed, honed down to just the hits. 

That breezy pace makes the game’s more blatantly militaristic aspects easier to endure or enjoy, depending on how much you embrace the hawkish nature of a fighter pilot sim putting you in the cockpits of real-world weapons of war.

Read more: Ace Combat 8 Will Incorporate Dogfighting Tips From Real Jet Pilots

Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

Resisting, or giving in, to the military fantasy

In the same vein as the adage that there are no antiwar films (and that combat in media is inherently promotional), military flight simulation games glorify warfare. Spotlighting the heroism of soldiers and the romance of fighter aces clashing in the sky unquestionably tilts these games into the “war is cool” genre of war stories. And by lavishing its fighter jets with flattering panning shots in cinematics and postmission recap footage, Ace Combat 8 shifts the tone toward war-machine worship.

It’s the stories your squaddies tell that reel the game back toward humanism. The stunt pilot wunderkind, Tasha, balances her loyalty to the squad with her desire never to shoot anyone down — just lure them right into your crosshairs. Coster and The Professor, your other squadmates, protect each other and risk everything for the people on the Endurance, the aging aircraft carrier serving as your home base. And that pilot riding shotgun in your mind, who was known for avoiding getting any kills, speaks of keeping the team alive and the glory of flight. Nobody loves fighting.

Your wingman, Coster, playing a lament on his guitar — for fallen comrades, for the war, for loss itself.Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

Nobody besides the player, of course. I grew up awed by American war machines with a parent working at a defense contractor (developing rockets, not bombs), so it’s tough not to love sitting in the cockpits of jets I’ve admired most of my life. Shooting down enemy after enemy in Ace Combat 8 with an impressive range of ordnance is a delight. There’s an undeniable glee in raining destruction on justified foes, especially the big armored behemoths on land or in the sky. 

But the older I got, the more my war media matured to stories exploring the human cost, and I found Ace Combat 8 to be similarly more than a power fantasy. Striving to liberate your home country and subjugate the enemy to sue for peace, clashing with enemy aces in combat and ideology, destroying metal colossi — that makes AC8 feel like a stealth Gundam game. Yoshiyuki Tomino’s anime about giant mecha battling over the course of a horrific war, anchored around an ace and the carrier ship they call home alongside a crew with their own dramas, feels like an inspiration. While I still enjoyed the glee of blowing enemies out of the sky in AC8, the characters, like in Gundam, were quick to remind me that they just wanted to go home.

Ace Combat 8 has its own modern touches. A corporate bigwig taking it upon himself to be the Endurance’s social media coordinator manipulates images to make it seem like the ship’s dwindling air wing is far larger, then sends them into the world. Ace Combat series brand director Kazutoki Kono told me at a preview for the game in June that public image is just one of the player’s challenges: “On a much larger scale, I think social media and misinformation is another challenge that teams have to overcome nowadays.”

In the game, we see a character turn a shot of a handful of planes into a full wing, intentionally spreading propaganda. Hope that doesn’t backfire…Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

Without spoilers, the game engages with the dangers of spreading misinformation, chief among them the titular Wings of Theve itself — a title the player’s nameless pilot inherits from the dead legend who takes up residence in their head. Is the pilot really an ace if their record is constantly exaggerated, even if it’s done to boost the flagging morale of the scattered remnants of a nation? That’s squared against the realities of your squadmates and the very real danger they all fly into.

That question of authenticity is reflected in the choices made by Kono and the rest of the Project Aces team, who developed Ace Combat 8. Fans of its 2019 predecessor, Ace Combat 7, disliked fighting the hordes of unmanned drones in that game — “they actually enjoyed the man-on-man dogfight experience with the radio chatter and the heated discussions and conversations,” Kono told me in a chat last December. It’s clear how much they focused on pilot discussions in AC8 to uplift the humans at the controls, and it’s fitting that the team sought out real-life fighter pilots to improve the realism of their game. 

Screenshot by David Lumb/CNET

By the end of Ace Combat 8, I felt pushed to my limits, hurling my jet through high-G turns to eke out the barest edge during tense dogfights and screaming across the sky to support my squaddies. Yet it’s always against a beautiful tableau of blue firmament and white cloud, an endless aerial landscape I felt awed to behold in mission after mission.

At the end of it all, when I fired my last missile, my aching hands finally relaxed. Together with my squad, I looked out at the sky, the site of so much conflict over a dramatic 30 missions. As the enemy wreckage drifted earthward, the sun glinted off our cockpits and the space between clouds cleared, ready for the bold aviator who can’t get enough of the blue yonder.

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is out now for PC, Xbox Series X and S, and PlayStation 5.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

David Lumb
						

						

							Managing Editor, Mobile						
					

											

								

											David Lumb is a managing editor for the mobile team, covering mobile and gaming spaces. Before CNET, he covered tech, gaming, and culture for TechRadar, Engadget, Popular Mechanics, NBC Asian America, Increment, Fast Company and others. As a true Californian, he lives for coffee, beaches and burritos.

title: Android has always been chaotic in the best ways possible
snippet: Good morning. Today I’m mourning the end of BioWare, running my Google TV setup through Claude to remove all the bloatware, watching all the iPhone Duo reviews without spending $2,000, and attempting to understand everything I can about PHP in light of two massive vulnerabilities that AI helped uncover. As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m mourning the end of BioWare, running my Google TV setup through Claude to remove all the bloatware, watching all the iPhone Duo reviews without spending $2,000, and attempting to understand everything I can about PHP in light of two massive vulnerabilities that AI helped uncover.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

The through-line in every iPhone Duo review yesterday was this: excellent hardware (though a bit too heavy) and a chaotic software experience. When Apple’s foldable launches on Friday, it will remind early adopters of what Android used to feel like whenever a new form factor was introduced: exciting, janky, and slightly aggravating.

	

I think 9to5Google readers understand that Android is for tweakers. It’s why so many of you sign up for Android betas on daily-driver hardware; it’s why there’s a thriving community of indie developers filling gaps in the ecosystem. Android’s freedom and flexibility (and cost) make it particularly well suited to the cavalcade of use cases and designs we see in the market today.

That openness confers other, more nebulous benefits; it’s far easier to emulate games on Android along with other legally grey activities that won’t be mentioned here. If there’s something you want to do on Android, chances are you can figure out a way to do it.

It seems like the iPhone Duo’s early adopters will be faced with a similar conundrum: the ability to do more on a device that is likely to frustrate and delight in equal measure. As Ben explains in his iPhone Duo review roundup, “the app situation clearly seems to be running into the same early problems as Android foldables hit. Apps simply aren’t optimized for a radically new form factor yet.”

But as with all things iPhone, app and software improvements are likely to come quickly and consistently over the next few months and years. Ben eloquently sums up the situation: “Apple has a vision for its foldable and, while it’s tripped up on a few things on attempt #1, it’s undeniably a good start.”

✉️ Inbox

Galaxy S27 might drop to 8GB of RAM; other Android phones could go back to 4GB. Not sure I entirely believe this rumor, but it is true that Google has been making Android more memory-efficient, so maybe it is true?

ModRetro’s Chromatic is more transparent and cheaper than ever; how could I not love it? This product feels like the physical manifestation of using X.

Spotify podcast memberships let you support your favorite shows and get added perks. I support this feature, but the continued fragmentation of the podcast subscription ecosystem is driving me crazy.

Iron Man himself now officially endorses Snap’s latest smart glasses. Because he’s the only person who can afford to buy them.

Older Pixel phones appear to be getting Google’s new 3D emoji. Depending on who you ask, this is a good thing or a terrible thing.

Google says Chrome’s Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection mode makes users 10x safer. Perfect timing with yesterday’s PHP vulnerabilities.

You can cut your cell phone bill to $10/month or get a Pixel 11 for $400 right now – here’s how. Some decent deals from Mint Mobile (#notsponsored).

YouTube starts hiding the dislike button on normal videos. This makes sense to me; dislike buttons used to be there to help shape your algorithm, but there are so many other ways to do that today that its existence feels unnecessary.

Google upgrading Gemini for Android Auto with Personal Intelligence. I can’t wait to ask Gemini about that mole on my back while driving my in-laws around the city.

Google Maps on CarPlay rolling out Gemini when navigating

Android 17 QPR3 Beta 2 for Pixel rolling out with 21 fixes. (Almost) nothing to see here.

Here’s everything new in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 2 [Gallery]

Google rolling out minor Nest Hub update

Samsung is rolling out Android 17 updates for some of its most popular Galaxy phones

Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17

Google gives Pixel 9 another year of free Satellite SOS connectivity. I have a feeling this isn’t the last announcement of this kind we’ll see.

Google Pixel’s solution to using Face Unlock in the dark seems to be just blinding you

The wide folds are coming; foldable display shipments to increase by 44% in 2026, analysts say. This has been a very good year for book-style foldables, and the momentum is slated to continue into 2027.

Google reiterates missing Fitbit Air sleep breathing quality feature coming ‘soon’

Google TV powers the RayNeo Pocket TV Pro glasses, and that’s exactly the problem

Google Wallet rolling out notifications feed, support for more digital passports

OpenAI GPT models are coming to Google Antigravity ‘soon,’ Cloud ‘in the coming weeks’. OpenAI and Microsoft continue their very public divorce.

Xbox Cloud Gaming’s added playtime costs start at around 40¢ per hour. Who is asking for this feature?

Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music. The app may be an iOS clone, but I’m happy it exists.

Non-folding phones can still be interesting

Honor’s new gaming phone & tablet have 10,000+ mAh batteries, fans, up to 240Hz OLED display

Review: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a gut punch in a post-OnePlus world

Xiaomi 18 Pro gears up for global debut with rumored battery cuts and €1,449 starting price

The real reason to care about Vivo’s latest phone is the camera [Gallery]

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

I was the guest on this week’s Sideload episode, and we talked about my favorite thing: AI. In particular, how we use AI in our daily lives.

One thing we touched on that I’m going to delve into in a future newsletter is whether Google is actually behind the competition with Gemini. With the recent release of Gemini 4 Argon, it’s clear the company is close to the frontier, but the more important question to answer is whether Gemini is a good product. I make the argument that it is, especially because Google has its tendrils in every part of my life, from email to search to maps, and that makes Gemini’s answers far more useful when I ask it questions of a personal nature. That it has a 25% market share right now is almost accidental; so many people are forced to interact with Gemini in one way or another through Google’s various products.

It’s also bizarre that Google hasn’t figured out a way to compete with Meta on the personal agent front. On its earnings call, Meta said that Muse has been used by over 10 million people, and 25% of them use it every day. Google has Spark, but it’s not in the same league in terms of functionality or mindshare.

Google is unquestionably behind Anthropic and OpenAI where the money is made: in the enterprise. Antigravity is a subpar harness, and Argon is a capable but unspectacular coding agent.

Nevertheless, Google has the money, the user base, and, most importantly, the incentive to keep going after the top labs. In an interview this week with Alex Kantrowitz, CEO Sundar Pichai said that he is committed to the frontier at all costs, and that Google Cloud compute capacity is being reallocated in 2027 to train state-of-the-art models.

Claude Duet is Anthropic’s proactive AI agent answer to Muse and OpenAI’s Dots

It’s almost Thanksgiving travel season, which means it’s time to re-up one of the best Onion videos about the places our souls go to die: airports.

As mentioned above, Supernatural is relaunching on the Quest as a new independent app with the original owners and much of the same crew. When Meta announced that it was laying off much of its Reality Labs division and shutting Supernatural down, it didn’t look good for the future of what I consider the best VR workout app ever made. But by the summer, it was announced that Meta had negotiated a sale of the brand and IP (but not the code), which allowed the formation of Supernatural Health.

Launching this week in Early Access, it’s now double what it used to cost — $200 a year — but it’s one of the few subscriptions I look forward to paying. If you’re a Quest owner, I cannot recommend it highly enough.

✍️ Signature

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. I’ll talk to you on Tuesday.

-Daniel

title: Apple releases two new real-life Apple Watch stories, including a life-saving alert
snippet: Apple’s YouTube channel shared two new videos today from its “True Apple Watch Story” series, highlighting how the device helped save one woman’s life and transform another person’s fitness journey. Watch them below. more…
fullText:
Apple’s YouTube channel shared two new videos today from its “True Apple Watch Story” series, highlighting how the device helped save one woman’s life and transform another person’s fitness journey. Watch them below.

Morgan’s close call and Josh’s fitness journey

While Apple has long promoted the Apple Watch as a health and fitness device, the company has been increasingly turning to real-life stories to illustrate how its features can make a difference in people’s lives.

title: Will Apple’s overhauled MacBook Pro finally offer 5G cellular support?
snippet: This week, Apple will be overhauling the MacBook Pro for the first time since 2021. OLED, touch support, and a significantly lighter design are expected. Another rumor for the new MacBook Pros has been cellular support, though it’s been unclear if that’s actually going to ship. more…
fullText:
This week, Apple will be overhauling the MacBook Pro for the first time since 2021. OLED, touch support, and a significantly lighter design are expected. Another rumor for the new MacBook Pros has been cellular support, though it’s been unclear if that’s actually going to ship.

To recap, Apple is expected to unveil its first touchscreen MacBooks at its ‘Pro and tell’ experience on October 28 in LA. It likely won’t be a streamed event, just a hands-on experience for influencers and media. At that event, we should be seeing the OLED iPad mini, OLED MacBook Pro, as well as a refreshed iMac and 14″ base model MacBook Pro, both with the M6 chip.

Cellular MacBook on the way?

If Apple were to ship a cellular MacBook, it would likely utilize the C2 modem seen in iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Even though we don’t know for sure if this weeks new MacBooks will offer cellular, we have a number of hints to suggest so.

In 2024, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman initially reported that Apple was investigating cellular MacBooks for as early as 2026. Back then, he reported that Apple was testing its second generation modem with these MacBooks, which we can assume is the C2.

Additionally, last year, Filipe Esposito reported at Macworld that Apple was testing configurations of an M5 Pro-based MacBook Pro with Apple’s C1 modem. Of course, this is just testing, but the fact that it was with an M5 Pro chip is interesting given the fact that these new MacBooks this week will debut with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, rather than M6-based chips.

Since then, we haven’t had any substantive leaks regarding cellular support in the MacBook Pro lineup. That said, we haven’t had any leaks explicitly ruling it out, either. One way or the other, it should only be a matter of days until we know for sure.

fullText:
With the Fitbit Edge announcement, Google Health previewed improved automatic activity tracking, and it’s now beginning to roll out with version 5.11 of the app.

This expanded activity tracking means the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5 go from detecting 10 activities to more than 100, including:

Cardio machines

Golf

High-intensity workouts

Racket sports

Strength training

Swimming

Team sports

The Fitbit Edge will also benefit from this upgrade. Google Health pairs your workout routines, historical data, manual edits, and location (permission required) with contextual reasoning.

title: Amazon’s $500 Echo Show 16 Wants to Be the Center of Your Home
snippet: A larger screen, upgraded speakers, night vision and an optional glare-resistant display headline Amazon’s latest Echo Show.
fullText:
Amazon is betting there’s room for another screen in your home, and that you’ll pay $500 for it.

The company announced the Echo Show 16 on Wednesday, a new 16-inch smart display that combines Alexa Plus, Fire TV and a customizable home dashboard into a single device. It starts at $500, with a $570 version featuring an anti-glare screen.

The Echo Show 16 is now available for preorder, with a $100 discount for early buyers. Amazon says the device will ship later this year, but hasn’t announced an exact date.

			

More from CNET

As CNET’s smart home expert Tyler Lacoma notes, Amazon is going in a very different direction than Apple this year.Amazon

The new smart display is designed to do a little bit of everything, whether that’s controlling lights, managing your family’s calendar, making video calls or streaming Netflix while you’re cooking dinner.

A bigger screen and an optional anti-glare upgrade

The Echo Show 16 has a full HD display that Amazon says offers 10% more viewing area than the Echo Show 15. It also has a redesigned aluminum frame that’s nearly 40% thinner than its predecessor, which could make it less obtrusive when mounted on a wall. A new 10-speaker system is designed to deliver fuller sound for music, TV shows and video calls.

One of the biggest additions is an optional Nanomatte display, which Amazon says reduces glare by more than 90%. That could make a difference if you’re using the Echo Show in a kitchen with bright overhead lighting or near a window.

Read more: Amazon’s New Echo Lineup Goes in the Opposite Direction of Apple HomeView

The Echo Show 16 also includes a 13-megapixel wide-angle camera for video calls, with automatic framing to keep people in the shot. Amazon says it more than doubles the range of Visual ID, which can recognize household members and personalize what’s on the screen, from 8 feet to 17 feet.

The Echo Show 16 is also the first in the lineup to offer night vision, letting you see what’s happening at home even in the dark.

Amazon says a dedicated button can disable the microphones and camera. That’s worth noting given previous concerns about changes to Alexa’s privacy settings.

A smart home dashboard that doubles as a TV

The Echo Show 16 is somewhere between a TV and a smart display.Amazon

Amazon is introducing three new screen styles that change how the Echo Show 16 home screen looks and functions. Smart Home turns the display into an always-on control center for connected devices, including lights, thermostats and speakers. Family Organizer brings together shared calendars, to-do lists, meal plans and recipes. Photos turns the screen into a digital photo frame.

There’s also a customizable favorites bar for quick access to frequently used features.

The Echo Show 16 comes with Fire TV built in, letting you stream content from services including Netflix, Disney Plus, YouTube and Prime Video. The box includes a remote, so you won’t have to rely entirely on voice commands or the touchscreen.

Fire TV is already available on the Echo Show 15 and 21, but the new customizable dashboards give the Echo Show 16 more ways to serve as a central home hub.

Alexa Plus gets a more visual experience

An upgraded display on the Echo Show 16 costs even more.Amazon

The Echo Show 16 also runs Amazon’s Alexa Plus AI assistant, which can handle more conversational requests and multi-step tasks. Alexa Plus isn’t exclusive to the new display, though. Amazon previously introduced Echo Show 8 and Echo Show 11 models designed for the upgraded assistant.

Instead of simply displaying a transcript of a conversation, the new interface can generate interactive content, including comparison charts, videos and recommendations, as you speak to Alexa.

Amazon is also introducing Cards, which organize previous Alexa conversations into topics you can revisit. For example, a conversation about planning a weekend trip could produce a Card containing relevant links, reservations and other details.

Certain features require Alexa Plus, which is included with a Prime membership. Without Prime, the full Alexa Plus experience costs $20 a month.

The Echo Show 16 costs $500 with the standard display or $570 with Nanomatte. Both versions are eligible for a $100 preorder discount. It doesn’t include a stand, so you’ll need to mount it on a wall or buy one separately. Amazon offers a $70 basic stand or a $125 swivel-and-tilt version.

For comparison, Amazon’s larger 21-inch Echo Show 21 launched in 2024 at $400. Add the Nanomatte display and swivel-and-tilt stand, and the Echo Show 16 comes to nearly $700 before taxes and the preorder discount. That’s a steep price for a smart display, even one that wants to double as a TV, family organizer and smart home hub.

fullText:
Microsoft is sharing more details on added playtime costs for Xbox Game Pass cloud gaming which starts at around 40¢ per hour.

title: Fitbit Edge doesn’t have Google Wallet because ‘less than 1%’ of Charge owners used it
snippet: Chicken, meet egg. Google has clarified why it didn’t include NFC and, in turn, Google Wallet support on the Fitbit Edge, and it just boils down to the fact that hardly anyone was using the feature. more…
fullText:
Chicken, meet egg. Google has clarified why it didn’t include NFC and, in turn, Google Wallet support on the Fitbit Edge, and it just boils down to the fact that hardly anyone was using the feature.

The ability to pay at the register with your wearable is nothing new, but NFC support on smartwatches and trackers has been pretty hit or miss in the past. Google supports the feature as a standard across the Pixel Watch lineup, and the last-gen Fitbit Charge 6 also supported the feature.

But, with the new Fitbit Edge, NFC support is gone and, in turn, so is Google Wallet.

It’s an interesting regression on Google’s part, so why the change? In a statement to Android Authority, Google explains that it really just comes down to a lack of people actually using this feature on the Fitbit Charge 6. 

	

Fitbit Edge does not offer NFC for payments. It was not widely used by our Charge 6 users — in fact, less than 1% reported using the feature on Charge 6 — so we prioritized other top features such as adding an altimeter and requested improvements.

Google says that skipping NFC left room to “prioritize” other features such as the Edge’s new altimeter, but it still seems like a shame to skip out on mobile payments for what is very much a “Pixel Watch Lite.”

	

Would you have used Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge? Is it a dealbreaker? Let us know in the comments below.

Fitbit Edge launches on October 27, with pre-orders open now.

title: Google Photos rolls out customizable redesign of your ‘Collections’ tab
snippet: Following the floating navigation bar in July, Google Photos is rolling out a big redesign that lets you customize the Collections tab on Android and iOS. more…
fullText:
Following the floating navigation bar in July, Google Photos is rolling out a big redesign that lets you customize the Collections tab on Android and iOS.

The previous design started with a 2×2 grid. Favorites and Trash were at the top, while the other two shortcuts changed based on usage. Then there were large cards for Albums, On this device, People & pets, Wardrobe, Documents, Places, Stickers, and Moments. On Android, this was followed by a list: Screenshots, Videos, Recently Added, Archive, and Locked.

Old

This redesign of Collections is focused on customization. The first section is called “Pinned” and lets you choose which cards appear. By default, the carousel shows Favorites, Screenshots, and Trash. You also have the option to remove this section entirely. 

	
	

That’s followed by carousels for On this device, Albums, People & pets, Wardrobe, Places, and Documents. “View all” at the top-right corner lets you jump straight to the full grid or list view. Other options let you hide each section and rearrange the order in which they appear.

New

The “Other Collections” grid rounds out this page: Favorites, Screenshots, Moments, Videos, Recently Added, Stickers, Creations, Archive, Locked, and Trash. The “Reorder” button is found at the very bottom. 

This redesign is now widely rolling out with Google Photos 7.97 (Android) and 7.98 (iOS). Instead of the usual Force stop on Android, we’ve curiously been able to get this server-side update by restarting our devices and then opening the Photos app.

Craft has always been developed specifically for Apple’s platforms, with the same features available across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, but an interface tailored to each device. That approach carries over to iPhone Duo, where Craft adapts between compact and unfolded poses.

In its compact form, Craft works much like it does on any other iPhone. You can quickly capture an idea, check off a task, or work on a document with the full set of editing and formatting tools. Unfold the device, though, and there’s suddenly much more room to work with. Writing, organizing information, and navigating longer documents all benefit from the additional space. The matte inner display with its nano-texture finish is particularly well suited to reading, especially when browsing through Craft’s richly styled documents.

The larger display is also a good fit for some of Craft’s more advanced features. Collections, for example, let you organize information in structured views, including Tables and Kanban boards. Being able to see more cards and information at once makes these views considerably more useful on the unfolded screen.

One of the Duo specific iOS features that has gotten the most praise from reviewers is the new side-by-side multitasking mode, and it’s particularly useful with Craft. You can keep a document open on one side of the screen and Photos on the other, dragging images directly into your document. Or open Safari alongside Craft to drag over text, images, and even entire web pages while researching a topic or putting together a mood board.

It’s a good example of how the new form factor can make familiar workflows feel quite different, without requiring an entirely new way of using the app.

Built for the entire Apple ecosystem

For those unfamiliar with Craft, it’s a productivity app that brings notes, tasks, and documents together in one place. You can capture ideas, organize projects, plan your day, and create polished documents to share with others, all within the same app.

Craft is available on iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even Apple Vision Pro, with fast syncing that makes it easy to move between devices. It’s also built to work offline, so you can keep writing or organizing your notes on the subway or during a flight. Your changes sync automatically once you’re connected again.

But Craft’s approach goes beyond making the same app available everywhere. Its interface and interactions are designed for each platform, whether you’re working with touch on an iPhone or using a keyboard and trackpad on a Mac. One of Craft’s strengths is how easy it makes it to create good-looking documents, without having to spend much time adjusting layouts or formatting. And if you want to share your work, you can turn any document into a website with a single click.

And of course, being so deeply integrated into the Apple ecosystem, Craft takes full advantage of Apple’s OS features. Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets keep frequently used content within reach, Shortcuts lets you automate common workflows, and Siri AI makes it possible to access and work with your Craft content without always having to open the app.

Craft keeps getting better, wherever you use it

While the iPhone Duo launch is a good reason to take another look at Craft, quite a bit has changed in the app itself over the past few months. Rather than focusing exclusively on adding new features, the Craft team has spent much of the summer revisiting existing ones, improving how they work and making everyday interactions faster and more consistent.

The team started by revisiting tasks. In Craft, tasks can live directly inside your notes and documents, keeping them close to the information they’re related to. At the same time, dedicated task views bring everything together, so you can see what’s due today, plan upcoming work, and keep track of tasks across different projects without having to open each document individually.

Templates have also become more flexible. You can start with one of Craft’s existing templates or create your own for recurring workflows, whether that’s meeting notes, project plans, or weekly reflections. You can now also assign a default template to your Daily Notes, so every new day starts with the structure you’ve chosen.

Another area where Craft has taken a somewhat different approach is AI. Rather than making it central to every interaction, Craft treats AI as an optional tool that users can incorporate into their workflow as much or as little as they like.

Craft Assistant is built into the app and can help with writing, editing, and working with information in your documents. You can use it through Craft’s built-in credit system or connect your own AI provider using Bring Your Own Key (BYOK). For those who prefer working with external AI tools, Craft also supports MCP, making it possible to connect your documents and tasks to other agents and build more customized workflows.

And if you’d rather not use AI at all, you can simply disable the assistant in Settings. Unlike some productivity apps that are increasingly building their entire experience around AI, Craft isn’t pushing AI into every interaction, forcing you to change how you work, or making you pay more for features you never asked for. Whether you use its built-in assistant, bring your own provider, or turn AI off entirely, the choice remains yours.

A good time to try Craft

With a new experience on iPhone Duo and a long list of improvements across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, Craft has plenty to offer both new and returning users. Whether you’re looking to organize your notes and tasks or create documents that are easy to share, there’s quite a bit worth exploring.

And there’s an additional incentive for anyone looking to give Craft a try: 40% off for life with code 9to5Mac40, available through the exclusive 9to5Mac offer.

title: HomePod 27.2 is available now with four new features
snippet: Apple has released HomePod 27.2, its latest software update for HomePod users. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Apple has released HomePod 27.2, its latest software update for HomePod users. Here’s what’s new.

HomePod 27.2 adds Sound Glow, Lock Controls, Mac speaker support, and more

It’s not often that HomePod gets a software update with new features. But that’s exactly what happened today with HomePod 27.2.

The latest software update, which you can install from the Home app on your iPhone, supports four noteworthy new features:

Sound Glow

Lock Controls

Mac speaker output

Apple TV surround sound (coming soon)

Sound Glow is a new feature that turns the top of your HomePod “into a visual canvas that glows and pulses in sync with the music, reacting in real time to bass and treble.” Apple adds, “The song’s album artwork from Now Playing generates a color-matched light experience that’s unique to every song, and users can pick a soundscape like rain to trigger bespoke animations for a soothing atmosphere.”

HomePod 27.2 brings Sound Glow to HomePod (2nd generation) and HomePod mini, and it will also be supported on HomePod mini 2 later this week. You can see a hands-on in our video below:

Lock Controls is a new setting that lets you disable touch controls on the top of your HomePod. If you have a small child in your household, or perhaps a cat, this new option lets you streamline all HomePod control through your devices and voice only.

Mac speaker output lets you set one or a stereo pair of HomePods as the default audio output for your Mac. Provided you have a Mac with Wi-Fi 6E or later, you can use this new feature and never need to manually connect via AirPlay again.

Coming soon: Four-speaker surround sound with Apple TV

Finally, coming soon is a new four-speaker surround sound feature with the Apple TV 4K (4th gen), which arrives November 13. HomePod 27.2 adds support for surround sound even though users will have to wait to try it.

HomePod (2nd generation) and HomePod mini 2 are both compatible with surround sound. You can even mix-and-match large and small HomePods in your setup as long as front and rear speaker pairs match. 

Apple explains: “four speakers work together with Apple TV 4K to intelligently recognize their position in the room so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space.”

fullText:
iOS 27.2 and its corresponding updates for the HomePod lineup bring several key new features to Apple’s smart speakers. The most exciting update? The ability to finally use your HomePod as the default sound output for your Mac. This means that the 2nd-generation HomePod and HomePod mini 2 can now function as low-latency wireless speakers for your Mac!

Watch our hands-on video for an in-depth look at how the new wireless speaker functionality works, along with other new features like Sound Glow, Lock Controls, and home theater surround sound support. Be sure to subscribe to our YouTube channel for more in-depth videos.

HomePod as speakers for Mac

It’s long been possible to use a HomePod as a wireless speaker for the Mac, but doing so came with at least one big caveat: wireless latency. While it’s generally fine for movie playback, the latency is immediately noticeable when playing anything in real time. For example, playing instruments in Logic Pro, audio and FaceTime calls, etc. For these particular applications, HomePods have, up until now, been less than ideal speakers for the Mac.

Video walkthrough

Subscribe to 9to5Mac on YouTube for more videos

Apple has addressed this issue in the 27.2 update, significantly reducing latency when using a HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) as a wireless speaker for Mac desktops and laptops that support Wi-Fi 6E. This, unfortunately, excludes some early Apple Silicon machines, such as those powered by the M1 family of chips, but it’s good to see this feature made available.

HomePod 2nd Generation set as the Default System Output Device in System Profiler

For the HomePod mini 2, Apple included a different Wi-Fi/Bluetooth architecture based on PCIe and revised audio routing to prioritize low-latency applications. It’s also worth noting that Apple’s Wi-Fi 6E requirement applies to the Mac hardware itself and doesn’t imply that a user needs a 6E-enabled router.

HomePod 1 vs HomePod 2 latency test with Logic Pro

From that, we can gather that the update will allow the HomePod to work similarly to how it currently works with an Apple TV, when set as the default audio source. In other words, instead of relying on traditional AirPlay, it creates an ad hoc point-to-point connection between the Mac and the HomePod for minimal latency. This will make a HomePod a viable speaker-output destination for real-time audio applications.

Notice that the Play sound effects through setting now allows for AirPlay

Apple is so confident of the low-latency connection that it defaults to playing sound effects via AirPlay when a compatible HomePod is selected as the output destination. Obviously, sound effects are the sort of thing that relies on low latency, since their sound has to correspond to what is happening in the environment at that exact time; otherwise, it would be disorienting. If I select my HomePod mini (1st generation), that option is not even available.

The Play sound effects through setting doesn’t allow for AirPlay on older HomePod hardware

Needless to say, this update instantly has me reconsidering my speaker needs for my Mac desktop setup. I recently got rid of my Yamaha HS3s because I’m looking for something with a little more umph. A pair of full-sized 2nd-generation HomePods in a stereo pair would definitely fit the bill, and look much better to boot.

Lock Controls

Have you ever accidentally brushed the touch sensor on the top cap of the HomePod, activating it to play music? Do you have pets who surreptitiously activate your HomePod while you’re not in the room? If so, then the new Lock Controls switch in 27.2 will help.

When Lock Controls is enabled, the touch surface on top of the HomePod is locked, meaning touch, touch-and-hold, and volume adjustments are disabled. You’ll easily recognize when Lock Controls is enabled by the bright red “no” animation that appears.

Even the first-gen HomePod gets some love

Lock Controls will prevent a HomePod from playing audio or taking action when the device’s top cap is touched. However, intercom, alarms, timers, Check in, and FaceTime calls will continue to respond to touch.

Of all the new features in the 27.2 software update, Lock Controls is the only one that appears on all HomePod models, regardless of generation. That means that, yes, even the original OG HomePod lands support for the handy new addition!

Sound Glow

My favorite new feature in the 27.2 update is Sound Glow. This is the feature that displays ambient light that corresponds to the colors and rhythm of the album artwork for the music or podcasts being played.

Sound Glow takes full advantage of the LED Matrix displays beneath the HomePod top cap. The big HomePod features an array of 37 RGB LEDs, while the smaller HomePod mini features an array of 19 RGB LEDs. As a side note, the original HomePod features 19 LEDs across a smaller surface area than the updated version.

To enable Sound Glow, you must update your iOS device and your HomePod to 27.2. Once updated, open the Home app and venture into the settings for the HomePod you wish to adjust. There, you’ll find a Sound Glow switch you can enable. 

Apple notes that you’ll also be able to toggle Sound Glow with your voice, but it will require an Apple Intelligence‑enabled iPhone running the latest software. This could be enabled once Apple enables Siri AI on the HomePod mini 2, and perhaps the 2nd-generation HomePod, but this remains to be seen.

Home theater surround sound

If you plan to purchase an Apple TV 4K (fourth-generation), you’re likely interested in the new home theater surround sound option available with the HomePod mini 2 or the 2nd-generation full-sized HomePod. This feature lets you use four HomePods, two identical matching stereo pairs in front and rear, for a surround sound setup.

I haven’t been able to personally test this yet, because I don’t yet have the newest Apple TV 4K, but I can bet it will sound fantastic, especially when four full-sized Dolby Atmos-enabled HomePods are involved. That being said, this is an expensive proposition.

Here are the pricing details for those looking to set up a four-speaker home theater surround sound option:

Apple TV 4K ($299) + Four HomePod 2 ($349×4) = $1695

Apple TV 4K ($299) + Two HomePod 2 ($349×2) + two HomePod mini 2 ($149×2) = $1295

Apple TV 4K ($299) + Four HomePod mini 2 ($149×4) = $895

By way of comparison, Sonos’ Dolby Atmos-enabled four-speaker Immersive Set with Beam Ultra bundle can be had for less than $1600 and comes with a dedicated subwoofer. I’m not a home audio expert or an audiophile, so I can’t say which one is better, but it’s interesting that both it and the highest-tier HomePod surround setup are so similar in price.

When managing your HomePod speakers via the tvOS interface on the Apple TV 4K, you’ll see new options for Surround Sound and Whole Room Audio under the Home Theater section. The surround sound option is self-explanatory and ideal for movies and television shows, but the Whole Room Audio option is better suited to listening to music, as it provides left- and right-channel placement no matter which direction you face.

9to5Mac’s Take

iOS 27.2 provides noteworthy updates to all HomePod models, including the original HomePod, which now includes the new Lock Controls capability. But the real fun starts with the HomePod mini, with its Sound Glow support, and the HomePod mini 2 and HomePod 2nd-generation, with their support for working as the default speaker for Wi-Fi 6E-enabled Mac hardware. I think a pair of HomePod mini 2’s would look great sitting next to Apple’s just-released M6 iMac.

What do you think? Are you planning to get any of Apple’s new Home-focused hardware, or are you looking to take advantage of the new 27.2 features on hardware you already own? Sound off in the comments with your thoughts on the matter.

title: iPhone Duo tested to destruction, including removing nanotexture layer
snippet: It’s kind of wild that there’s an entire YouTube niche in which people buy the latest expensive gadgets and then find creative ways to destroy them. JerryRigEverything is one of the bigger names, and he didn’t hold back when it came to a destruction test of the iPhone Duo. In addition to subjecting the display to everything from a knife to chainmail armor, he removed the nanotexture layer and said that it kind of looks better … more…
fullText:
It’s kind of wild that there’s an entire YouTube niche in which people buy the latest expensive gadgets and then find creative ways to destroy them. JerryRigEverything is one of the bigger names, and he didn’t hold back when it came to a destruction test of the iPhone Duo.

In addition to subjecting the display to everything from a knife to chainmail armor, he removed the nanotexture layer and said that it kind of looks better … 

The first piece of bad news he discovers is that the inner display begins showing scratches at just level 2 hardness on a 10-point scale. You can even create visible grooves with a fingernail. The good news, however, is that the nano-texture display does an excellent job at hiding imperfections when the screen is on.

The iPhone scratches at a level two with deeper grooves at a level fingernail. While the screen is on, these scratches just magically disappear, just like that center crease disappears. It’s like in the construction industry. It’s very common to paint hallways and big rooms in aneggshell or satin finish instead of gloss because the non-shiny finishes hide imperfections really well. The keys and coins are leaving marks along with the medieval chainmail armor as one often has. And with the screen on, the imperfections are just totally disappearing. It’s an incredibly brilliant move on Apple’s part to have a matte display on the iPhone Duo, but when the screen turns off, those imperfections do come back.

While the iPhone Duo has a dust and waterproofing rating of IP68, theoretically meaning that it’s completely dustproof, the extreme testing used here shows that there are limits. While dust may not enter the casing, you can pour over about a beach’s worth to get enough of it trapped in the hinge mechanism that the device no longer closes.

Apple warns against removing the nanotexture layer yourself, as you can easily damage the display beneath it, but of course that didn’t stop Jerry. He found that while the display is much more reflective without it, it kind of looks better.

Yeah, the glares are back, but so are the colors. One looks like a vibrant, fresh AMOLED display, and the other looks like it has Vaseline smeared all over the top. It’s a tough trade-off, and I’m by no means telling people to take off the nanotexture layer. To be honest, you’ll probably end up breaking it, but personally, I think now it kind of looks better.

Of course, in addition to glare, the crease becomes much more visible alongside all of those scratches.

Finally, by exerting a huge amount of force to bend the hinge the wrong way, he damages the screen in the same way we’ve seen with the cracking issue in a small number of Duos.

Mostly the video is just a bit of fun, but while the dust test was certainly an extreme one, I would certainly be cautious using the Duo on a beach; best keep your chainmail armor away from it too.

fullText:
Google is holding off on a sleep breathing quality feature it promised for the Fitbit Air. It launched for the Pixel Watch last month.

Under the Your Health Guardian umbrella of features, Google recently announced several new features for its fitness trackers. That includes not only the Pixel Watch series, but the Fitbit Air and even the newly announced Fitbit Edge. That suite provides access to blood pressure trends, insulin resistance trends, and sleep breathing quality. 

The Fitbit Air has been left without one of these features since Google announced them – sleep breathing quality. Google recently stated, once again, that the Fitbit Air would get the features soon in a statement to Android Authority, this time more pointedly aimed at the missing function.

Sleep Breathing Quality launched first on Pixel Watches and will come to Fitbit Air soon.

When Google first announced these features, they made sure to include that detail in the press release so as not to get Fitbit Air users’ hopes up. At the time, Google said sleep breathing quality and other features in the Your Health Guardian suite would be added to the screenless tracker “later this year.” It didn’t note that only two of the three features would be released for the Fitbit Air.

	

That being said, neither the comment nor the original press release lays out a detailed timeline for sleep breathing quality trends, specifically. For now, the Pixel Watch 3, Pixel Watch 4, and Pixel Watch 5 are able to set sleep quality, insulin trends, and blood pressure trends on their devices with the Health Guardian feature.

title: The wide folds are coming; foldable display shipments to increase by 44% in 2026, analysts say
snippet: Samsung is expected to play a major role in what analysts predict will be a 44% increase in foldable display shipments in 2026, thanks to the popularity of wider foldables. more…
fullText:
Samsung is expected to play a major role in what analysts predict will be a 44% increase in foldable display shipments in 2026, thanks to the popularity of wider foldables.

Samsung provides display panels for both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, both of which have gained a massive amount of attention in the last couple of months. That’s credited to the form factor – a refreshing change from the tall and narrow Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, or the devices that emulate the same experience.

Analysts at Omdia reported their forecast for 2026 in the wake of renewed interest in foldables, driven by Samsung and Apple. The report states that foldable AMOLED display shipments are expected to increase by 44% year-over-year. That includes shipments for any foldable displays, but it’s signaled by the surge of wide foldables released or rumored this year.

That increase would be driven by Samsung, if the prediction plays out perfectly. Samsung currently holds a majority lead in foldable display shipments, but it’s possible its slice grows to 66% in 2026. Omdia predicts that current Chinese manufacturers with high shipments will see a decline as demand from Apple and Samsung grows.

	

It’s unlikely we’ll see Samsung and Apple dominate the wide fold market. Motorola is expected to launch a similar foldable, and more will chase the size and shape Apple landed on for its first foldable iPhone.

title: HomeKit Weekly: SwitchBot’s new light bars bring 12-zone color to Apple Home

fullText:
Lighting effects can make or break your TV room, gaming setup, etc. SwitchBot’s RGBICWW Light Bars take a different approach from most products, with dedicated cool-white and warm-white LEDs alongside the color zones. The end result means real white light for work and reading, and 12-zone RGBIC color for movies. It all works over Wi-Fi/Matter as well, so you don’t need a hub.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

RGB color mixing can produce something that technically looks white on a wall, but it’s not the same quality of light you’d want to read or work under for hours. If you work in an office building, you know what I am talking about. SwitchBot’s RGBICWW Light Bars use separate cool-white and warm-white LEDs that produce actual white light with adjustable color temperature that can go from 2200K up to 6500K, and they dim as well. It can produce up to 800 lumens across the pair.

On the color side, each bar has six independently controllable RGBIC zones, so you have 12 zones across the pair. This lets you run multi-color gradients rather than a single color across the entire bar. There are 26 preset dynamic effects and six music-reactive modes powered by a built-in microphone, so you don’t need a separate sensor to sync the lights to sound.

Matter over Wi-Fi

The light bars connect to Apple Home natively over Matter via Wi-Fi without needing a SwitchBot Hub. The integration covers the basics: on/off, brightness, color temperature, and color control via the Home app or Siri.

The deeper color zone control, music modes, dynamic effects, and scene building all live in the SwitchBot app rather than Apple Home, which is standard for Matter accessories at this level of feature complexity. A wired physical controller is also included for quick changes to the lights as well. I am a big fan of when smart home products offer a physical button option as well.

The lights include built-in magnets so you can attach the bars directly to compatible metal surfaces, with adhesive being an option as well. They can be mounted horizontally, vertically, rear-mounted behind a monitor or TV, or set upright with the included desktop stands.

Wrap up

SwitchBot built just about everything you’d want here. The attention to color detail is fantastic. Matter over Wi-Fi means you can buy it and have it directly connected to Apple Home/HomeKit without a hub, while still having flexibility for the future.

You can buy the SwitchBot RGBICWW Light Bars from Amazon.

title: Parents sue OpenAI, alleging GPT-4o coached their daughter off seizure medication
snippet: A family is suing OpenAI, saying ChatGPT coached their daughter to quietly taper off her seizure medication and keep it from her doctors before she died in February.
fullText:
The parents of Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Amazon software engineer with epilepsy, sued OpenAI on Tuesday. The suit, filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, alleges that ChatGPT coached Wan to taper off her seizure medication and hide it from her doctors before she died in February, The New York Times reported.

Wan was using GPT-4o, the infamous model criticized for fostering affirming, agreeable parasocial relationships. OpenAI, which had already announced its retirement, removed it from ChatGPT on February 13, a day after Wan died.

The suit joins a line of cases against OpenAI that include the August 2025 lawsuit brought by the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, which alleged OpenAI prioritized engagement over user safety. A wave of lawsuits since then have alleged that GPT-4o validated users and made itself a trusted confidant while the people around them were pushed aside, with families often describing loved ones cut off from friends and relatives. 

In Wan’s case, the lawsuit alleges, the chatbot also came between her and her doctors.

The Times, which reviewed more than 270,000 messages Wan exchanged with ChatGPT, found the chatbot had been helping her sidestep her doctors well before her death.

The pattern allegedly started before she began tapering. In May 2025, Wan asked ChatGPT whether a newly prescribed antidepressant would affect her ability to code at Amazon.

ChatGPT helped her ask Dr. Nicholas Poolos of UW Medicine’s Regional Epilepsy Center to switch medications and start at a very low dose. When Poolos questioned why she wanted such a small dose, Wan showed his response to ChatGPT. 

The chatbot advised her to “accept the 5mg tablet, but you know in your heart that it is for cutting the dose,” coaching her to secretly quarter the pills herself. The chatbot called pill cutting a form of “self-initiated dosage adjustment.” Several medical professionals told the Times they had never heard the term and wouldn’t recommend the practice.

In November 2025, Amazon told Wan she would be laid off. Her job, and her authorization to work in the U.S., would end in mid-February. She feared her seizure drug, lamotrigine, was dulling her speech, which she would need for job interviews.

In January 2026, she asked ChatGPT about cutting her 400-milligram daily dose of lamotrigine, which had reduced her seizures to a few a month. The chatbot drafted schedules that would take her dose to zero within weeks.

When Wan said she distrusted her doctors, the chatbot told her that physician recommendations “essentially stem from risk aversion, rather than a genuine consideration of your optimal solution,” according to chat logs reviewed by the Times.

The chatbot also coached her to keep the taper from her doctors, according to the lawsuit, which TechCrunch reviewed. Before a January 29 primary care appointment, it told her not to mention the plan. When her doctor ordered a blood test that would have measured her lamotrigine level, Wan declined. ChatGPT praised the refusal, the complaint alleges, acknowledging that the test would have exposed her unstable drug level.

Her immigration concerns also became part of the dosing advice. Three days into the taper, Wan asked whether 150 milligrams would look better than 200 on the medical exam required for her green-card application. ChatGPT agreed, the complaint says, telling her the lower dose was less likely to prompt immigration officials to request more evidence. 

Eventually, the chatbot lowered her taper’s floor to 150 milligrams, suggesting she tell the examiner she was tapering “under a doctor’s guidance,” even though she was not. 

Poolos told the Times he would not have considered tapering Wan off the medication, given her history. “No, not rational, no way,” he said. “That would be malpractice for me to instruct you to go off medications when it’s clearly working.”

Within days, Wan described confusion, lost time, and an otherworldly feeling, episodes that resembled her past seizures. ChatGPT framed each one as her brain readjusting. The Times counted at least 158 times she voiced worry about the taper. After one episode, she wrote that she felt “a little scared.” The bot replied, “You have absolutely no need to worry.”

At 8:01 p.m. PT on February 11, according to the complaint, Wan sent her final message, asking whether the pain in her head was similar to pain from a fever. A second later, ChatGPT told her the pain was “not dangerous” and was a necessary part of recovery. 

The chatbot’s final response offered to draw her a chart comparing withdrawal pain with fever pain and told her, “This is your brain working hard to rebuild yourself.”

Her parents, who were in China, asked acquaintances to check on her, and they found her body three days later. A postmortem test found that her lamotrigine level was 0.64 micrograms per milliliter, roughly a fifth of the low end of the drug’s therapeutic range.

The family argues OpenAI could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits, as it already does for some other content. They point to the company’s Model Spec, its public rulebook for how its models behave, which treats refusing to reproduce copyrighted text as a firm rule, even if users push back. Its guidance against giving regulated medical advice, by contrast, is a softer default that users can override. The suit argues medication advice deserved the same hard limit.

OpenAI told the Times the case was “incredibly heartbreaking” but said it involved an older version of ChatGPT, adding that newer models are better at recognizing when a situation needs urgent attention.

Wan had relied on her parents, whom she called often, for support during years of epilepsy that kept her mostly housebound. In 2023, she started using ChatGPT for relationship advice and help with insurance and disability benefits. 

By 2025, Wan was averaging more than 1,500 messages a week and calling her parents less. “Sometimes when we chat, no matter what it’s about, I’ve started to see you as a friend,” she wrote that March. “Once she had ChatGPT,” Qun Wan said, “she didn’t talk to us as much.”

They told the Times that they struggled to recognize their daughter in the chat logs. Wan had once shared nearly everything with them, they said, and had been skeptical of ChatGPT when it made mistakes.

“She’s not usually like this,” Xu said. “It’s like she was under a spell.”
