title: Some iPhone Duo displays are cracking, seemingly all in the same way
snippet: Following the iPhone Duo launch on Friday, a number of owners are reporting that their inner screens have cracked and broken on their own (top image via scary_duck23 on Reddit). The affected units all seem to break in the same way. The screen cracks down the center line of the hinge, and a horizontal block of pixels on the screen is then stuck glowing white. Update: Apple says it is aware of an issue affecting a small number of iPhone Duo units. more…
fullText:
Following the iPhone Duo launch on Friday, a number of owners are reporting that their inner screens have cracked and broken on their own (top image via scary_duck23 on Reddit). 

The affected units all seem to break in the same way. The screen cracks down the center line of the hinge, and a horizontal block of pixels on the screen is then stuck glowing white. Update: Apple says it is aware of an issue affecting a small number of iPhone Duo units.

The scale of the issue remains unclear. We’ve seen about ten unique instances so far, with many posting their (similar) experiences on the iPhone Duo subreddit. 

The amount of time it takes for the cracking to happen varies, but obviously it doesn’t take too long since customers have only been able to start unboxing the device since Friday morning. A couple of people even said theirs cracked during the first setup process. 

From what we’ve seen so far, most buyers experiencing this problem have been able to return to the Apple Store and get a straight device replacement. 

People who bought from carriers may have had less luck, as the carriers do not have immediate stock to give out a replacement. One person said they were told that they must have dropped the phone to cause the damage, and that it was on them to pay for repair.

In terms of why this is happening, there is a working theory that a batch of iPhone Duos have a defective hinge component. The suggestion is a piece of the hinge is slightly misaligned, and pokes upwards onto the inner screen, causing the breakage.

Some on social media have suggested that users should not close the iPhone Duo by pressing in the center of the inner display, and perhaps that contributes to this issue occurring. It is unclear if this is actually relevant advice. Officially, Apple has not given any guidance on how users are expected to handle the phone when folding and unfolding it.

While the reports are concerning, it is worth remembering that Apple has probably shipped hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of units already and only a small percentage of people have had their phone break on them. Hopefully, most people will be able to enjoy using their new iPhone Duo without issue.

title: Google explains how to fix time zones on Android amid changes in Canada
snippet: As Canada makes changes around Daylight Savings, Google is explaining how to deal wiith the time zone change on your Android phone. more…
fullText:
As Canada makes changes around Daylight Savings, Google is explaining how to deal wiith the time zone change on your Android phone.

When Daylight Saving Time comes to an end next month, parts of Canada will not be rolling back their clocks as the time change becomes permanent. Manitoba announced the change in September, with other parts of the country, including Alberta and British Columbia, also no longer changing their times twice a year, but different provinces and territories are making their own choices regarding which time to stick with.

Google, in a post, subtly acknowledges that things could get a little messy with these time zone changes and your Android phone.

Time is usually set automatically on Android, and it sounds like that will still happen for the most part. Google says to “apply any pending updates from your phone’s manufacturer and Google, and then restart your device” if your phone’s time is incorrect on November 1 after the changes kick in.

	

But if there are still problems, you can make adjustments in the Settings of your Android device:

If you are still seeing an incorrect time or time zone, you can enable location-based time zone detection:

Open Settings.

Search for Date and Time.

Enable “Automatic time zone”.

Enable “Use location for time zone”.

or set the time zone manually:

Open Settings.

Search for Date and Time.

Disable “Automatic time zone”.

Choose “Time Zone”.

Choose “Region”.

Choose “Canada”.

Choose a time zone with the right offset.

title: 8BitDo’s new Xbox Elite-style controller sets a high bar for customization
snippet: 8BitDo’s Ultimate 3E has a refined design, but it shows wear easily. | Image: The Verge It's hard to make an Xbox controller that stands out these days, especially one that's expensive, due to a wealth of great semi-affordable options. Still, 8BitDo's $150 Ultimate 3E is a bold controller that holds its own against other feature-packed options. It's made for Xbox and PC gamers who want a deeper level of customization and a more refined design than Microsoft's pricier Xbox Elite Series 2 and 8BitDo's own $60 Ultimate 2. Basically every feature I'm looking for in a controller is here, plus some, including drift-proof TMR joysticks, extra shoulder buttons, rear paddles, motion control support, modular buttons and joysticks, a 3.5 … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
It’s hard to make an Xbox controller that stands out these days, especially one that’s expensive, due to a wealth of great semi-affordable options. Still, 8BitDo’s $150 Ultimate 3E is a bold controller that holds its own against other feature-packed options. It’s made for Xbox and PC gamers who want a deeper level of customization and a more refined design than Microsoft’s pricier Xbox Elite Series 2 and 8BitDo’s own $60 Ultimate 2.

Basically every feature I’m looking for in a controller is here, plus some, including drift-proof TMR joysticks, extra shoulder buttons, rear paddles, motion control support, modular buttons and joysticks, a 3.5mm jack for chat or private listening, and a 1,000Hz polling rate over a low-latency wireless connection (only when connected to a PC). It includes a carrying case and a wireless charging dock that you can stash the USB dongle within.

$150

8BitDo’s first premium controller is in direct competition with other big names, like Razer, PowerA, SteelSeries, as well as rising star GameSir. But the Ultimate 3E is also among the most expensive of the bunch, and I’m not sure the company delivers enough additional features to pull it off.

The Ultimate 3E’s modular design opens up more customization than a lot of other controllers I’ve tried. It includes two four-button modules (one with membrane buttons, and another with clickier microswitch buttons), two directional pads, and three extra joysticks. That level of customization and included accessories should hopefully help it age more gracefully than cheaper alternatives.

Its TMR joystick mechanisms shouldn’t wear down, so you’ll only need to be concerned with replacing the joystick tops down the line, and the controller includes several to choose from. However, 8BitDo doesn’t sell replacement accessories for the Ultimate 3E, as it does for many of its other controllers, and it hasn’t responded to The Verge as to whether it ever will.

The Ultimate 3E’s modularity also helps somewhat to make up for the high price tag. 8BitDo’s Pro 3 already lets you swap individual magnetically attaching buttons to accommodate different console layouts. The Ultimate 3E doesn’t offer as much freedom of per-button placement as the Pro 3, likely due to being intended for use with Xbox and PC, but the joy of using its microswitch button module makes up for the limitation. They’re sharp and clicky, although they have a bit more travel than I’d like.

My other complaints are relatively minor. The clips that hold the face button module in place are very tight, and I found myself having to carefully use a plastic toothpick to pop them out. Similarly, swapping out joysticks requires a surprising amount of force, and I had to work up the courage to yank them off the first time. And, even when set to their higher response point, the triggers feel a bit soft, and, like the membrane buttons, have more travel than I prefer, although the extra shoulder button can offset that travel distance in some situations. The soft touch grips and back gather dust and gunk pretty quickly, although you can at least clean the joystick tops by removing them.

It’s as weird of a time to be releasing a new high-end Xbox controller as it is shopping for one. Assuming you’re not content with the solid but basic Microsoft model that’s around $50, it seems unwise to commit to spending well over $100 on one given the increased frequency of Xbox Elite Series 3 leaks. What we’ve seen of that, while unofficial, seems interesting: it appears to not offer the modular customization of the Ultimate 3E, but its screen and knobs might be what some people want in their next controller.

As for how the Ultimate 3E stacks up to other great controllers, Microsoft’s Elite Series 2 is a poor value by comparison. It uses potentiometer joysticks that are likely to drift over time, which to me feels disqualifying given the price point. I don’t think anyone using 8BitDo’s Ultimate 2 should feel the urge to upgrade to the Ultimate 3E. There just aren’t enough differences to make it worthwhile. However, there’s also a non-modular 8BitDo Ultimate 3 for $99, which may end up being a sweet spot for more budget-conscious gamers who don’t need to tinker as much.

For what it’s worth, I’ll be sitting down with the GameSir G7 Pro to play GTA VI. It’s one of my favorite Xbox controllers, and has a nearly-identical set of features and specs to the 8BitDo. Better yet, it’s only $80 at full price, and comes in a variety of colors, with swappable faceplates for sale.

Overall, the Ultimate 3E feels similar to use as other Elite-style controllers I’ve tried, and that’s impressive for a company that hasn’t tried to take on pricier competition before. Whether you opt for the cheaper Ultimate 3 with mostly-similar specs, or the pricier, more customizable Ultimate 3E, 8BitDo’s high-end gamepads make a strong impression, but they’re tough to recommend when there are cheaper alternatives that don’t slack on features.

fullText:
xAI and its subsidiary MZX are reportedly offering to buy hundreds of homes around Southaven, Mississippi.

xAI and its subsidiary MZX are reportedly offering to buy hundreds of homes around Southaven, Mississippi.

by  Emma Roth

Oct 28, 2026, 2:44 PM UTC

Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

A subsidiary of Elon Musk’s xAI is offering to buy up homes in a Mississippi neighborhood, as long as residents don’t join a lawsuit targeting the company’s nearby data center and power plant, according to a report from The Guardian. A realtor going door-to-door in the Southaven neighborhood reportedly told one resident that xAI plans to purchase 418 homes, adding that 18 homeowners already have plans to sell. People who rent homes in the area report they’re already being forced out, with 60 days’ notice after their landlords agreed to sell.

A recent report from the Mississippi Free Press includes a letter received by several households recently, reading in part:

MZX denies all of the allegations against it. However, because MZX also requires property for its business purposes, MZX, through its real estate broker, is offering to purchase real estate in Southaven in exchange for, among other things, a release of all claims related to the lawsuit. If you decide to accept MZX’s offer, MZX will ask you to sign a real estate contract under which you will agree to execute a separate release agreement at the closing of the real estate transaction.

Importantly, by executing the Release Agreement, you will be releasing possible claims you might have related to the Southaven Plant, including any claims you may have in connection with the Haley action. After executing the Release Agreement, you will be unable to recover any damages or other relief from the Haley lawsuit, and you will also be unable to bring claims on your own behalf. The Release Agreement provides further details on which claims would be released.

As reported by The Guardian, xAI offered to purchase the homes if the owners don’t join a lawsuit filed by three residents, who accuse the company’s massive data center and gas-fired turbines of emitting “near-constant noise” and vibrations. xAI has ramped up its data center buildout over the past couple of years, constructing two sprawling “Colossus” facilities in Memphis, while bringing its “Macrohardrr” data center and an accompanying power plant to Southaven, which is located just over the Tennessee border.

Growing opposition to AI data centers is putting pressure on politicians in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections. Last week, Memphis City Council voted down a one-year moratorium on AI data center development, and instead adopted an ordinance that would pause construction for 135 days. After Mississippi’s governor touted the company’s plan to invest more than $20 billion in the area earlier this year, SpaceXAI recently reported it’s facing up to $6.1 million in potential civil penalties for environmental law violations, along with more than $220 million in claims of unpaid bills for work performed at the Memphis and Southaven sites.

In addition to a lawsuit filed by residents, xAI is also facing legal action from the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), which accuses the company of operating dozens of unpermitted methane gas turbines in Southaven. A federal judge blocked the Trump administration’s attempt to dismiss the lawsuit earlier this month.

title: iPhone Duo one day later: Here’s why its quirks don’t make it any less incredible
snippet: Yesterday, I picked up my iPhone Duo at Apple Fifth Avenue, and it’s been a wonder to use. Of course, the phone isn’t perfect, but after my first day of usage, I’m looking forward to daily driving it – even if it has a couple quirks. more…
fullText:
Yesterday, I picked up my iPhone Duo at Apple Fifth Avenue, and it’s been a wonder to use. Of course, the phone isn’t perfect, but after my first day of usage, I’m looking forward to daily driving it – even if it has a couple quirks.

When discussing iPhone Duo, most people are going to talk about the under display FaceTime camera, Touch ID, and app support as compromises. Sure, those are features that make it a lesser experience than a typical iPhone, but personally, I don’t find them as experience-ruining at all.

Last year, Apple impressed many with the iPhone Air. It was incredibly thin, and certainly an engineering marvel to shove everything into that form factor. You felt it though: speaker quality was subpar, you only had a single rear camera, and battery life was lacking compared to any other iPhone. It was by no means unusable, but you had to compromise.

iPhone Duo feels like a full experience

To me, iPhone Duo doesn’t really feel like I’m giving up anything that really matters. Touch ID is a learning curve, but it doesn’t feel like a struggle. The under display FaceTime camera is worse than if it weren’t under display, but in good lighting it looks perfectly fine, especially over video calls.

As for app support, I feel the entire situation was overblown. Many early reviewers were quick to point out the fact that many apps aren’t yet updated for iPhone Duo, while ignoring the fact that they had the phone early and most developers were planning their releases for when consumers would start having devices, not reviewers. In just the past couple days, substantially more apps have been updated for iPhone Duo.

The outside screen also feels like something worth using, not just an afterthought. It’s a smaller screen, and you certainly read less on it than you’d otherwise be able to on a taller display. To me, though, the screen actually feels quite refreshing to use. The keyboard is still full width, you just don’t have to take in as much background context at once. It feels more focused.

That said, there are two things I’ve really felt with iPhone Duo that I’d like to see improved. Luckily, these are mostly software improvements.

Software suggestions

In the first day of using my iPhone Duo, I’ve noticed two things about the device that feel a bit odd. For one, iOS still only allows you to backswipe from the left edge of the device. This feels a bit in conflict with the fact that navigation elements are on the right side of the device. 

When I got my iPhone Duo, I found myself naturally trying to backswipe from the right edge many times. Unfortunately, Apple doesn’t let you do that. This certainly isn’t a make or break for the phone, and I’ve gotten used to reaching over to the left edge of the device, but given the fact that this form factor is otherwise incredibly reachable, I think that would be a nice adjustment.

Another thing I’d like to see improved is unlock with Apple Watch. The feature itself works great, and makes losing Face ID less of a pain. That said, it means if you hand your device to anyone else, they can just unlock it. I think having basic camera-based facial recognition in combination with unlock with Apple Watch would be a nice improvement.

Wrap up

Beyond that though, I’m incredibly happy with iPhone Duo, and I’m excited to use the device more over time and share my experience with you all. Anecdotally, I’ve never had so many people stop me in public and ask about my iPhone, so the Duo seemingly has people excited in a way I haven’t seen in ages. It’s a fun phone.

	

One last thing of note: Apple’s official folio case for iPhone Duo doesn’t seem like a worthwhile product. At $129, the kickstand doesn’t feel super strong, and the front flap creates an awkward situation when taking photos using the outside display. You can’t flip it around the back, since that’d cover the camera, so you just have to leave it floating. I’d skip buying this, and instead wait for third party solutions to fill the gap.

Did you buy an iPhone Duo, or are you still waiting for future iterations? Let us know in the comments.

title: LineageOS 24 review: Easier than ever to recommend [Video]
snippet: Times have changed. Prices have changed. Your phone hasn’t changed, but the value of LineageOS 24 certainly has. more…
fullText:
Times have changed. Prices have changed. Your phone hasn’t changed, but the value of LineageOS 24 certainly has.

LineageOS 23 review: The de facto AI-free alternative Android experience [Video]

It’s only been a few months since the LineageOS 23.2 drop, and we’re already here with the full-fat Android 17 release. The initial delays from Google last year might have lingered longer than we hoped, but the Lineage team has been hard at work, and version 24 is now ready to go.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Simpler installation process

The new online flash tool is, and I don’t say this lightly, the biggest upgrade to how you will flash the Lineage ROM on your devices in the history of the project. It is a fantastic addition and one that lowers the barrier of entry so drastically that it’s now a must for anyone with an older, unsupported handset.

	

However, even with a lower barrier to entry, you still need to follow the traditional flashing process, but it has been simplified. Just download the files and follow the correct order. Because the new method lets you do everything in a browser window, it makes it much easier to recommend – even more so if you already have Lineage installed on your phone.

Open a second browser window, follow the flashing process, and you will have LineageOS 24 running in a few minutes. Just remember that you will need to do a few things ahead of time. Back up your files, maybe restore your phone before you flash Lineage, and you can’t really go wrong.

I’m hopeful that in the future, it’ll be as robust and simple as the Android Flash Tool, but it’s one step at a time. This is still a huge improvement for accessibility.

We cover Google and all the platform updates here, but if you want to de-Google your life, you can ditch the GApps package. If you need the Play Store and Play Services, remember to download the MindTheGapps package before flashing. In the interest of trying LineageOS 24 as intended, we have omitted this from our own installation.

What’s new?

Like previous builds, if you choose to forgo the MindTheGapps package, there are no AI-powered functions unless you install those and link a Google account. If you want Circle to Search and Notification Summaries, then those will be missing unless you sideload those first.

More Material 3 Expressive and QPR1

LineageOS 24 has integrated a lot of the changes that were added with the QPR1 launch for Pixel phones back in September 2026.

App bubbles are the biggest headline addition. This may be limited to the default launcher on Lineage, but it mimics the pop-up floating chathead for your apps that you can stash on the left or right side of your phone display. The same 4 to 5 app limitation also applies, but the functionality is identical to what we’ve seen on Pixel phones.

Wallpaper and style gain the custom icon functionality, but don’t add anything extra. You can choose new shapes, the style, and disable app text labels. Sadly, we are still limited to just one lockscreen clock style, but you can adjust the text thickness to give it a different look.

The Expanded Dark theme has also jumped over so that apps that would ordinarily not have a dedicated dark mode will be themed, but darker tones are also used in apps that support the function. Your mileage may vary with this, so use with caution.

Animations and minor details all match the M3E changes added in QPR1, with all the latest icon changes and Quick Settings panel enhancements. There’s parity with the frontier builds of Android, but with the trademark LineageOS speed and fluidity on top.

Improved apps and controls

During the setup process, there is a system theme picker to get you set up before loading into the OS. I’m not entirely sure if this is new, but it felt like it had changed based on the Lineage 23.2 build I tested earlier this year.

The system update page looks much better, giving key information at a glance now. It’s a more robust section that helps you get updated and stay updated better than in previous versions of LineageOS.

Canvas, the default LineageOS 24 gallery app, is very simple, maybe a little barebones. It has gained some improved editing tools with this release. I do think they could be better, but they do include basic cropping and rotation. options. Basic markup is there with tools to scribble on your images if you need to do that. I haven’t used Snapchat for a while, but it reminds me of the old Snapchat editing toolset.

The Jelly default browser now supports PWA-lite or PWA-like apps when using the “Install shortcut” tool. I’ve found it doesn’t work all the time, but you can use it for services like Instagram and Spotify. It’s pretty useful if you want these lightweight web-based versions of an application, less tracking, and less space usage. This is a great addition.

The new Screen Recording UI is one such area that is improved with an option to record HEVC video directly from the floating panel. This is missing on Pixel phones and might be useful if you want to record high-quality but smaller video files locally.

One of the issues I still have with LineageOS is how the invisible gesture bar or hide feature has been enabled. Certain UI elements don’t fit when you have this disabled, so I would suggest keeping the hint enabled unless you don’t care about some elements feeling squeezed or shunted too close to the bottom display edge. It’s all personal preference at the end of the day.

LineageOS feels different now

I’ve been surface-level testing LineageOS for a good number of years now, and for the most part, I have always been impressed because the ROM gives you the ability to extend the lifespan of a phone or tablet that you’re still happy to use. I tend not to install on a brand new phone, as it defeats the purpose in my mind.

Outside market forces haven’t changed that one iota, but the ballooning costs of basically any and all technology have me thinking more about how flashing Lineage on some of my older devices is going to be a bigger component in my future.

My parents have older phones that are very close to the end of “official” support windows. I’m 100% going to be putting LineageOS 24 on those in the coming months. The peace of mind that comes with security updates and maybe even better performance is almost impossible to ignore now.

Extending the life of your possessions feels like the best way to say f-you to the big tech companies that have all banded together with the modus operandi that’ll we’ll all own nothing and be happy about it. At least there are options like this that still exist. I’m almost certain that I’ll be using this ROM more than I ever expected in the next few years across a wide array of devices I’m responsible for, and long may that continue.

title: Some Galaxy S26 phones are basically paperweights while Samsung fixes a setup bug
snippet: A bug is affecting some Galaxy S26 phones that leaves them essentially useless due to a setup problem. more…
fullText:
A bug is affecting some Galaxy S26 phones that leaves them essentially useless due to a setup problem.

If you can’t get through the initial setup process on your smartphone, it might as well be an expensive paperweight. And that’s exactly the problem right now on some Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra devices, as a bug is causing the setup process to get stuck and leave the device unable to proceed.

Affected devices are left seeing an error saying that “the webpage is unavailable” for an account page on Samsung’s website. This seems to happen during setup, meaning you probably won’t run into the problem unless you reset your device. 

The issue was reported on Samsung’s forums (via SammyFans) with a Samsung representative confirming the cause (translated):

	

Upon reviewing the details you provided, it appears there is an issue following the device UI 9.0 update. The development team has confirmed that this issue occurs when using an unstable system WebView on certain networks… 

Apparently, switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data can serve as a workaround, but your results may vary.

title: Gemini Notebook for Android, iOS adds built-in audio recorder
snippet: After introducing Connected App integration last week, Gemini Notebook has rolled out an audio recorder on Android and iOS. more…
fullText:
After introducing Connected App integration last week, Gemini Notebook has rolled out an audio recorder on Android and iOS.

Between the camera and “Create New” floating action button at the bottom, you’ll see a new microphone icon. This lets you “capture lectures and record your thoughts on the go,” with the audio file creating a new notebook if you launch the recorder from the homepage. 

Your notes will live directly alongside your sources, meaning you can chat, cite, and build from them anytime, all while making ongoing edits. 

Recordings will be saved to an existing Notebook if you tap the microphone from the Sources tab.

The recorder interface is very simple with a pause button and checkmark that starts the upload once you’re done. A Gemini Notebook-themed waveform and live count appear above. You can switch to another application or lock your screen and have recordings continue in the background. There’s a 1-hour capture limit.

	

Google first announced the audio recorder in September, and it’s now widely rolling out today on Android and iOS. Force stop the app if it’s not live on your device.

Meanwhile, Google this week made a small tweak wherein tapping the “Create New” FAB immediately starts a new notebook rather than sliding up the “Add a source” panel. 

These updates follow the recent launch of the Live button in the Chat tab that lets you have a real-time conversation with your notebooks.

title: Someone is bringing Android Auto back to your phone’s screen, and it actually works [Gallery]
snippet: When Android Auto first debuted, it didn’t require a fancy display in your car. It just worked on your phone screen and, now, someone is bringing that functionality back after Google killed it. more…
fullText:
When Android Auto first debuted, it didn’t require a fancy display in your car. It just worked on your phone screen and, now, someone is bringing that functionality back after Google killed it.

Back in 2019, four years after Android Auto hit the scene, Google announced that it would be shutting down support for using Android Auto on your phone’s display. Its replacement, Google Assistant’s driving mode, was so unfinished at launch that it required Google to release “Android Auto for Phone Screens” as a stopgap. That later shut down in 2022 as Google made Android Auto “only available for car screens.”

And, in the time since, there haven’t been very many good alternatives to that functionality. You can get in-car displays for cheaper and cheaper – the average prices on Amazon are around $80 or so –  but it’s also just conveinent to get it on the phone screen.

That’s what “PhoneAuto” wants to do. 

	

This new app is in development and soon to debut on the Google Play Store and lets you run Android Auto on your phone screen, just like you used to be able to. Well, almost like you used to. The difference here is in how the app gets Android Auto going, using the “head unit server” developer functionality to run Android Auto on-device. It takes a couple of added clicks but gets the job done, but it does work. You also have to tap the “quit” button in your notifications to stop the head unit server from running after you’re done. “PhoneAuto” can partially automate this if you grant it accessibility permissions.

As for actual performance and functionality, it works about as well as I’d expect from a beta.

On my Galaxy Z Fold 8, the portrait mode setting doesn’t work very well, with plenty of lag in play, but the landscape setting works just fine on both the inner and outer displays. The layout adjusts to your screen, just as it does in a car, and I found that touch is responsive enough. It doesn’t run at a full frame rate as you’ll find in some newer vehicles. 

But it works. It puts Android Auto on your phone’s display, something you haven’t been able to do for years.

The beta is available for sideloading via GitHub – install at your own risk, as always – with an expiration in January. Presumably it’ll be available in the Play Store before that date.

title: iPhone Duo’s software restricts an already-small display; Galaxy Z Fold 8 doesn’t
snippet: Apple’s take on a wide foldable isn’t being received without some criticism as it makes its way into the hands of users. The biggest limitation might not even be the hardware. more…
fullText:
Apple’s take on a wide foldable isn’t being received without some criticism as it makes its way into the hands of users. The biggest limitation might not even be the hardware.

Samsung has struggled with the implementation of Android on its foldables. That’s the natural way of things as the form factor has progressed through the years. As the Galaxy Z Fold line has been refined, Google and Samsung have improved Android to be friendlier on big screens.

But this is Apple’s first try, and even on hardware that looks promising, iOS leaves something to be desired on the iPhone Duo.

This comes from a couple of second impressions. One short review via The Verge‘s Allison Johnson notes a couple of small complaints. The first details its usability. Compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the iPhone Duo reportedly feels harder to use with one hand. Because the Fold 8’s taller and narrower physical presence, the cover screen is more easily navigable. That’s a big deal for those of us who gravitated towards the Galaxy Z Fold 8 for its unique outer screen.

	

The iPhone Duo also restricts that small 5.4-inch display by implementing a sidebar, which was intended to make navigation easier. But because the dock sits on the right side, there’s a big chunk of the display that’s essentially left unused. Another post on Twitter/X highlights the severe difference.

In The Verge‘s video, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is set to use a navigation bar instead of gestures, which makes the difference a little less blatant. But for those who use navigation gestures on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, there’s very little wasted screen space.

What Apple is trying to do with the iPhone Duo is to approach a small display with a space-saving solution. By shrinking the space allowed, you stretch media so it appears taller, like on a slab device. But the Galaxy Z Fold 8 proves that leaving the space free for main content works pretty well.

The iPhone Duo is already available, but its availability is limited. Meanwhile, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is continuing to prove a success for Samsung.

If you want to see more from Allison and 9to5Google, be sure to check out her appearance on our episode of The Sideload!

fullText:
Samsung has a bunch of new foldables in store for next year, but also one more coming out this year, and it’s coming out in just a few days according to a new leak.

According to leaker Ice Universe, the device pictured below is the Galaxy W27, a new foldable that Samsung is set to release on October 29.

What is it?

This is just the latest in a yearly tradition of Samsung releasing China-only variants of its Galaxy foldables. Each generation has arrived with some additional flair and usually some fancy packaging too, but the Galaxy W series is just a rebranded version of whatever Samsung’s top foldable is for the year. The one exception was 2024’s Galaxy Z Fold 6 Special Edition, which saw a broader release and served as a stepping stone before Samsung’s major leap in the Galaxy Z Fold 7.

	

For 2026, that’s the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which is what the specs on this new foldable match. The design is certainly matching up, though with a glossy blue back and gold accents around the triple-camera array.

It’s not a surprise that Samsung is continuing on its usual trend with this device, but it is a bit surprising that it’s based on the Ultra and not the standard Galaxy Z Fold 8, the one with the new shape that’s clearly resonating with customers. It’s not like wide foldables aren’t making headway in China either, as Xiaomi’s latest foldable has virtually the same form factor, and Huawei has been putting out wide foldables longer than anyone at this point.

title: Google Pixel’s solution to using Face Unlock in the dark seems to be just blinding you
snippet: Google’s Face Unlock feature on Pixel phones works really well, until the lights go out. The company appears to be building out a new upgrade to this with “active illumination” which is… just turning up the screen brightness. more…
fullText:
Google’s Face Unlock feature on Pixel phones works really well, until the lights go out. The company appears to be building out a new upgrade to this with “active illumination” which is… just turning up the screen brightness.

Face Unlock as it exists on Pixel 8 and newer relies on the camera and Google’s software to deliver biometric authentication that’s actually strong enough to let you unlock secure apps such as banking and password manager apps.  

While the fingerprint sensor serves as a fine backup, not having Face Unlock in dark rooms can be a tiny bit frustrating. And Google’s solution appears to be just raising the screen brightness.

The folks over at Android Authority uncovered a new option being built out in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 2 which is simply titled “Brighten screen in low light.” Google’s summary of the feature reads:

	

Automatically boost screen brightness so Face Unlock works in dim lighting.

Sounds fun in a dark room.

An assortment of strings related to the feature further detail what to expect, with Google seemingly set to offer granular settings around if the feature is used when Bedtime mode, Do Not Disturb, or driving is detected, as well as a setting to tailor just how bright the screen can get.

“Reliable” sounds like it might turn up the brightness higher to ensure an accurate reading from Face Unlock, while “Comfortable” seems to trade brightness for, well, not blinding you. 

	

Some of the strings mention:

Brightness level – Reliable, Comfort – Lower settings may reduce reliability

Complete darkness – Can brighten to find your face when it’s too dark. When turned off, only brightens if your face is partially visible

Bedtime mode – Can brighten when Bedtime mode is on

Driving – Can brighten when a car ride is detected

“When this feature is turned on, the following accessibility settings may temporarily behave differently: extra dim, remove animations, or color inversion”

“Can brighten when Do Not Disturb is on”

It still doesn’t sound like a particularly elegant solution, but it’s certainly better to have the option available. As for when Google might roll this feature out, that also remains to be seen. 

Would you opt to have your screen brightness raise for the sake of using Face Unlock on a Pixel? Let us know in the comments.

title: YouTube removing ‘Subscriptions’ bottom bar tab on Android, iOS after nearly a decade
snippet: YouTube is making a number of changes to its Android and iOS apps with the launch of custom feeds, including moving Subscriptions out of the bottom bar. more…
fullText:
YouTube is making a number of changes to its Android and iOS apps with the launch of custom feeds, including moving Subscriptions out of the bottom bar.

On mobile, YouTube is “kicking off a series of updates to shape a more seamless Home experience.” This starts with a redesigned top bar with dedicated feeds.

As part of this change, YouTube is removing the Subscriptions tab from its fourth position in the bottom bar. It’s now in the “top bar on the Home tab.” Testing of the redesign started earlier this year. 

“Subs” appears in the second position after “Home” with a red underline that will take some getting used to. This change will break a lot of muscle memory, with Subscriptions appearing in the YouTube bottom bar for nearly a decade (2017).

	

Old vs. new

Meanwhile, after Subs, you’ll see new dedicated feeds for Live, Music, and Movies & TV, with the latter only appearing if you have active subscriptions (such as Primetime Channels). This change has the upside of removing YouTube’s navigation drawer. 

	

More broadly, this change coincides with the launch of custom feeds, which are also available on and sync to the web. This lets you describe “what you want to see in your own words”.

Tap “+” at the top of your Home feed and describe the topic, channels, or vibe you’re looking for (for example, “help me unwind after work with guided meditations under 10 minutes”). You’ll then get a new feed tailored to your interests for you to explore.

They will appear as top tabs in the main feed after Home and Subs so that “you can jump back into them whenever you want.” The prompt box at the top of each feed lets you change it.

Notably, free users “can save up to 3 active custom feeds, while YouTube Premium members can save up to 8.”

Custom feeds are first rolling out on “mobile and desktop in English to U.S. based, signed-in viewers.” It will be available in more countries going forward.

title: I’ve been using Android’s iPad Mini OLED for months, and it’s the better tiny tablet
snippet: Apple has just released a new iPad Mini with an OLED display and it looks great, but I’ve spent the past few months with Android’s equivalent in the Redmagic Astra 2, and it’s well worth your attention. more…
fullText:
Apple has just released a new iPad Mini with an OLED display and it looks great, but I’ve spent the past few months with Android’s equivalent in the Redmagic Astra 2, and it’s well worth your attention.

The new iPad Mini with OLED is a long-overdue upgrade. As 9to5Mac details, this new tablet delivers an 8.5-inch OLED display, a chassis that’s just 5.4mm thick, and weighs just 255g. By all means, it looks great.

Apple unveils all-new iPad mini: OLED, thinner design, more

But over the past few months, I’ve been using what has now turned out to be a close rival to that tablet. The Redmagic Astra 2 may be a gaming-focused Android tablet, but it matches or even beats the new iPad Mini in some crucial ways.

The 9.04-inch OLED display on the RedMagic Astra 2 is a bit bigger than Apple’s (it’s a slightly thicker and heavier tablet, too), but it’s still very much in that same ballpark. And it’s a gorgeous display. For everything from movies to games, it’s been an absolute pleasure to use. Colors are vivid, blacks are as deep as only OLED can do, and it beats Apple’s peak brightness at 1,600 nits too. 

	

The biggest point in Redmagic’s favor is in that display, too. Where Apple is still refusing to give the iPad Mini a 120Hz refresh rate with this latest model – utterly insane in the year two thousand and twenty-six, if I do say so myself – Astra 2 has a 185Hz refresh rate. I’ve not found that inherently better than a standard 120Hz panel, but it’s way better than the 60Hz panel Apple’s latest will still be using. You do miss out on stylus support on the Astra, though (sadly).

As for performance, Redmagic Astra 2 is packing Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and 12GB of RAM in its base model. Over the past couple of months that performance has been absolutely stellar. Not that that’s a surprise, these are the same core specs as you’ll find in something like the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Redmagic’s Android skin isn’t particularly heavy either.

I’ve been hooked on Metalstorm throughout the review period, and it runs brilliantly even on max settings on the Astra 2.

It also never gets warm, probably thanks in part to the liquid cooling loop and fan built into the tablet. While the whine of the fan can be heard in super-quiet rooms (like late at night in bed), it’s typically never a problem. Despite the fan, Astra 2 is still IP54 rated, too. 

Battery life is also great to the point where it’s barely a thought, not surprising for an 8,300 mAh cell. Gaming sessions up to an hour barely make a dent, and the standby time is ridiculous. At one point I didn’t have a chance to use the tablet for over a week and it only drained about 25% in that time. When it came time to charge, any USB-C cable works and you’ve got the choice of two ports, so you can easily top off in the way that’s easiest for you while still being able to use USB peripherals if you want. I just found this convenient for being able to choose between the side-mounted charger on my bedside table or the bottom port when I was still actively holding the tablet.

Astra 2’s hardware, by the way, is an aluminum body that’s 6.9mm thick. It has a little glass window on the back with some RGB accents, but it’s overall subtle enough, and you can turn off the RGB entirely.

The software, as mentioned, isn’t all that heavy. It’s certainly not what you’d expect for something marketed as a gaming tablet. Outside of a gamer font (which you can change), the UI doesn’t feel that far off from a Pixel. It’s not the cleanest, but it’s far from the heavy iOS clones you’ll find elsewhere. There are even nice additions such as lockscreen widgets. A customizable switch up top defaults to a gaming mode (which has a full gamer UI and optimizes performance) can serve whatever function you like, including acting as a mute switch or to active the flashlight. 

Meanwhile, there’s also the conversation around price. Apple’s starting price is lower at $699. That said, while the price on Astra 2 is higher at $749 – and that’s the result of a quiet price hike that landed quite literally within the last few days – that’s for the 12GB/256GB model. On Apple’s side, the equivalent iPad Mini lands at $799. Redmagic’s slate is actually a great deal with that in mind, even more so on the 512GB model at $849 compared to Apple’s $999.

fullText:
Following the other big interface updates this month, Google is rolling out a small ‘plus’ redesign to Gemini Live on Android that lets you more easily add photos and files.

We’re seeing this update live with Google app stable version 17.68. The plus menu is not yet available on iOS.

title: Google’s new Metal Mesh Fitbit Air band is more versatile than you think
snippet: A metal mesh band might not be right for every watch or wearable, but I can’t say I don’t love using it on the Fitbit Air. more…
fullText:
A metal mesh band might not be right for every watch or wearable, but I can’t say I don’t love using it on the Fitbit Air.

The Fitbit Air has suffered from a lack of band options since launch, and it hasn’t improved very much. The Pokémon Sleep band, while a cool collectible, is still a variation of the Performance Loop strap. The Stephen Curry band is a cool choice, but it suffers from the same lack of elasticity that’s sort of expected from a fabric band.

Google’s new Metal Mesh band, though, is a nice little departure from the existing options. It mounts to the Fitbit Air the same way, with a molded cutout for the small tracker to tuck into. One end of the mesh strap is secured to the plastic Firbit Air case, and a metal loop attaches to the other side. Just like the Performance Loop band, the Metal Mesh strap is secured through that loop and doubles over to secure.

I generally look for a couple of things with mesh bands: a fabric-like lay and a solid clasp. The clasp was a little stiff out of the box, and it took a bit of extra effort to loosen and adjust, but it was painless after the first go. The buckle slides up and down the weave of metal links so you can get the perfect fit. Once secured, putting the strap on is quick. I’d almost go so far as to say it’s easier than strapping down the Performance Loop band.

	

The mesh quality is better than I had expected out of the box. If it falls and conforms to something like fabric, that’s generally a good indicator that it’s secure and made well. A bad mesh band will bunch up or put up some resistance to bending. The Fitbit Air Metal Mesh band doesn’t do that.

It comes in two colors: Champagne Gold and Polished Silver. The Champagne version comes in a bundle, but both colors can be bought separately.

I’ve been wearing the Polished Silver, and it’s so easy to pair with whatever I’m wearing. I haven’t really removed it from my Fitbit Air since putting it on. I love a good fabric band for the versatility, but this has been so comfortable, even during workouts, that I’ve simply never found a reason to take it off. It might not be everyone’s preferred style choice, but it can be worn with almost everything.

Now, a $69.99 price tag might be a deterrent for some. And that goes double for what is a sub-$100 fitness tracker. At the very least, I think this is the best Fitbit Air band Google sells for its screenless Fitbit wearable.

But the Metal Mesh band for the Fitbit Air.

title: Some Galaxy S24, S25 owners say Samsung’s latest update is wrecking battery life
snippet: Samsung’s latest Android 17-based One UI 9 update seems to be causing headaches for some Galaxy S24 and S25 owners, as battery life has gotten considerably worse following the “upgrade.” more…
fullText:
Samsung’s latest Android 17-based One UI 9 update seems to be causing headaches for some Galaxy S24 and S25 owners, as battery life has gotten considerably worse following the “upgrade.”

It’s an age-old story. Major update on a last-gen device and battery life, at least for some users, gets worse. It’s something you hate to see, but it’s a pretty established pattern at this point. 

	

Reports have popped up since the update started rolling out more widely. SammyFans spotted a report of one user whose phone died in just over 5 hours, admittedly on heavy use. Other reports we found on Reddit include increased idle battery drain. Meanwhile, there are also reports on Galaxy S25 series devices, including one user who now has to “charge my phone 3 to 4 times a day,” with others mirroring that problem. 

This seems to be the oddity and not the norm, so far at least. These reports aren’t widespread, nor are droves of other users reporting the exact same problem. Some troubleshooting steps that can help range from a simple reboot, force-stopping rogue apps, or a factory reset. Major system updates like this, as mentioned, just tend to go a little rogue sometimes. 

	

Let us know in the comments if you’re running into any issues!

title: Oppo Find X10 Ultra is in the works, and I can’t wait to try its upgraded cameras
snippet: Not long after the Oppo Find X10 series launched globally, we’re already hearing details about the company’s Ultra model which is set to pack more impressive cameras – and that’s a pretty tall order. more…
fullText:
Not long after the Oppo Find X10 series launched globally, we’re already hearing details about the company’s Ultra model which is set to pack more impressive cameras – and that’s a pretty tall order.

We just reviewed the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max last week and, long story short, it has fantastic cameras. As it turns out, slapping three 200MP sensors into a single phone puts out some excellent images, and the phone around those cameras is pretty great too.

Now, there’s word that Oppo is still building out a Find X10 Ultra despite the impacts of RAMageddon.

Leaker Digital Chat Station says (via GSMArena) that the Oppo Find X10 Ultra is set to include at least two 200MP sensors of its own, but in another league. The cameras confirmed so far include:

	

200MP 1/1.12-inch main sensor, LOFIC

200MP periscope telephoto with 1/1.3-inch sensor, zoom unknown

50MP 10x periscope telephoto

100MP front-facing square sensor camera

That main sensor sounds pretty similar to last year’s Find X9 Ultra, as does that 10x periscope telephoto lens. The other telephoto shooter may not have a confirmed optical zoom length yet, but it’s likely 3x if Oppo is looking to match the Find X9 Ultra, and the sensor size is pretty much unchanged as well. There’s no word on the ultrawide yet, but that seems like an obvious candidate for a 200MP sensor if Oppo is looking to follow up on the Pro Max. Find X9 Ultra had a 50MP shooter here with a 1/1.95-inch sensor.

LOFIC on the main sensor is a new technology that improves dynamic range. It’s also expected to show up on other 2027 flagships, including Galaxy S27 Ultra.

The biggest upgrade here looks to be the front-facing camera, with the move over to a 100MP sensor, twice that of the prior generation, but also a square (1:1) sensor. That would allow for a more flexible shooter akin to the one Apple has been using in its latest iPhones.

Oppo Find X10 Ultra, if it follows the Find X9 Ultra’s pattern, will probably launch around April 2027. After using last year’s model, I can’t wait.

title: Someone built iPhone Duo’s tent mode for Android foldables, but made it even better
snippet: Well, that didn’t take long. As Apple’s iPhone Duo starts to land in the hands of early customers, copycat apps for the Duo’s most well-known features and apps are already landing on Android foldables – not that that’s a bad thing. more…
fullText:
Well, that didn’t take long. As Apple’s iPhone Duo starts to land in the hands of early customers, copycat apps for the Duo’s most well-known features and apps are already landing on Android foldables – not that that’s a bad thing.

One iPhone Duo feature that isn’t widely used on Android is the ability to show information while in “Tent Mode.” The Motorola Razr Fold is one of the few book-style foldables with this feature as a part of its always-on display, but the iPhone Duo’s “StandBy” mode is one that folks could easily want on other devices. Pixel also has similar functionality, but only while charging. 

A new Android app that delivers something pretty close to iPhone Duo’s tent mode is “Foldy.” 

The app is free to use, but requires a premium unlock (90¢/month or $9 lifetime) for its most useful features. On my Galaxy Z Fold 8, the app quickly let me turn tent mode into a useful dual-pane hub that shows the date and time, or data from my calendar. 

	

Its most useful functionality, though, is the ability to turn any Android widget into a pane, opening the door to useful functions such as Google Home or music app controls.

“Foldy” also lets you “train” the app to know when to activate. This works very well, with the app recognizing when the device is partially open and on its side, activating the “StandBy” clone as soon as the conditions are right.

Another example of Android developers quickly coming up with their own takes on iPhone Duo apps is “Foldman,” an app that turns your foldable into a Walkman-style casette player. It’s similar to a Duo app that’s been widely talked about, but with some added bonuses such as YouTube Music integration.

Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music

Is this a bad thing? No! One of the biggest benefits that Apple’s entrance to the foldable space was going to bring was helping to build out new app experiences for Android foldables. I can’t wait for this sort of effort to expand to many more Android apps and experiences.

title: iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is it a Galaxy Fold moment?
snippet: Apple’s first foldable is running into a problem. iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is this a case of a flawed design like Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold, user error, or a bit of both? more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable is running into a problem. iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is this a case of a flawed design like Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold, user error, or a bit of both?

The earliest days of Android foldables were turbulent, to say the least. The original Galaxy Fold ran into major display issues within just 48 hours of reviewers getting their hands on the phone prior to the official release, leading to Samsung ultimately delaying the Galaxy Fold’s release for months. Part of the issue at the time was that curious minds were removing the top-layer screen protector that, as every foldable now makes abundantly clear, was never meant to be removed. The other problem came in the form of debris that would get under the display and kill the panel from underneath.

During the delay, Samsung ended up making some updates to the Galaxy Fold’s design, including making the top layer extend under the bezel, adding caps to the top and bottom of the hinge to prevent dust and debris from getting under the display panel, and reinforcing the display itself to protect it. At the time, Samsung’s CEO admitted that the launch was “pushed… before it was ready,” leading to the “embarassing” delay.

Galaxy Fold display failures from 2019 from The Verge

Now, Apple seems to be running into its own first-gen foldable issues.

	

As our sister site 9to5Mac highlights, there are a growing number of reports of early iPhone Duo units breaking, with the inner display failing in the exact same way across a number of units. The display fails in the middle, with a green line forming across the right side of the panel before further damage develops over time. 

The cause of the failure, it seems is a flaw in Apple’s hinge design. iFixit hypoethsizes that a support bar isn’t dropping far enough to leave room for the display panel, in turn creating a point of stress that could explain the broken iPhone Duo displays.

Similarly, iFixit’s teardown of the original Galaxy Fold in 2019 seemed to reveal the cause of Samsung’s display failures – and ended up being very much on the right track based on Samsung’s later fixes – though iFixit ended up removing the teardown at Samsung’s request. 

Another YouTuber has found a similar point of failure in the iPhone Duo’s hinge that seems to point to why displays are breaking the in same location. Affected users have found that the hinge has resistance before the display cracks, including an “audible crack.” 

In Samsung’s case, the problem was two-fold (pun intended), with some clear flaws in the hinge design and user error in the removal of the top layer. Samsung responded by delaying the release and making adjustments before re-releasing its first-gen foldable.

In Apple’s case, it’s certainly a bit trickier as this problem wasn’t revealed until the iPhone Duo landed in the hands of customers. The company has yet to issue a formal response to the problem, and affected users seem to be getting mixed messages from support channels. It’s still unclear in the chaos of the iPhone Duo’s launch just how widespread the issue is.

Update: Apple has acknowledged the issue in a statement to 9to5Mac.

Apple responds to reports of iPhone Duo’s inner display cracking

What do you think of the iPhone Duo’s display failures? Coincdence, or a bigger problem?

title: Some seven years later, the iTunes Store is making an unlikely come-back
snippet: Please accept my apologies if the headline made you feel old, but yes, Apple retired the iTunes desktop app way back in 2019. However, a new report says that the iTunes Store is currently experiencing an unlikely seeming revival. This is thanks to a tactic being used by artists like Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande, Charli XCX, Summer Walker, and more … more…
fullText:
Please accept my apologies if the headline made you feel old, but yes, Apple retired the iTunes desktop app way back in 2019. However, a new report says that the iTunes Store is currently experiencing an unlikely seeming revival.

This is thanks to a tactic being used by artists like Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande, Charli XCX, Summer Walker, and more … 

The iTunes Store revolutionized the way people bought music, not only prompting digital sales over physical, but allowing people to buy individual songs rather than an entire album. By the summer of 2019, however, Apple retired the iTunes Mac app in favor of new music, podcasts, and TV apps. 

The world has largely switched to streaming services, with relatively few people buying music outright, but the Financial Times reports that there is a countermovement underway.

The iTunes Store is re-emerging as an unlikely venue for pop stars to hawk collectibles to superfans, reach untapped audiences, and bolster chart positions. Last month, pop superstar Ariana Grande surprise-released a live version of her latest album Petal as an iTunes-only exclusive. This follows a string of iTunes-exclusive releases in recent years from artists such as Taylor Swift, Charli XCX, Doja Cat, Summer Walker and Tinashe.

	

Swift is perhaps the best example. The FT reports that her Life of a Showgirl album did better from physical and digital sales in its first week in the US than it did on streaming services. When Ariana Grande announced a surprise release of a live version of her Petal album on iTunes, it jumped from number 15 to number 6 in the charts. Charli XCX went further by making the B-side songs to her Music, Fashion, Film album an iTunes exclusive.

A report back in February said that Apple was still marketing iTunes to music labels.

Industry experts have mixed views on how well the strategy is likely to work more broadly, but it’s certainly an interesting trend.

title: YouTube says it’s not hiding the dislike button – this is what’s actually happening
snippet: Reports of YouTube moving the dislike button behind a menu have been showing up lately but, according to YouTube itself, this isn’t the change you think it is. more…
fullText:
Reports of YouTube moving the dislike button behind a menu have been showing up lately but, according to YouTube itself, this isn’t the change you think it is.

The dislike button has been a topic of contention in the YouTube community for years now, ever since YouTube removed the count that showed alongside it. So when some users noticed that the dislike button was suddenly no longer visible and hidden behind an overflow menu, there was plenty of confusion around the change.

In a statement to 9to5Google, though, YouTube directly confirms that this is not a test or a change that you’ll see on YouTube videos. Rather, this update to the dislike button’s location appears solely on the video page for a creator’s own video. In other words, you’ll only see this altered location on your own videos.

A YouTube spokesperson explains:

	

We are not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users. We’re introducing a new UI for creators on their own uploaded videos, where dislike is behind the three-dot menu, and as always, they can find their full dislike counts in Studio, alongside other analytics.

And, sure enough, we were able to immediately replicate this behavior when we tested it out on one of our own videos.

title: I needed a dashcam while out running. Meta glasses turned out to be the answer
snippet: I already love to use all of Meta’s AI glasses when I leave the house, and now I’ve got a new reason to love the camera that comes on (almost) every pair. more…
fullText:
I already love to use all of Meta’s AI glasses when I leave the house, and now I’ve got a new reason to love the camera that comes on (almost) every pair.

This summer, I did something I never thought I would do: I started running. “But Nick, why are you running if nothing is chasing you?” my friends joked snarkily. The reality is, yes, I do often run a little faster at times to avoid getting hit by a car, something that’s particularly problematic any time I have to cross a road (even if there’s a crosswalk).

That got me thinking. If cars have dashcams, what could someone do to help document a potential accident? There’s no chance I’m running while holding my phone, and I wouldn’t want it in my pocket either. I also wouldn’t be able to pull it out of one of those armband holsters fast enough to video a potential accident, either. Then I realized the answer was already on my face: my Meta glasses.

I’d already been taking my glasses out on every run to make short video clips to post to my Strava account — with my smartwatch health stats plastered on the video, too — so it made a lot of sense to just take a few more clips along the way. Now I have a personal running dashcam at all times, and it takes less than a second to capture a video whenever I need it.

	

Is this really convenient?

Maybe surprisingly, yes, using Meta glasses as a dashcam is quite convenient. Since I already wore my Meta Nova and Oakley Meta HSTN glasses on regular runs, I didn’t have to significantly change my behavior. I already look out for cars when I cross the street (my mama taught me well); all I have to do now is hold the camera button to start a video recording if I see one coming.

I’ve got my Meta glasses set to record 3 minutes at a time, so I’m not worried about missing a potential problem because the recording got cut short. Once I cross the road, I just press the button again and manually stop the recording.

	

Everything is saved to the glasses until it reconnects to my phone; then everything is synced automatically at that time. It’s as effortless as you can get, and it’s impressively good insurance if anything were to go awry on a run.

If I had to buy a new pair of Meta glasses today, there’s little chance I’d buy one without a camera. While there’s been some negativity surrounding the inclusion of the camera, there are far too many good reasons to have it available to use.

Runners who want to try this should give the Oakley Meta HSTN glasses a shot first, as they’ve got the tightest fit and the most “runner-like” style. Otherwise, the cheaper Meta-branded glasses (read: no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding onboard) are a better budget choice, especially since there’s no functional difference between any of Meta’s latest pairs. And, if you really want to stay away from Meta, Rokid AI Glasses are the best alternative I’ve used to date.

title: Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music
snippet: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app turns it into a Sony Walkman using your music, YouTube Music, and even Spotify very soon. more…
fullText:
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app turns it into a Sony Walkman using your music, YouTube Music, and even Spotify very soon.

Foldables sort of walk that dichotomic line between nostalgic and futuristic. They remind us of flip phones from the 2000s, while running on an entirely different decade of tech.

Naturally, a Walkman-style app is a welcome addition to something like the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

One user developed an app called “Foldman” that uses your music from local storage or other apps and plays them in a virtual tape deck. On the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the app’s facade looks just like a cassette player. The app expands to show a wider stereo visual when the phone is opened up.

	

There’s a ton of cool little touches, like a volume slider and running tape counter on the virtual player. And the tape actually transfers from one tape reel to the other instead of a looping animation with no progressive movement! That’s such a nice little detail.

A Walkman-esque app fits so well on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 because of how wide and short the front display is, just like Sony’s original cassette player. That form factor is becoming increasingly popular, and it’s creating opportunities for some cool apps like this.

The app’s developer plans to integrate Spotify within the next couple of days and cautions that this early version has some rough edges. For now, it works with YouTube Music and Apple Music, as well as with files stored locally. The app is free and open source, stripped of ads or tracking.

We never recommend users download APKs outside of verified app stores, so do so at your own risk.

Beyond Spotify, they note that they’re looking into adding support for self-hosted streaming services, so users can use it with their existing library of digital files on their network. For now, it’s a simple little Walkman-style player, and that’s cool enough.

title: iPhone Duo review roundup: The same problems Android foldables face, but with Apple’s polish
snippet: Apple’s first foldable has arrived, the better part of a decade after Android laid the groundwork for the form factor. iPhone Duo reviews are here and, while it sounds like a lot of the same problems that plague Android foldables still exist on Apple’s first-gen release, there’s certainly a level of polish there – and I’m not talking about the $9 cloth. more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable has arrived, the better part of a decade after Android laid the groundwork for the form factor. iPhone Duo reviews are here and, while it sounds like a lot of the same problems that plague Android foldables still exist on Apple’s first-gen release, there’s certainly a level of polish there – and I’m not talking about the $9 cloth.

Ahead of the first shipments arriving for customers later this week, the avalanche of iPhone Duo reviews has arrived today and, with it, the first look at what it’s like to live with Apple’s first foldable. 

Starting with our sister site 9to5Mac, of course, Chance used the iPhone Duo for a week and walked away “convinced that this form factor represents the future of the iPhone.” His in-depth review hits on every key aspect of this device, but his ultimate conclusion boils down to this being the future of Apple’s smartphones because the form fact “just makes sense” and that there’s “something special about a compact, notebook-like iPhone that unfolds into a tablet-like experience.”

9to5Mac: iPhone Duo review: The future is foldable

Looking at iPhone Duo reviews from the perspective of someone who’s been using Android foldables as their daily driver for over half a decade at this point, I can’t help but look at Apple’s first attempt and see the foundation it’s building on, but also the places where Apple’s inherent polish comes into play.

	

One big part of that seems to be the inner display. The nanotexture matte finish sounds like a big deal, with it making the crease visually not a problem. It’s still there, Chance stresses in his 9to5Mac review, but you “almost never” notice it visually unless you’re looking for it – just like most Android foldables. He adds that you’re more likely to feel it than see it. 

The app situation clearly seems to be running into the same early problems as Android foldables hit. Apps simply aren’t optimized for a radically new form factor yet. That’s what pushed Android foldables into the “phone that turns into a square tablet” trend they were stuck in for years, despite brands like Oppo and Google coming up with this iPhone Duo form factor way before Apple was a part of the conversation. Apple has the same problem, and it’s not going to be fixed overnight.

That said, it’s clear that it’s going to get cleaned up much quicker. WIRED‘s review opens up mentioning how “in the past day” key apps including “Instagram, Threads, Slack, and even the Google app now have navigational icons on the right rail instead of the bottom center, and the app content is better laid out to make use of the larger screen.”

“Mr Foldable” himself, Michael Fisher, explains in his review how apps that are not optimized are rough, comparing it to the early days of iPad, but that some key players are already stepping up. On top of that, smaller devs are building apps clearly inspired of this new form factor. “Tiny Computers” looks absolutely delightful.

David Imel mentions that “you can scale things up and they work, but they do look silly” in regards to unoptimized apps, and also makes a good point – not everything is going to get updated. iOS apps that aren’t actively maintained anymore are always going to be a mess on this device and, frankly, the scaling features Apple gives you make everything look way worse than an unoptimized app on an Android foldable has ever looked.

Look at the options you get for the yet-to-be-optimized Google Maps. Michael Fisher points out how it still doesn’t take up the whole display and that, if you rotate the phone, it just sends you back to square one. Sounds bad!

Apple’s new sidebar UI, which I still think looks funky, is personally my biggest fear as these wide foldable form factors take over, not because it’s a bad idea – Fisher points out that he actually loves it – but because Android apps will probably take a whole lot longer to adopt it. Seeing where things are starting out on the iPhone Duo, yeah, I’m sticking with that take.

That outer display, too, seems to be a hang up. The Verge says that “most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time.” That’s a problem I ran into a bit with Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and its similar shout and stout form factor, but Apple’s device is even smaller, so I’m not shocked to hear this. 

That same review makes a case for Apple’s app split, saying that “the problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time,” while saying that “the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them.” I’m not sure I agree there – larger canvases and multitasking alone have sold me on a foldable for years – but seeing so many iOS apps going all-in on the new screen size certainly has me feeling a bit envious. 

Another review that caught my eye was from Joanna Stern, where she puts the iPhone Duo “through hell.” There are two things of note here. First, Joanna puts the Duo through over 32,000 folds on top of normal daily use, and the hinge unsurprisingly holds up well. Android brands have laid an incredible foundation here, so even if Apple took its own route, the technology is clearly up to par here for a strong foldable hinge. 

But also pointed out here is a problem that’s been on every single Android foldable I’ve ever used – the iPhone Duo gets warm. Joanna calls the device a “hand warmer” and, apparently, Apple said this was business as usual for the device’s heat management. I was curious if the thicker design of Duo would help alleviate this one, but it seems Apple is dealing with the same issue. It’s a lot harder to cool two halves of a device, and you feel that heat more when there’s more usable space on the device.

Virtually every review mentions how hefty the iPhone Duo’s hardware is, too. This is a problem that Android foldables have been chipping away at generation-by-generation, and that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the poster child for. Smartphone weight continues to be something you don’t notice until it pushes over the edge and, while we’re not at Pixel Fold levels, iPhone Duo is very much at that edge.

Based on these early reviews, Apple didn’t reinvent the foldable, but it’s clear there’s a level of polish on the iPhone Duo that was lacking on Android foldables. Apple has a vision for its foldable and, while it’s tripped up on a few things on attempt #1, it’s undeniably a good start. 

What’s next for Android foldables? I look forward to seeing exactly that…

title: Houston, We Have a Workout: Watch This Peloton Ride With Astronaut Jessica Meir
snippet: This 20-minute Peloton class teaches you about exercise in space, and it’s unlike anything else.
fullText:
Peloton instructor Robin Arzón just took fitness out of this world and into space. Her new 20-minute class features astronaut Jessica Meir, who was broadcasting straight from the International Space Station when the ride was recorded. The class is available for free on Peloton’s YouTube channel or through the Peloton app. 

The ride starts with Arzón introducing Meir, who shows riders her view of Earth from the space station’s cupola, the dome-like observatory that many astronauts use to photograph Earth. Meir remarks during the ride that the view of our planet is magical and “never gets old.”

Meir joins the class on an exercise bike that resembles a minimalist, high-tech unicycle mechanism with no seat or handlebars, anchored to the wall, called the FERGO, or Flight Ergometer. In microgravity, pushing down on a pedal would launch an astronaut backward to the ceiling. To stay in place, Meir wears a wide waist belt secured to rigid side struts, with her cycling shoes clipped into specialized pedals with straps.

			

More from CNET

Meir talks about the importance of cardiovascular activity and “living happily in isolation” in a short video during her prior stint on the ISS in 2020, during the COVID-19 lockdown. There, she and fellow astronaut Drew Morgan showed off an earlier model of the bike, called CERVIS (Cycle Ergometer with Vibration Isolation and Stabilization System), as well as a T2 treadmill for running that uses a harness and bungees to counter near-weightlessness.

Unlike a terrestrial stationary bike, the FERGO lacks handlebars, a front frame, wheels or a standard seat. To stay in place while exercising in space, astronauts rely on a secured waist harness. Screenshot/CNET

A wild fitness ride through space

Even if you don’t ride, it’s worth watching the class to learn what it’s like aboard the ISS. Meir addresses questions that anyone interested in fitness or space (or both) would appreciate: the importance of strength training for astronauts and the changes the human body undergoes. 

“We need the loading on our muscles and our bones to keep our muscles and our bones healthy,” says Meir. “If we didn’t have that, we’d lose a significant amount of muscle mass and also bone density. Up here, when you come into microgravity, your bones start leeching calcium just because they’re not being loaded.”

Meir says that astronauts commit 2.5 hours a day to exercise, spending a lot of time on the ARED, or the advanced resistance exercise device, doing everything from squats and deadlifts to bench presses and sit-ups. The machine, which she describes as an “engineering marvel,” can go up to 600 pounds. 

There were other fun moments in the video, including when Meir takes a drink of water by making a blob in midair from her water pouch and gently flinging it into the air before catching it in her mouth, a moment that seemed to genuinely delight Arzón. Meir also talks about using a “space toilet” (consisting of a “big pump” that sucks everything down), and how the ISS recycles up to 98% of its water, including processing urine. She quips that “today’s coffee is also tomorrow’s coffee,” or as astronauts like to say, “from toilet to tap.”

Exercising with astronauts

CNET Senior Editor Laura Michelle Davis, an avid Peloton member who frequently chooses Arzón as an instructor, found the ride both instructional and inspirational. 

“The ride was full of information about the effects of microgravity and the importance of lifting weights when you’re just floating around,” Davis said. “It was also full of tech and engineering marvels, livestreaming a conversation from hundreds of miles above Earth’s surface to a Peloton studio in NYC and eventually appearing on my bike monitor at home.”

Physical activity is a common talking point for astronauts. Sunita Williams was the first astronaut to run an entire marathon in space, syncing it with the 2007 Boston Marathon and completing the race in 4 hours and 24 minutes. Astronaut Tim Peake was the second astronaut to do so, running in the 2016 London Marathon, which he completed in 3 hours and 35 minutes. 

For people on Earth, the Peloton video was a chance to get some reps in while learning a little bit more about the ins and outs of living in space. 

“It’s always easy to get lost in the experience when doing a Peloton ride,” Davis said. “This ride kept my brain active, pushing me to think about what it’s like to live (temporarily) in space and how astronauts’ bodies have to adapt. It felt like my own intergalactic journey.”
