title: Apple exploring fix for Safari’s cramped layout on the iPhone Duo’s outer display
snippet: In a new post on the WebKit blog highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, Apple’s Jen Simmons said the company is exploring ways to let websites make better use of the iPhone Duo’s outer display. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new post on the WebKit blog highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, Apple’s Jen Simmons said the company is exploring ways to let websites make better use of the iPhone Duo’s outer display. Here are the details.

Apple knows Safari isn’t making full use of iPhone Duo’s outer display

One issue singled out in multiple iPhone Duo reviews (including ours) was the fact that Safari’s right-aligned controls take up a significant portion of the outer display’s limited screen space, leaving websites with an unusually narrow area to show their content.

Here’s what Chance Miller had to say about this in his review, published earlier this week:

But the awkwardness of the iPhone’s 5.4-inch outer display shows up in Safari. The web simply isn’t optimized for this form factor. I’ll talk more about this later, but the right-aligned controls on iPhone Duo eat into the usable screen real estate in Safari especially.

[…]

I can see why Apple chose the design it did for Safari on the iPhone Duo. I don’t think overlapping the controls with the website would’ve made sense. Still, scrolling in Safari is one of the best examples of something that’s better on the inner screen.

For new iPhone Duo users who have also been frustrated by this issue, Apple’s Jen Simmons shared some good news today.

In a post highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, including how websites adapt to the iPhone Duo’s different screen sizes and folding positions, Simmons acknowledged that websites currently can’t extend behind the controls on the device’s outer display, and said Apple is exploring ways to address that limitation.

From her post:

We would like to give web designers and developers the ability to design and use that space in more creative ways. Perhaps you want to extend your header background across the full width of the display, for example. It might seem like there’s just one obvious way to make this possible, but really there are many possibilities.

Simmons went on to explain that simply using the HTML viewport meta tag with viewport-fit="cover" to extend websites behind Safari’s controls could cause problems, because many websites don’t properly account for those areas, potentially leaving important content obscured.

Instead, she invited developers to share their ideas as Apple explores a better approach:

We are investigating if there’s a better way to accomplish the same result — something more foolproof and perhaps easier for you to use. If you have ideas, we’d love to hear them. And stay tuned.

If you’re a web developer and have ideas on how Apple could address this limitation, you can read the full WebKit post for details on how to share your feedback.

title: Gemini Notebook now available as Connected App for deeper integration
snippet: Gemini Notebooks are already available in the Gemini app side panel, but Google is now adding deeper Connected App integration. more…
fullText:
Gemini Notebooks are already available in the Gemini app side panel, but Google is now adding deeper Connected App integration.

As a Connected App like Google Workspace or Photos, @Gemini Notebook “allows you to manage and query notebooks directly within your chats using natural language.”

This integration lets you retrieve information from existing notebooks, create new ones, add sources, and save notes. The Gemini app will “automatically detect when to use the Gemini Notebook Connected App for relevant prompts.” For example: 

Create, edit, or delete a notebook (“Create a Gemini Notebook about solar farm market trends”)

Add, update, or delete sources in a notebook (“Add a copy of this chat to my notebook about Bio 101 course”)

List notebooks and their sources (“Show me a list of all the sources in my notebook about US National Parks”)

Answer questions using context from your notebook (“What do my Gemini Notebooks say about butterfly migration?”)

This integration is available now and has been enabled by “default for users globally, except in the European Economic Area, where it will be OFF by default.”

	

@Gemini Notebook is “available to all Google Workspace customers, Workspace Individual subscribers, and users with personal Google accounts.”

title: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 still feels refreshing in all the best ways [Video]
snippet: With the iPhone Duo now a thing, it puts the Z Fold 8 in an even more interesting position. Yes, it’s an attempt by Samsung to get ahead of the curve, but, in truth, it really has worked. more…
fullText:
With the iPhone Duo now a thing, it puts the Z Fold 8 in an even more interesting position. Yes, it’s an attempt by Samsung to get ahead of the curve, but, in truth, it really has worked.

So now that Apple is here, there is no doubt that the Z Fold 8 faces its fiercest competition, but to me, it highlights so much of what Samsung did so well with. I do not think that the Duo renders Samsung’s design obsolete. Apple’s entry into the market only sharpens the contrast between these competing design philosophies. It even underscores precisely why I’ve come to prefer Samsung’s passport-size footprint.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

I’m not even sure it’s Samsung that has pushed the form factor forward too drastically. 

	

I’m not alone in realizing that, for a lot of people, passport size makes the most sense. The outer screen is just enough of a taster without being too big; switch to the inner if you want a little more playroom is immediately obvious from the get-go. Everything feels reachable on the outer screen, while the inner screen is the big canvas for all other content.

Sure, the Z Fold 8’s outer display isn’t perfect. Some UI elements can feel cramped; you will need to adjust how tall your keyboard is, but it isn’t as rigid as what Apple seems to have done on the Duo. That’s a good thing as the flexibility of Android just suits the multi-sized form factor.

The thing is, you’re going to fall into one of two categories. Those of us who want a smaller, tablet-y shape, or a phone that happens to open to run more apps side-by-side.

Objectively, the “traditional” folding phone size and shape will be more useful in basically most scenarios. Subjectively, I don’t really care about those as much. I’m in the privileged position of having a decent selection of handsets on deck at any one time to test-drive, and those satisfy something else entirely.

As I was saying, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has arguably been the most interesting and, now, my most-used phone throughout 2026. Of course, that is alongside the Pixel 10 Pro in early 2026 and now the 11 Pro. It has my backup SIM permanently tucked inside. Backup because I don’t get distracted as much with so many notifications, but that SIM has free roaming, making it my favorite travel companion…and my Balatro on-the-go handheld.

Every week, I’ll download a few movies and TV shows, like a sort of digital “prepper,” so I can be on a flight or a train and just know I have something to watch on a screen that tucks neatly into my side bag or jacket pocket. It is a mini tablet that weighs less than most other phones. You barely notice it. As I keep repeating: It feels so fresh.

One thing I have to appreciate about the slimline design is that I haven’t babied it; I have put a screen protector on the outer display for basic protection. It has handled a couple of days at the beach as an e-reader, and as yet, it’s accrued just one minor ding on the top frame edge, no major damage. That’s a good thing to me, as I haven’t found a Z Fold 8 case I really love yet. It’s super light and razor-thin; I never want to dull that sheen. It’s like the perfect realization of what the Flip ought to have been and likely won’t ever become.

I’ve seen a lot of complaints online about the inner display being both glossy and having a very visible crease. It’s not something I’ve dwelled on too much. They’re not big problems for me, in all honesty. I would like to see some enhancements, but it is what it is. That sounds like me handwaving away those complaints. I’m in agreement that we need to see Samsung make changes, especially now that Apple has a foldable with an almost-invisible crease and, frankly, a beautiful anti-reflective coating. Samsung is the undoubted king of displays, so we need more from the company in the future. That said, I still love the inner screen once I’m zipping around the system.

Against my better judgment, I have recently tried a “matte” screen protector from Amazon. So far, so good, but it’s nowhere near as matte as advertised. It does dull reflections, but I’m still on the lookout for something that might mimic the iPhone Duo display to see what the fuss is about. The screen protector I picked up does make a difference by reducing smears and fingerprints, but you might not want to put something on the inner screen, as Samsung doesn’t entirely recommend it, and it can be a bubbly mess if you get it wrong. It took me a few attempts to get the fit just right.

Back to the software: It helps that One UI is basically the perfect starting base for a foldable, and I think that is what has sealed the deal in a lot of ways. I’m a steadfast Material 3 Expressive fan, and while it’s still my preferred way to experience Android, One UI has continued to evolve in ways that Google likely doesn’t care about. I liked the Pixel 9 Pro Fold and 10 Pro Fold, but they felt less playful than the Fold 8 because I don’t think that Google does quite enough to truly optimize for the non-standard dual UI experience.

Sure, you need to use some of the Home Up and Good Lock plugins, but it opens up the door to vast customization that most other brands can’t really compete with. I like being able to make even minor adjustments to things like the volume UI or icon layout. Don’t get it twisted, I’m not doing insane things on my Z Fold 8, but even the minor adjustability holds weight on a device that acts as both a phone and a tablet, depending on which screen you’re about to use. Even the bottom dock is better placed than what I can glean from how Apple has added a right-sided dock on the iPhone Duo, while the volume buttons are just sensibly placed on the Fold, too.

The “big” apps are all well optimized. Instagram on the inner screen is awesome because you can see the comments and your feed in one instance. It feels like a tablet UI, probably because it is. There’s a little jank when running two apps side-by-side, but nothing that a little resizing can’t fix. I stick to two apps, as adding that third makes things cramped.

To expand on that a little further, I am actually really happy that Apple is about to wade into the foldable waters. For starters, it means we’ll hopefully get even better application support from the biggest developers. 

From launch, the Z Fold 8 has had a few apps tuned to take better advantage of the smaller outer display, and while they’re not quite perfect, at least some work has gone into them. I’m really excited about the prospect of more apps being refined, and with so many big corps effectively relying on AI for faster ports, surely the next few years might prove to be a golden age for foldables. The truth is that most Android apps already scale reasonably well, so no major issues. The odd UI section might feel cramped here and there, but I don’t think I can complain too much.

Now, for a few of the weakest portions of the Z Fold 8 that can’t really be glossed over too much.

Yes, the camera is not quite as good as the best in the business. 

At its worst, it’s purely functional, and ordinarily that would be a complete dealbreaker, but I’m at an age where a sharp, clear photo that does the job is more than good enough. Maybe I’m a glutton for this kind of punishment, as I find myself working around the limitations to get acceptable shots. It’s not ideal, but foldables compromise here more than any other devices, save the affordable options. So in that regard, you are well aware of that going in anyway.

It probably helps that I haven’t given up the Pixel 11 Pro as my mainstay photography phone. Not everyone can do that, so it’s arguably the biggest complaint you can have on the Z Fold 8 in my opinion – save the price, of course.

Battery life is another one of the weakest points. It will withstand most people’s usage patterns, but nobody should spend nearly £2,000 or $2,000 to have the Fold 8 not reach the end of the day. I think we all know by now that folding phones are going to compromise in this one area quite substantially. Luckily, it does manage to do movies and TV shows more than enough justice with longevity. I have watched multiple episodes of Widow’s Bay back-to-back on a couple of flights recently, and it doesn’t sap the battery all that much so long as you put the thing in flight mode.

In fact, I have been impressed when you’re not glued to the screen. It isn’t amazing, but I wouldn’t call the battery bad on the Z Fold 8 by any stretch. I have a super-slim Anker power bank in my bag at all times, so on a long-haul flight I’d just plug it in to be sure I can keep enjoying that lovely inner display. I can charge while watching and then just unplug, ready to go at my destination.

Now for the brief section where I will unashamedly just say some truly out-of-touch things (although this entire post is debatably out of touch): this is the most special phone I have used this year. Not even because it’s the best at any one thing. It could simply be a symptom of so much being “samey” or feeling so incremental in Western markets right now. This is a luxury product, and that instantly marks it down in most people’s eyes.

If Apple, the tastemakers of the non-tech buying public, are ready to give this form factor a real college try, then Samsung has made the right decision. The Z Fold 8 is easily the most elegant Android phone I’ve used in a while. I’m smitten with it. It’s something I want to unfold, fondle, and play with. What’s somewhat annoying is that, because I’ve enjoyed it so much, I’m giving in to a phone addiction I have tried so hard to curb over the past 18 months, since there is something refreshing here that is hard to truly quantify.

I’ll try my best to quantify it, though.

In my mind, there’s a Swiss Army Knife feel about the Z Fold 8 that no other phone has had for me for a long time. A tablet, gaming screen, reading screen, webpage dream all rolled into a passport package that respects my pockets – or the space in my sidebag. 

It’s a really versatile gadget that isn’t just a siloed phone, and that is probably why it’s resonating with so many people – myself very much included.

If you’re bored with your current phone and ready to switch, the Z Fold 8 might be worth taking a look at, provided you can stomach the price.

I’ll drop some of the best deals currently available on the Z Fold 8 down below, but expect to see discounts and sales soon, now that Apple has entered the fray and we’re on the cusp of Black Friday sales in the coming weeks.

So now that Apple is here, there is no doubt that the Z Fold 8 faces its fiercest competition, but to me, it highlights so much of what Samsung did so well with. I do not think that the Duo renders Samsung’s design obsolete. Apple’s entry into the market only sharpens the contrast between these competing design philosophies. title: MagSafe Monday: TESSAN’s 6-in-1 charging station replaces every charger on your desk
snippet: One hub/cord to rule them all is a goal most people have for their desk. The TESSAN Magic 65W Charging Station is built to collapse your pile of cords into a single compact hub, and a couple of its design details are really handy as well if you like to hide your power cables. Let’s take a look at it. more…
fullText:
One hub/cord to rule them all is a goal most people have for their desk. The TESSAN Magic 65W Charging Station is built to collapse your pile of cords into a single compact hub, and a couple of its design details are really handy as well if you like to hide your power cables. Let’s take a look at it.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

The Magic 65-watt brings six charging options into one base: two traditional AC outlets, two USB-C ports, a USB-A port, and a MagSafe wireless charging stand. The main USB-C port delivers up to 65 watts, which is enough to fast-charge a MacBook Air or an iPad, so you can leave your power brick in your bag. Keep in mind that 65 watts is the max from that single port, so expect the power to be shared if/when you have several devices plugged in at the same time.

The two AC outlets are a nice touch here for a desk setup, since an external monitor, lamp, or speaker can plug right into the base station. This is super handy if you are trying to snake cables under your desk, etc.

A magnetic stand with a single trade-off

The MagSafe wireless charger doubles as a stand that tilts up to 65 degrees, which puts your iPhone at a nice angle for FaceTime, watching a YouTube Short, or Standby mode. It also handles AirPods charging at 5 watts.

Here’s the trade-off worth knowing before you buy: this isn’t Qi2 certified, so iPhone wireless charging tops out at 7.5W. If you’ve moved to a Qi2 or Qi2.2 charger elsewhere in your house, this will feel slow compared to them. For a quick top-off, it’ll be slow, but for an all-day or overnight charge, it’ll be fine.

The Apple Watch charger, which is built into the station and can be pulled out for use or tucked back in when you don’t need it. I personally don’t wear an Apple Watch, so I love when it’s optional. That’s one less cable dangling off the side of your desk if you do wear one, though 

One of my favorite details is that it has a 0.32-inch ultra-thin flat plug with a 45-degree right-angle design, so the hub can sit flush behind the desk without sticking out from the wall. It also leaves the other outlet on the wall plate open.

Wrap up

The TESSAN Magic 65W Charging Station isn’t the fastest MagSafe charger you can buy, and it doesn’t try to be. What it does well is consolidate your charging and power for your desk, including your external monitor, lamp, and other Apple gear.

You can buy the TESSAN Magic 65W Charging Station from Amazon.

title: Fitbit Edge Review: Too much and too little at the same time
snippet: When Google announced the Fitbit Edge, my assumption was that it would be a great in-between for the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air. In a way, that’s true, but this isn’t the product I thought it was – it’s just a new, slightly better Fitbit that leaves me wanting more. more…
fullText:
When Google announced the Fitbit Edge, my assumption was that it would be a great in-between for the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air. In a way, that’s true, but this isn’t the product I thought it was – it’s just a new, slightly better Fitbit that leaves me wanting more.

At $180, the Fitbit Edge is closer to the lower end of Google’s wearable lineup than it is a proper middle ground. It’s closer to a Fitbit Air with a screen than it is a “Pixel Watch Lite.”

That starts in the software, which has been updated to visually resemble this new era of Google Health. The main “Clock” face brings about a new assortment of options that draw inspiration from the Pixel Watch. There’s a baker’s dozen of these faces available, with the “Modular” series being my personal favorite. 

These support complications just like on Pixel Watch, allowing you to quickly see various data points around fitness tracking, or even pull in weather conditions. It’s not nearly as flexible as Pixel Watch – personal favorite weather data points such as UV index and sunset are missing, for example – but it’s a good glanceable bit of information, something the Air completely lacks.

	

What’s more frustrating than anything about the faces is that it’s all powered through the same basic and clunky interface that Fitbit trackers used for years. It’s incredibly slow and clearly not native to the Health app. It gets the job and works better than I remember it being the last time I used a Fitbit tracker, but it’s still a poor experience compared to the rest of the software.

Using the software on the tracker, you’ve got notifications below the clock and Quick Settings above, with Tiles to either side. It’s very familiar for Pixel Watch owners, and it’s visually a huge upgrade over the Fitbit Charge series. Google’s Material design language is felt throughout and everything is very clean with smooth animations. You can only customize the Tiles via the Google Health app on your phone (through the same clunky UI as faces), with the overwhelming majority being health/fitness-related, with weather and media controls also mixed in. This was the place I found the Edge most useful over the Air. Where tracking a workout on Fitbit Air either required relying on automatic tracking or starting it on your phone, Edge’s display lets you quickly jump into the workout of your choice. The “Quick Start” tile is helpful here, saving your most recent workouts. This was the biggest upgrade I found over the Fitbit Air outside of just, well, having the time shown on the thing on my wrist.

On the note of smartphone notifications, this is where I felt the biggest lacking from Pixel Watch. Inherently, a tiny display like this isn’t going to be as capable or useful as a full smartwatch, but the experience is just not very good. Notification previews can’t scroll through more than the first couple of words from a notification unless you tap “Open,” and incoming notifications also stack in the UI. The side button is used to go “back” in the software, but each notification is treated as its own layer, at least up until a certain point. When several notifications come in at once, this is a dreadful experience. They’re also not working consistently. I couldn’t get notifications working for much of the review period and, after many troubleshooting attempts, they just randomly started working on their own. Jordan Floyd on our video team says he still hasn’t managed to get them up and running. Google tells us that an upcoming Health app update will address notification issues.

Don’t get me wrong, notifications on Fitbit Edge are a huge step forward beyond the Fitbit Charge series, but they’re still not good either.

Apps on Fitbit Edge include the usual Health suite, as well as an alarm clock, Google Maps, a stopwatch, a timer, and a very basic weather app. The Google Maps experience leverages the Edge’s GPS but is really just a mirror of walking directions from your phone. You can’t start navigation on the Edge. The Weather app gets the job done, but it’s incredibly basic and lacks information I’d want outdoors such as UV exposure.

The biggest missing app here is Google Wallet, as the Edge lacks NFC support. Google says hardly anyone used it on the last generation, but I disagree with that logic – the Charge had many other downsides that prevented it from being appealing to those who also wanted Wallet, where the Edge is much closer to a fully usable smartwatch. Lack of mobile payment support is ultimately the biggest dealbreaker for me.

On hardware, Fitbit Edge is very much just an Air with a display.

Compared to a Pixel Watch, wearing the Fitbit Edge feels like wearing nothing. It’s very lightweight and, in turn, comfortable. Google’s bands from Pixel Watch also make the jump here, with the included Active band being just as comfortable as it is on Pixel Watch – though it is a hair magnet, picking up dog hairs far more readily than my Pixel Watch bands ever have. Google also sent over the Magnet Band which, personally, I’m not a fan of. It’s uncomfortable when on and, at least for my wrist, is difficult to put on. The two halves of the band are the same length and, if you sit in between the small and large sizes, it’s hard to get it on since there’s nothing for the band to grip on to until it’s fully connected. I’d rather go for something like the default Fitbit Air band here.

I was disappointed to see a problem from the Charge era make its way to Fitbit Edge. One multiple occasions through the review period, my Edge just fell off my wrist because the band connector failed. This happened once overnight and once as I was just walking through my home. It’s a disconcerting feeling, and was the eventual deal-breaker for me on Fitbit Charge 5 – I nearly lost the tracker while snowboarding, and it was shelved not long after that trip. Fitbit Edge doesn’t seem nearly as prone to this issue, but having it happen twice, with official bands, during my two-week review period is not exactly faith-instilling. A good habit would be to pull on the band to ensure it’s fully seated, but I’d argue this shouldn’t be necessary if you hear it click into place.

The connector here works well for switching bands quickly, but I would have appreciated seeing something new from Google here, especially seeing as it’s not like Fitbit Edge can use bands from the Charge series anyhow.

I reviewed the “Fog” setup with a silver tracker, and I do really appreciate that this splits the difference between a smartwatch and tracker in the looks department. With the right band, this is totally passable in a dressy situation.

Easily my favorite hardware decision here is the physical button on the side of Fitbit Edge. Prior Fitbit tracker toyed with a haptic button that was not at all a true button replacement. Not once was I fooled into thinking I was pressing a button, and the illusion only broke further when trying to turn the device on from an off state. It wasn’t the worst idea in theory, but a physical button is so much more satisfying. Fitbit Edge’s button isn’t the most premium, but it’s very much good enough and a welcome change on Google’s part.

But of course, none of that matters without fitness tracking to back it up.

I wore Fitbit Edge for the better part of two weeks – and only needed to charge once during that time, battery life is great, at least with the always-on display disabled – and used it mainly for tracking treadmill and strength workouts, with stats roughly lining up with the baselines set by Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5. You should never take stats from a fitness tracker as absolute truth, but the Edge is certainly more than capable enough at helping you to establish trends and work towards goals.

That’s all done in conjunction with the Google Health app, which I’ve been using with the Air and Pixel Watch for months at this point. Google Health, like virtually any AI tool, is inherently not perfect, but I’ve certainly come to appreciate it. The app opens to a simple overview of your cardio, steps, and other key data sets before diving into insights from the “Coach” – i.e. Gemini – around your trends. You can speak with “Coach” in natural language to set your goals around fitness, weight loss, strength training, or any number of things.

In that way, this is not the classic Fitbit of years past. This is very much a new experience built on the foundation of the old Fitbit, and one that you’ll either probably come to love, or come to hate. Personally, the experience has really grown on me. The app’s daily notifications summarizing my movement are a good last-minute way to get in some extra movement on quiet days, or a good morale boost when I was particularly active. As a workout novice, it’s also great for helping me figure out strength training workouts that suit my day. If I have more time or want to focus on a specific area, the “Coach” is pretty easy to work with in tailoring your workout. 

It’s not perfect, of course. It still tends to randomly get automatic workouts wrong, but for my needs it has done quite well. As we learned in our Fitbit Air review, though, your results may vary – at the end of the day, this is an AI-powered experience we’re talking about and, as Google itself repeatedly stresses, “AI may make mistakes.”

Of course, you’ll need to pay Google for a monthly subscription to use most of those features. Without Google Health Premium, the Edge is still capable, though, with support for basic step, heart rate, and workout tracking. Health Premium is bundled into the AI Pro plan which also includes Google Home Premium.

As a side note, kudos to Google for continuing on with the ability to use Fitbit Edge in tandem with other Google wearables in the Health app. While I used the Edge almost exclusively over the testing period, there were a couple of short Pixel Watch 5 stints mixed in for specific needs, and the Health app does a great job and syncing everything across not just the app, but each device. That said, it’s a less useful feature on the Edge. Where using a Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch in tandem is a fantastic experience, there’s almost no scenario I can imagine where it makes sense to have a Fitbit Edge alongside either one of those devices.

And therein lies my main takeaway with the Fitbit Edge.

This middle-ground wearable exists in a weird little bubble. It’s not a Pixel Watch, not even close, actually, but it’s also not a Fitbit Air.

I’ve found myself coming to appreciate the Fitbit Air as a way to find some reprieve from a connected lifestyle, with the Pixel Watch then stepping in when I need that connection or the added functionality of apps. The Fitbit Edge gets everything right on the fitness tracking side, but it also doesn’t really feel like it knows what it wants to be. It’s too connected and complex compared to the Air, but also too restricted compared to the Pixel Watch. It’s somehow both too much and too little at the same time.

That said, the Fitbit Edge might just need to be thought of in a specific light – it’s just not something new. This is a Fitbit tracker, an updated version of the same Fitbit tracker that millions have known and loved for years. In that light, it’s rather good, it just depends on whether or not you’ve moved beyond that point. I think I have.

Fitbit Edge starts shipping on October 27.

Fitbit Edge at Google Store

Fitbit Edge at Amazon

Fitbit Edge at Best Buy

					

Inherently a good and capable fitness tracker, Google’s new Fitbit Edge sits in a place where it’s somehow managing to bring too much and too little to the table at the same time.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Excellent battery life

											

Much better software than Fitbit Edge

											

Google Health is a good fitness coach

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Limited functionality outside of fitness

											

Clunky clock face selector

											

Paid subscription to unlock most features

title: Google Health 5.11 rolling out with Fitbit Air Health Guardian, improved sleep tracking, & more
snippet: Google Health 5.11 is rolling out this week as a rather big update for Fitbit trackers and the Pixel Watch. more…
fullText:
Google Health 5.11 is rolling out this week as a rather big update for Fitbit trackers and the Pixel Watch.

The Improved Automatic Activity Tracking is available now for the Fitbit Air, Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5, with the Fitbit Edge getting the capabilities at launch on October 27.

Tracks more activities: We expanded the number of activities your Fitbit tracker or Pixel Watch can detect from 10 to up to 100, including strength training, swimming, and racket and team sports.

Uses more context: Powered by contextual reasoning, we now factor in more context — including your workout routines, historical data, manual edits — to deliver nearly 2x more accurate detections and cut missed workouts by more than half.2

Logs workouts automatically: Workouts that meet your minimum duration threshold (15 minutes by default) with a sustained elevated heart rate are automatically logged, and a summary is sent to the Google Health app, typically within 30 minutes.

Learns your patterns: When you confirm or edit an activity, you’re improving a feature that learns your unique patterns and uses them to refine its predictions.

The Fitbit Air and Edge are getting two Health Guardian features if you’re a Google Health Premium subscriber. You can set up blood pressure and insulin resistance trends now, with the first report available at the beginning of November.

Blood pressure trends, which allow you to track blood pressure patterns before they can put strain on your heart, will be available in the Health Guardian section of the Health tab if you’ve worn your Fitbit Air for 5 or more consecutive days in October.

Insulin resistance trends, which track monthly shifts in your metabolic health, will be available if you’ve worn your watch for 7 or more days and nights in October.

Blood glucose is now “Glucose” throughout the Google Health app with updated charts and graphs. Additionally:

	

Custom time-in-range goals: You can now set specific time-in-range goals for glucose data from connected continuous glucose monitors. To set a goal, go to the Metabolic section of the Health tab, tap Glucose, open Settings, and select Set goal.

Faster syncing with Lingo by Abbott (US only): You can now connect Lingo by Abbott directly to the Google Health app so your glucose data syncs faster — displaying in the Google Health app within 30 minutes of a reading. If you have a Google Health Premium membership, Google Health Coach³ can also answer questions about your glucose trends. To connect, tap your profile icon in the Google Health app and select Partner Apps.³

Finally, there’s improved Sleep Tracking across wake detection and nap editing:

More accurate awake detection: We’ve improved our sleep tracking to better factor in your steps data so that we can more accurately track short awakenings, like getting up to use the bathroom. 

Easier nap editing: You’re always in control of your sleep data. If a nap ever shows up that doesn’t match your day, you can now easily remove it directly from your nap card.

Version 5.11 is available on iOS and still rolling out for Android users.

title: Apple publishes iPhone Duo support documents covering hinge, Touch ID, cases, more
snippet: Apple is publishing a slew of support documents today corresponding with the launch of iPhone Duo, as it does for every iPhone launch. The support documents cover Touch on iPhone Duo, troubleshooting hinge issues, and much more. more…
fullText:
Apple is publishing a slew of support documents today corresponding with the launch of iPhone Duo, as it does for every iPhone launch. The support documents cover Touch on iPhone Duo, troubleshooting hinge issues, and much more.

In one support document, Apple outlines what to do if you’re having any of the following problems with the hinge on your iPhone Duo:

Device won’t open or close completely

Unexpected noise while opening or closing the device

Loose hinge

Bent or broken hinge

Enclosure damage that affects hinge operation

Apple also has a support document outlining the software accommodations for using a case on iPhone Duo that partially covers the left edge of the outer display:

After applying iPhone Duo Case, a message appears on the display of iPhone Duo with the option to adjust the screen size to accommodate for the case. Follow the onscreen instructions to make the changes.

You can adjust the screen at any time: open Settings and tap Display & Brightness. Turn on Shift Left Edge. This shifts the outer display content to accommodate the front portion of the case.

title: Apple’s website has fun new easter egg: a fully interactive iPod
snippet: Today is the 25th anniversary of Apple unveiling the first iPod. And as discovered by Kian on X, the company’s website now has a fun new iPod easter egg. more…
fullText:
Today is the 25th anniversary of Apple unveiling the first iPod. And as discovered by Kian on X, the company’s website now has a fun new iPod easter egg.

Apple marks 25th anniversary of iPod introduction with new easter egg

The iPod is 25 years old and has long been discontinued, but it lives on in the hearts of many fans.

And now, a digital version lives on as an easter egg on Apple’s website too.

If you visit music.apple.com and add a path that doesn’t exist, the ‘Page Not Found’ screen now features a fully interactive original iPod model.

You can try it out by visiting music.apple.com/ipod or any other nonexistent version of the domain.

The iPod on the page lets you click through using its buttons to find pre-installed songs. The scroll wheel even works by clicking and dragging it around.

Apple first introduced the iPod on October 23, 2001, and the music you’ll find on this interactive model comes from artists that were popular at the time.

	

You can select songs to play 90-second previews right there in the web interface.

It’s a fun easter egg to play around with and celebrate the iPod’s legacy.

title: Shrinking season 4 just got exciting release timing update
snippet: Shrinking just aired season 3 earlier this year, but all signs point to a refreshingly quick return, as one of the show’s stars just confirmed season 4 is officially done filming. more…
fullText:
Shrinking just aired season 3 earlier this year, but all signs point to a refreshingly quick return, as one of the show’s stars just confirmed season 4 is officially done filming.

Shrinking season 4 has finished filming ahead of expected early 2027 premiere

TV’s streaming era has brought a lot of advantages over linear TV, but undoubtedly one drawback is that shows tend to have much longer waits between seasons.

Traditional broadcast television usually schedules shows to premiere in the fall and run through the spring, then return after a short summer break for a new season in the fall.

In streaming, viewers are shocked when a show comes back after only a year.

Apple TV has slowly been getting better at this. Slow Horses is the best example, but another recent one is Your Friends & Neighbors. And we’re seeing signs of other series getting quicker turnarounds between seasons, including Shrinking.

Shrinking aired its season 3 finale this April, and by May we heard that filming on season 4 was about to start.

Now Jessica Williams, the star who plays Gaby, has confirmed that season 4 has officially wrapped production. This means the series will almost certainly return in early 2027.

On a show like Shrinking, post-production is a much quicker process than with series that are heavy on CGI and other special effects. So we could see Shrinking season 4 premiere in late January, exactly one year after season 3 debuted. 

More conservatively, the show returning by spring 2027 seems a safe bet.

You can watch Shrinking seasons 1-3 here on Apple TV.

title: Trying an iPhone Duo at the Apple Store? Don’t Leave Without Testing These 6 Things
snippet: The iPhone Duo is now in Apple stores, even if most buyers won’t get theirs until January. Here’s how to make the most of a hands-on demo.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo went on sale Oct. 23, and anyone who didn’t preorder the device on Oct. 16 is now looking at a delivery date in late January. Apple stores have demo units on display, though, so you can spend time with Apple’s first foldable long before one could arrive at your door. A few minutes is enough to check what a spec sheet can’t tell you: how the hinge feels, how visible the crease is, how the phone sits in your hand folded and unfolded and how apps behave when you open it up. Here are six things worth testing on your next visit to an Apple store.

Here’s what should you be looking to do when you actually pick up the iPhone Duo. Because while the foldable phone might have a fun, unique design, you may run into things you’re unfamiliar with — or even dislike — when using it day to day. You’ll want to be confident that the device is a good fit for your needs before plunking down $2,000 or more for the folding phone.

We’re going to break down a series of things you should check out when you finally get to play with it at the Apple Store.

			

More from CNET

The opening animation

The iPhone Duo’s unfolding animation is neat.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

When the Duo was first revealed, Apple showed off a very intriguing animation when you unfold the it. Leave it to Apple to make a function so simple look so aesthetically pleasing. 

It’ll likely be the first thing you notice when you first open the Duo up to see its inner display, and there’s a good chance you’ll continue to open and close the device to see the effect. At the end of the day, it’s a parlor trick — but a very good one, adding delight to ordinary use. 

Admire the matte screen and minimal crease

Foldables, well, fold, and they typically come with creases. The Duo has a minimal crease and a matte display, both of which are wins. That said, even the most noticeable creases tend to “disappear” when you’re viewing content — you just get used to them while watching TV shows or YouTube videos. The Duo’s minimal crease should be even easier to ignore.

And let’s not forget about the matte screen. Several foldables ship with glossy displays, but the iPhone Duo will have a less shiny screen, making it easier to view in bright environments without annoying reflections.

Apple demonstrated how Netflix will be optimized for the Duo’s displays — from the cover screen to the main display to this half-open configuration with controls on the bottom half. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Watch videos

The outer passport-size display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for watching videos because of how it crops content to fit the new aspect ratio. Still, it’s handy to prop the phone up in tent mode and watch shows that way. You also have a large inner display to work with, but because of its passport-style design, even that screen has a different aspect ratio than the widescreen format people are used to on regular phones, so there will likely be some letterboxing in videos.

Try watching something with the phone set up in both ways to see if it bothers you enough to dissuade you from buying the phone.

Again, it’s not an iPhone Duo issue but a foldable phone issue — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the same size and format. The aspect ratio of the display might crop the top or sides of videos, so it’s worth trying out if you expect to watch a lot of full-screen videos. 

The Duo supports drag-and-drop functionality when multitasking.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

See how apps act in different orientations

Like videos, apps on foldables can sometimes appear a little weird, and that could be the case with the iPhone Duo‘s aspect ratio. When you’re at the Apple Store, check out how your most-used apps look and feel on both the inner and outer displays, and make sure you rotate the inner screen to see how apps behave in this orientation, too — that wide screen could be great for watching vertical videos or scrolling through social media. 

If some apps, such as Instagram, look a little different or are wonky, it’ll hopefully be just a matter of time until the developers make an update that optimizes the experience for this new design. Keep in mind that you can also have two apps open onscreen at once, making it easier to multitask.

Explore the cameras

The iPhone Duo has two 48-megapixel rear cameras.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

If you want the best camera experience on an iPhone right now, you should be looking at the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, but that doesn’t make the Duo a slouch for shooting photos, either. 

Yes, the Duo is missing a third camera (telephoto), and if that’s important to you, then you probably shouldn’t even be considering Apple’s foldable. But still, if you’re going to shell out this much money for a new phone, test out those cameras — even if it’s in a controlled environment like an Apple Store.

Another thing to check out before you pull the trigger is your selfie shots with this new phone. There are two main ways to do this: with the phone closed, holding it up in the regular way you’d take a selfie using the outer screen’s 12-megapixel front-facing camera, or with the inner display open and shooting with the twin 48-megapixel rear cameras (the outer screen will show a preview of the shot).

There’s also a front-facing camera underneath the inner display, which is mostly for video calls — and which we suspect would produce the least-impressive shots from the device. Try them all and see what you think of the pics. And since you’re at an Apple Store, make sure you delete them afterward.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Try typing on both displays

The odd but interesting aspect ratio of the front display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for typing, so it’s best to do a typing test when you have one in front of you. While the inner display will provide a roomier and more comfortable typing experience, you probably won’t want to have to open up the Duo every time you want to shoot off a quick text to someone. If you have bigger hands, typing on the front screen could be a bit of a nightmare. 

Typing one-handed on the small cover screen should be manageable, but try it out to see if it works for you. Some may find it convenient; others may find it cumbersome.

And when you’re typing on the inner display, try the Duo in both portrait and landscape orientations to see which feels better. You can also choose between a split keyboard and larger keys. It’s thoughtful of Apple to offer options that let you tailor the typing experience to your preferences, but you may find that none of them suit your style.

title: This clever USB-C cable doubles as a stand for your phone [Gallery]
snippet: One of my favorite things about the rise of magnetic wireless charging has been the prevalence of chargers that hold my phone upright on my nightstand. But, when travelling, that tends to be a bit more cumbersome, or at least a little more expensive. The folks over at Statik have come up with a clever solution, a USB-C cable that has a kickstand for your phone with no added bulk. more…
fullText:
One of my favorite things about the rise of magnetic wireless charging has been the prevalence of chargers that hold my phone upright on my nightstand. But, when travelling, that tends to be a bit more cumbersome, or at least a little more expensive. The folks over at Statik have come up with a clever solution, a USB-C cable that has a kickstand for your phone with no added bulk.

The Statik PowerStand is a pretty straightforward idea. A USB-C cable that has a kickstand at the end. Simple idea, plenty of room for a poor implementation, but this is really quite well done.

One end of the braided cable is a standard USB-C plug, while the other side has a right-angle plug on an extended base. Admittedly, it feels a little clunky on its own, but it makes sense once you plug in a device. The USB-C plug is angled slightly and on a raised base, easily connecting to your phone even if it’s in a case. Two foldable “feet” swivel out and let you either stand the phone up vertically – perfect for charging – or put it horizontally for something like watching a video.

The implementation here is really quite good. The vertical orientation is surprisingly well-balanced and I never felt like my phone would just fall over. Don’t get me wrong, a shove will definitely let it fall over, but it’s not just going to fall on its own. The spacing for cases also worked perfectly on a Nomad case I have for my iPhone or my wife’s Peak Design Pixel 10 Pro case, but the plug didn’t feel insecure on my case-less Pixel as a result. 

	

The foldable “feet” also slot into place quickly and lock into position pretty well. It’s a good balance between strength and easily being able to adjust the position.

This isn’t some shoddy cable either. It’s a 240W cable with USB 2.0 data transfer speeds and is measures 6.6ft long too. The braided texture feels sturdy and it’s nice that the design still lets you use the kickstand end with a laptop. 

	

The Statik PowerStand easily earned a permanent spot in my travel bag, and for $20, it’s definitely worth your consideration too. 

Statik, by the way, is the same brand that makes those magnetic cables that are easier to store because they attach to themselves. Another cable in its lineup that the company sent out with the PowerStand is the PowerPivot Pro, an all-in-one cable with USB-C and USB-A ends on one side with a USB-C tip on the other end that can rotate in any direction. I’m not quite as keen on the functionality there, but Statik points out the one place it might come in handy – the car. For Android Auto/CarPlay, I could see this one being good for having your phone perhaps stuffed into a tight spot. It’d been even better, though, if both ends of the cable had these rotating tips. If nothing else, Statik says this is 20x tougher than a normal cable, and I believe it after feeling it in person.

PowerPivot Pro is also available for $20.

title: Google TV powers the RayNeo Pocket TV Pro glasses, and that’s exactly the problem
snippet: The Google TV platform is amazing on the big screen, but its limitations make it more frustrating than it should be on the mobile RayNeo Pocket TV Pro. more…
fullText:
The Google TV platform is amazing on the big screen, but its limitations make it more frustrating than it should be on the mobile RayNeo Pocket TV Pro.

Google TV is the best thing that’s possibly ever happened to my TV. I switched to the Google TV Streamer about a year ago after my Roku streamer broke down, and I haven’t looked back. So when I got the chance to try the Google TV-powered RayNeo Pocket TV Pro — a TV remote-like device that hooks up to RayNeo smart glasses and even has 12-bit Dolby Vision support — I was ecstatic. This would be a dream come true on my next flight!

The setup was dead easy, and I was on the Play Store downloading all my favorite streaming apps within a minute. I loaded Netflix, found a few shows to keep me occupied for a few hours in an uncomfortable coach airplane seat, and went to hit that shiny red download button. Alas, the download button didn’t exist.

Surely this was a mistake? Maybe that show just didn’t support offline downloads. I found another one and ran into the same problem. Turns out, the Netflix app on the Google TV platform doesn’t support offline downloads. Major bummer, but that’s alright; I’ve got like half a dozen other streaming apps to choose from.

	

Unfortunately, every single streaming app doesn’t support offline downloads on the Google TV platform. Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, HBO, even YouTube all don’t support offline downloads on the entire Google TV platform. I was befuddled. How could this have possibly slipped past testing, let alone into a final product? The RayNeo Pocket TV Pro went back into the box, and there it sat for over a week until I returned from my trip.

The personal pocket TV for your home

Essentially, I was in the “you’re holding it wrong” kind of scenario with this product, but I imagine I won’t be the last person who thought you could use it like this. For me, this is now a useless product, because there’s never a time when I want to sit and watch something without my family. For someone else, however, this might be the actual dream product I originally thought it was, just for a very different individual.

Let’s say you love watching live sports, but your family outvoted you and is now on the main TV. A quick tap of the “Live TV” button on the remote will take you to the Google FreePlay app, where you can find a metric ton of free live content, including plenty of games to catch. You could also load up Hulu, ESPN, Amazon, or whatever other service might be airing the actual game you want to watch, too, since this is a full Google TV device.

Or, hey, maybe you want to catch up on the latest Knives Out movie, but you’ve got little kids who probably would have nightmares if they watched a murder mystery before bed. Slap on a pair of RayNeo GT smart glasses, plug it into the RayNeo Pocket TV Pro, and you’re watching Knives Out in a perfectly private cinema while your kids watch Moana for the 400th time.

RayNeo Pocket TV Pro at Amazon

RayNeo GT smart glasses at Amazon

All this is aided by a piece of hardware that feels absolutely perfect. The remote looks virtually identical to any Google TV streamer you can buy and weighs 208g, which is the same weight as the average smartphone. The large, circular directional pad makes navigation a breeze, and the prominent microphone button calls up Gemini instantly, so you can find anything in a few seconds.

Even the battery life is quite good, lasting around 5 hours or so on a single charge. It’s got a dedicated USB-C port on the bottom for smart glasses output, and a separate port for charging, so you could plug this into an outlet or any portable battery (like this Anker Prime one) and keep it going for even longer. There’s even a microSD card port on the side for people who own digital copies of movies or TV shows, which would have fixed my problem if I did.

And as a full-fledged Google TV device, this one has every single app you know and love from your actual TV in your house. There’s quite literally no difference in the software; it’s just ultra-private now that it works on a pair of smart glasses. The only way it would get better is, of course, if the same streaming apps that allow offline downloads on phones worked here.

title: Review: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a gut punch in a post-OnePlus world
snippet: OnePlus is dead. The enthusiast-focused brand turned Oppo for the rest of the world was shuttered, ironically only for the rest of the world, earlier this year and its memory loomed large over my past few weeks using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max. For as great is this phone is, it’s a sad reminder that phones like these are going to be lacking in some parts of the world going forward, and that’s a crying shame. more…
fullText:
OnePlus is dead. The enthusiast-focused brand turned Oppo for the rest of the world was shuttered, ironically only for the rest of the world, earlier this year and its memory loomed large over my past few weeks using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max. For as great is this phone is, it’s a sad reminder that phones like these are going to be lacking in some parts of the world going forward, and that’s a crying shame.

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a beast on paper, though not quite the Find X9 Ultra I fell head over heels for earlier this year. To quickly summarize what you’re getting here (specifically for the EU variant):

6.78-inch AMOLED display (144Hz, LTPO, 3,600 nits peak brightness, 3,840Hz PWM)

MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro

12GB RAM

512GB UFS 4.1

7,150 mAh battery

80W wired/50W wireless charging (no Qi2 magnets)

Ultrasonic fingerprint sensor + camera-based face unlock

Cameras: 200MP main, 200MP 13mm ultrawide, 200MP 70mm (3x optical) telephoto, 50MP front-facing

By basically every measurement, a true flagship. The cameras, as mentioned, aren’t quite at the level of the Find X9 Ultra, but it’s still impressive to see three 200MP sensors on board here.

And those cameras perform very well.

	

Oppo touts killer video from this setup, including 4K/60fps, 4K/120fps, and 8K/30fps from every rear-facing lens, as well as improvements to HDR and stabilization. These can certainly go a long way in creator spaces, and I was impressed at the quality even in more casual use cases. Oppo worked with Instagram, for example, to improve uploads from the Find X10 series and the results speak for themselves.

As per usual, I found myself mostly using the camera here for stills, and I still find myself loving the experience of shooting on an Oppo flagship. Shots are generally crisp and clean, and the app is very easy to use despite all of the options it builds in. Compared to the Ultra I last used, I found myself wishing the telephoto lens had more range, as the 3x optical zoom quickly felt its limits kicking in. Oppo supports up to 120x hybrid zoom, but the quality falls off long before that, and the AI-powered enhancements really struggle to bridge the gap on anything beyond 10x. I wish the company had just used a 5x lens here rather than 3x. Still, most shots I took were excellent, and that 3x lens is the best shooter of the bunch, producing excellent natural bokeh in its shots. The 200MP sensor and Oppo’s software go a long way in ensuring that anything in the 3x-8x range, give or take, comes out at full quality. Not to mention the color processing – it nailed the colors of an absolutely gorgeous sunset I captured a couple of weeks ago. My Pixel would never. 

Adding on Oppo’s 10x teleconverter takes the whole thing up a notch, with levels of natural bokeh that just aren’t achievable on a smartphone otherwise. It’s not as crisp as a “real” camera with the same lens setup, but the results are often stunning.

View full-size samples on Google Photos.

But, outside of the camera, how does the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max hold up?

Frankly, very well. 

The hardware itself is fantastic. I reviewed the “Lumos White” trim which is a tiny bit lighter than others, but it’s still a fairly hefty phone regardless. I don’t mind the weight, though, when a phone is delivering powerful camera hardware. The same goes for the camera bump which pops out of the back quite a ways. I do loathe that Oppo opted for this dual-size camera bump where the main square off to the left is taller than the secondary bump used to house the flash and color-focused camera lens. It results in a phone that rocks back and forth on a table when not in a case, despite such an obvious solution sitting right there. It’s annoying, but I do appreciate other touches here such as the knurling around the camera lens and the splash of orange from the Hasselblad partnership (though the little ridge picks up dust like crazy).

This is where I’ll throw in the mention that I found myself using Oppo’s carbon fiber case throughout my entire review period, not because I felt the phone needed a case, but because this is yet another Android flagship forgoing built-in Qi2 magnets. The excuses are just lame at this point, especially with Oppo pretty heavily investing in magnetic accessories. It’s getting old saying this in every review, but I’m going to keep bringing it up until it becomes the standard it should be.

The frame has power and volume buttons off to the right side and they’re as tactile and satisfying as ever, while a “Snap Key” on the opposite side is a blatant clone of Apple’s Action Button, right down to the UI used to customize it. Still, I appreciate the shortcut and use it for the flashlight/torch, but I wish Oppo would take this up a notch with single-press and double-press actions, rather than limiting it solely to the long-press that Apple uses. While we’re on that topic, I wish Oppo would finally adopt the double-press power button gesture for activating the camera in global markets. This phone has a great camera, but lacking this shortcut is an absolute pain.

The display is gorgeous, as you’d expect from any modern flagship, and the built-in screen protector has held up remarkably well over roughly a month of use. 

As for the software, ColorOS 17 very much leans into the whole Liquid Glass clone trend, and I’m not a fan. But, to Oppo’s credit, you can easily tone down the transparency to get a much more visually pleasing design. That won’t change the Apple copycat looks found throughout system apps, but it makes it a much better experience on the whole.

I’ve always been more of a fan of Pixel UI and even One UI over most Chinese Android skins, but ColorOS has grown on me. Once you get over the initial learning curve, it’s a very user-friendly experience in so many ineffable ways. It’s truly hard to describe why it’s a pleasure to use, but I find myself with fewer complaints. They’re still there, of course – just a couple of quick hitters: Notification icons disappear inconsistently, the lockscreen shows notifications on top of the fingerprint icon which leads to a lot of misclicks, etc – but I find myself overall still feeling comfortable using ColorOS nowadays.

And it runs smooth just as promised. That’s probably in part thanks to Oppo’s continued optimizations, but also the MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro under the hood. The chip also stays cool. I threw everything from high-GPS use, 90°F days to video exports and more at this phone, and it never once warmed up even a little bit. Are we missing out without these MediaTek flagships in the States? Maybe!

Finally, let’s talk battery life.

The silicon-carbon battery here gives the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max a whopping 7,150 mAh battery in the EU, and the endurance rocks. This is not quite a 2-day phone in my testing thus far, but even heavy days won’t kill it. Whether I was running hotspots, editing videos, or playing games, Find X10 Pro Max never ended a day below 30%. I would imagine the 8,000 mAh version found in other regional variants pushes it over the edge of being a 2-day phone, but the point is you’ll be happy with this battery life. And, thanks to speedy SuperVOOC and USB-C PD charging on board, I never found myself needing to plug this phone in overnight. It almost acts like a smartwatch – a quick charge while I’m in the shower and getting ready for the day has been plenty to keep it topped off most of the time.

And after using all of that for a few weeks, I’m just about as sad about the situation surrounding this phone as I have been happy in using it.

The end of OnePlus means that Oppo phones like this one simply aren’t coming Stateside anymore. Of course, OnePlus’ versions were typically diluted compared to Oppo’s anyway (and that’s even true with the OnePlus 16), but it was better than nothing. It’s increasingly frustrating to be losing out on devices like these in the States, because Android brands like Oppo have been massively stepping up on quality in recent years.

Pricing, though, is against this one. In Europe, the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is €1,799. That’s a crazy amount of money for a smartphone that doesn’t fold.

If you live in a region where the Find X10 series is for sale, I think you’ll be thrilled by the Pro Max. The standard Find X10 Pro is not one to sleep on either. It’s a bit smaller despite having the same battery, and the cameras aren’t too far behind. 

					

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a complete package, with excellent cameras and battery life, and speedy software.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Triple 200MP cameras

											

Excellent battery life

											

ColorOS is quietly one of the best Android skins

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Smaller battery on EU models

											

No Qi2 magnets

											

Very high pricing

fullText:
Amazon swapped its usual big fall hardware showcase this year for a series of smaller launches throughout October. So far this month, it has announced new Fire TV devices, new Kindles, the Alexa Tablet Pro 12, Ring’s first smart lock, new hardware from AI-wearable startup Bee, and new Blink 4K cameras.

Then this week, it hosted journalists at a small event in New York City’s financial district to showcase its new Echo hardware.

Panos Panay, senior vice president of devices, Alexa, and Leo at Amazon, kicked off proceedings by explaining the company’s approach this year. “We have so many products we’re launching that are meaningful,” he said. “However, we get to this point when we do everything at once; not all your children get enough attention.” This longer rollout allows for more focus on each launch. He also teased two more launches still to come — from Ring and some “Echo on the Go” news — before explaining that today’s focus is “the most important focus we have, which is the home.”

He then spent about 45 minutes introducing five new Echo smart speakers and displays — the Echo Show 16, Echo Time, Alexa Photo Frame, Echo Studio with Home Camera, and a new Echo Dot — with each product sitting on plinths in the warehouse-like space.

He demoed several new software features for the Echo Show smart displays that will start on the Show 16 and trickle down to existing Show products, including dedicated home screens, an interactive 3D map view for smart home control, and a meal planning feature.

Panay also revealed that they have “opened up Alexa Plus’ brain a little bit more,” unlocking a new layer of understanding in the generative-AI-powered smart assistant. He pointed out that AI in the home is still relatively new, and while it’s everywhere else, from your computer to your phone, the home has been harder to unlock.

Amazon is looking to change that with Alexa’s “new brain” — an updated version of Alexa Plus with new capabilities including the ability to do “deeper research” alongside its usual use cases, such as controlling lights, setting timers, and playing music.

To manage these deeper conversations, a new “Card” interface on Show devices collects each chat. Cards also appear in the Alexa app and on Alexa.com, so you can continue chats with the assistant wherever you are.

Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

The event continued in a selection of small rooms designed to feel like home spaces, where product engineers and designers demoed the new devices and explained their features.

title: Apple’s ‘Pro and Tell’ Event: Everything Announced So Far This Week
snippet: It’s another big week for Apple, with a new iPad Mini, MacBook Pro and iMac, and more yet to come.
fullText:
Apple’s Pro and Tell experience week is here, and it’s off to a strong start, with the new iPad Mini unveiled on Monday morning and a new MacBook Pro and iMac on Tuesday. But there’s more to come: We’re also expecting a long-anticipated touchscreen laptop.

Apple’s had a busy few months, launching the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in September alongside the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the AirPods 5, followed by the iPhone Duo going on sale at the end of last week.

Apple’s refreshed smart home lineup, revealed during its recent Welcome Home event, is up next: the HomePod Mini 2 will launch on Friday; the Apple HomeView and Apple TV 4K on Nov. 13; and availability for the Home Collection products begins in December.

			

More from CNET

This week will culminate with Apple hosting a special event on Wednesday, and CNET will be on the ground capturing all the latest details. We’ll update this article as more details are revealed.

One of the two new iPad Mini colors: midnight.Apple

Apple’s new iPad Mini

Announced on Monday, Apple’s new iPad Mini is available to preorder on Wednesday and will go on sale Nov. 6. It starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, $799 for 256GB and $999 for 512GB. 

Setting it apart from the last iPad Mini, which came out two years ago, the new tablet has an 8.5-inch OLED screen (versus an LCD), IP67 water and dust resistance, an Apple A20 processor, a repositioned front-facing camera and a through-screen speaker system called Acoustic Display, as well as being thinner and lighter than before.

Apple’s new iMac M6 comes in a choice of seven colors.

A new iMac

The latest iMac, announced Tuesday, features Apple’s M6 processor with a CPU and a GPU each having up to 12 cores, two more cores apiece than before, Apple said. A new dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers AI compute that’s up to twice as fast as the previous generation, the company said. The iMac also has a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display.

Preorders for the iMac M6 will begin Wednesday, Oct. 28, with availability to follow on Nov. 6. Pricing starts at $1,499 for an iMac with M6 featuring a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU. It’s available in seven colors: blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver.

Apple

MacBook Pro refresh

The new 14-inch MacBook Pro, also announced Tuesday, similarly features the M6 processor with 12-core CPU and GPU and dual 16-core Neural Engine for AI tasks. Apple says the battery life runs up to 24 hours. The laptop features a Liquid Retina XDR display, a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and a six-speaker sound system.

The MacBook Pro with M6 can be preordered starting Wednesday, Oct. 28, and will be in stores and delivered to customers starting Nov. 6. Pricing starts at $1,999.

Apple Creator Studio updates

Tuesday also brought updates to the Apple Creator Studio software suite. For instance, Final Cut Pro for Mac now includes built-in MotionVFX, a collection of visual effects, plug-ins, transitions, templates and motion graphics tools; the curated Content Hub now includes video assets and is available in Final Cut Pro; Pixelmator Pro introduces Generate Fill, which lets creators transform selected areas of an image using natural language; and Keynote, Pages and Numbers introduce new AI features in beta, including assistants that understand document contexts.

The Apple Creator Studio updates will be available in November to subscribers for free.

And as for the iPhone Duo launch last week, check out CNET’s ongoing folding test — you can watch the livestream here and tune in on Tuesday as we continue testing how many times the iPhone Duo can fold without cracking in the CNET lab.

							Senior Editor

She holds degrees in law and communications, and currently writes news, analysis and features for CNET across the topics of electric vehicles, broadband networks, mobile devices, big tech, artificial intelligence, home technology and entertainment. In her spare time, she watches soccer games and F1 races, and goes to Disneyland as often as possible.

title: Moto Tag 2 brings its UWB and Android Find Hub integration back to $20
snippet: After briefly ending the promo earlier this month, Motorola has dropped Moto Tag 2 back to $19.99. more…
fullText:
After briefly ending the promo earlier this month, Motorola has dropped Moto Tag 2 back to $19.99.

Moto Tag 2 is, at the moment, the only Android Find Hub tracker that supports UWB precise finding alongside Bluetooth, and it’s an excellent option for Android users. With upgraded battery life compared to the last generation, compatibility with AirTag accessories, and everything else you’d want in an item tracker, it’s a hard one to say no to. 

That math got a bit more complicated, though, when Motorola stripped away a long-running offer that had raised the price of Moto Tag 2 to its actual retail price of $30. Before that, it had been available for months for just $20. 

Now, Motorola has dropped the price yet again. Moto Tag 2 is available for $19.99 in a 1-pack from both Motorola.com and Amazon, with a 4-pack at $69.99.

	

Moto Tag 2 at Amazon – 1-pack | 4-pack

It’s easily the best deal in an Android Find Hub tracker, at least assuming you don’t need one of the dual-network finders available from the likes of Pebblebee and Chipolo. 

As a reminder, you can only get the orange “Arabesque” color through the purchase of a 4-pack.

Meanwhile, Google is gearing up to launch the Pixel Tag as its first-party Find Hub tracker, complete with UWB support. But that will cost $30 and also lacks the AirTag accessory compatibility that Moto Tag 2 offers.

title: Android Find Hub app reveals how ‘Left Behind’ and ‘Ring your phone’ alerts work on Pixel Tag
snippet: We’re just weeks away from the launch of Google’s first Android Find Hub tracker, the Pixel Tag, and that’s also going to bring new options to the Find Hub app, as revealed in a new app update. more…
excerpt:
We’re just weeks away from the launch of Google’s first Android Find Hub tracker, the Pixel Tag, and that’s also going to bring new options to the Find Hub app, as revealed in a new app update.

Google confirmed that “Left Behind” notifications would be coming to Find Hub when it announced the Pixel Tag earlier this year. The company explained that these alerts were designed to “proactively help prevent leaving your items behind.” Earlier this month, Google further prepared for support including configuring this feature during the setup of a new Find Hub tracker.
